Ltd. breached its contractual obligations by providing inadequate software services, failing to deliver a stock control program, and not meeting UIC's particular requirements. requested_remedy: UIC Factory Ltd. alleges that Zung Fu Co. UIC also claims that Zung Fu was negligent in its performance and seeks recession of the contracts, damages, and repayment of sums paid.

facts.F1: UIC employed Zung Fu to provide a computer system in 1981.
facts.F2: The contracts included a computer hardware sales contract, computer software services contract, computer software license and maintenance contract, and computer maintenance contract.
facts.F3: Zung Fu delivered payroll and work-in-progress programs, but UIC alleged that these programs did not meet its requirements.
facts.F4: UIC claimed that Zung Fu was negligent and failed to deliver the stock control program.
facts.F5: Zung Fu withheld further training due to UIC's non-payment of various charges.
facts.F6: UIC made no complaints about the payroll programs until pleadings commenced in June 1983.
facts.F7: Evidence from computer systems analysts suggested that the payroll programs were capable of performing the required functions, but UIC's operator, Miss Chui, may not have been trained properly.
facts.F8: UIC fell into arrears of payment for installation charges, software licenses, and maintenance contracts.
facts.F9: Zung Fu alleged that it withheld delivery of the stock control program due to UIC's non-payment.
facts.F10: UIC accepted delivery of the software programs without complaint.
facts.F11: UIC did not press for earlier delivery of the software programs.
facts.F12: The contracts provided that payment and delivery were concurrent conditions.

requested_remedy: claims damages for injuries sustained during employment
parties: Defendant: Hyundai Engineering & Construction Company Limited

facts.F1: The Defendant was the principal contractor at Tung Chung Station Development Package II Phase site.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff was employed by the Defendant as a direct labourer (hacker).
facts.F3: On 31 October 2001, the Plaintiff was working on the site and fell from an aluminum ladder, landing on the ground covered with bricks and construction debris.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff alleged that he complained to the Defendant about the instability of the ladder prior to the accident but was ignored.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff was hospitalised for about 6 days after the accident and was given sick leave for about 10 months.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff suffered a compression wedge fracture L2 vertebrae and contusion of the abdomen.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff had worked as a security guard or cleaner before working on a construction site.

claim: Wong lent $10,000, $60,000 and $20,000 to Sung Siu Wai in July/August 2005, November 2005 and January 2006, with a total amount of $90,000. Sung repaid $15,000, and $75,000 is still outstanding.
requested_remedy: Wong lent $10,000, $60,000 and $20,000 to Sung Siu Wai in July/August 2005, November 2005 and January 2006, with a total amount of $90,000. Sung repaid $15,000, and $75,000 is still outstanding.
parties: Plaintiff: Wong Wai Yin (the holder of the cheques)

facts.F1: Wong lent money to Sung at various times in 2005 and 2006.
facts.F2: Sung issued three post-dated cheques (000028, 000030 and 000035 of the Bank of Communications) as security for the debts.
facts.F3: When repayment was due, Sung failed to repay Wong the money she owed, and the cheques were not honoured.
facts.F4: Wong thus sued Sung for the outstanding debts.
facts.F5: Sung's husband, Chan Wai Man, had borrowed $60,000 from Fong at the end of 2005/beginning of 2006 at a high interest rate (total repayment, including interest, being $70,000 if repaid within a month, or $10,000 per month as interest otherwise).
facts.F6: Chan's record and reputation of repaying debts on previous occasions had not been good, so Fong required Chan's wife Sung to issue cheques to be used as security for the loan.
facts.F7: Sung signed her name on a pile of cheques and gave them to Chan to put down the amounts, dates, payees and other information.
facts.F8: Chan and Sung gave all the cheques signed by Sung to Fong as security for the $60,000 loan.
facts.F9: Chan repaid about $130,000 to Fong by the end of 2006/beginning of 2007.
facts.F10: Wong pressed Chan and Sung for payment of the outstanding amount, telephoning Sung many times, and sending letters demanding that Chan and Sung deal with the debt they owed Fong.
facts.F11: Wong is deemed to be a holder in due course of the cheques as the holder.
facts.F12: The cheques were given by Sung as security for the loan by Fong to Chan at an excessive interest rate.

facts.F2: The agreement was made in exchange for the plaintiff withdrawing its objection to the resumption of its land for a drainage project.

facts.F10: Despite the plaintiff's repeated enquiries, the signs were never erected.
facts.F11: The defendant's statutory powers grant discretion to the Commissioner, not the plaintiff, to exercise control over traffic flow.
facts.F12: The agreement would have the effect of transferring the exercise of the statutory discretion from the Commissioner to the plaintiff.

claim: The plaintiff claims damages for personal injury sustained on 9 May 2002 in the course of his employment with the defendant company.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims damages for personal injury sustained on 9 May 2002 in the course of his employment with the defendant company.
parties: Defendant: NG KWONG YUI trading as NG YIU KEE TRANSPORTATION CO.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was employed by the defendant company, which is in the business of unloading cotton bales from containers and arranging for their transportation to a textile factory.
facts.F2: The plaintiff's duties involved removing cotton bales from containers using a handcart or trolley with short metal prongs.
facts.F3: The plaintiff claimed to have been injured on 9 May 2002 when the trolley 'flipped' while he was removing a bale, causing him to sprain his neck.
facts.F4: The defendant disputes the plaintiff's account of the accident and claims that he had pre-existing degenerative changes in his neck and shoulders that were asymptomatic until 8 May 2002.
facts.F5: The plaintiff's colleague, Mr. Zhau, corroborated the plaintiff's account of the accident, stating that he heard the plaintiff shout that he was injured and then reported the incident to their superior, Mr. Ng.
facts.F6: Mr. Ng denies the plaintiff's account and claims that the plaintiff told him on 9 May that he had sprained his neck on the previous day, 8 May, while removing a bale.
facts.F7: Medical notes from the plaintiff's hospital visits on 9 and 15 May 2002 record the plaintiff stating that he had neck pain for a few days, with no trauma, and that he had sprained his neck two to three days prior to the visit.
facts.F8: The plaintiff had performed his duties without incident for 17 years prior to the alleged accident.
facts.F9: The industry-wide practice is to use handcart or trolleys with short metal prongs to remove cotton bales from containers.
facts.F10: The container floor would have been damaged if a forklift truck was used to remove the cotton bales.
facts.F11: The work of removing cotton bales from containers does not require a fine touch and the workman can rely on their sense of feel to remove the bale.

requested_remedy: The Plaintiffs claimed that the Oriental Daily News had been defamed, and the 2nd Plaintiff had a separate cause of action in that it had been expressly referred to in the article in a defamatory way.
parties: Plaintiff: Oriental Daily Publisher Limited (東方日報督印有限公司)
Defendant: 1st Defendant: the proprietor of Ming Pao, 2nd Defendant: the publisher of Ming Pao, 3rd Defendant: the editor of Ming Pao, and 4th Defendant: the printer of Ming Pao

facts.F1: Oriental Daily Publisher Limited is a subsidiary of Oriental Daily News Limited, which is in turn a subsidiary of Oriental Press Group Limited, a public company listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong.
facts.F2: Ming Pao published an article written by Dr. Lui Tai Lok, which the Plaintiffs claimed was defamatory.
facts.F3: The article referred to a previous article published in Ming Pao on 14th February 1995, which was not the subject matter of the complaint.
facts.F4: In 1995, there were two main local television stations, Hong Kong Television Broadcasts Ltd. (TVB) and Asia Television (ATV).
facts.F5: The Oriental Daily News carried daily listings of the programmes to be shown on television, with a routine format that TVB's Chinese channel programme schedule would precede ATV's Chinese channel programme schedule, and TVB's English channel program schedule would precede ATV's English channel programme schedule.
facts.F6: On the evening of 23rd January 1995, a programme called the Pearl Report was broadcast on the English channel of TVB, which contained allegations relating to the Eastern Express.
facts.F7: One and a half days after the Pearl Report, the Oriental Daily News changed its television programme listings format, with ATV's schedules preceding TVB's, the size of print for TVB's listings being smaller, and TVB's logo being omitted.
facts.F8: The Oriental Daily News maintained this changed format for several days, with articles publicising TVB's declining audience ratings.
facts.F9: On 16th February 1995, TVB retracted parts of the offending Pearl Report, and two days later, the ATV logo disappeared from the Oriental Daily News television programme listings.
facts.F10: The Plaintiffs claimed that the article published in Ming Pao on 19th February 1995 was defamatory of the Oriental Daily News and the 2nd Plaintiff.
facts.F11: The 2nd Plaintiff was involved in and influenced the Oriental Daily News to attack TVB, and this was a deliberate act of humiliation.
facts.F12: The 1st Plaintiff was not the proprietor or publisher of the Oriental Daily News, and therefore had no cause of action.

facts.F2: The contract works were completed in 1996, but no final account has been agreed between them.
facts.F3: The plaintiff is a bank that provided Sum Tat with credit facilities and obtained an assignment of monies due to Sum Tat from the defendant under their sub-contract.
facts.F4: After the assignment, the defendant had to pay monies due to Sum Tat to the bank instead.
facts.F5: The full claim of the plaintiff is that Sum Tat is owed approximately $20.2 million by the defendant and that sum is therefore due to the bank.

facts.F7: The defendant's figure of $12.7 million is calculated on the basis of a gross sum due to Sum Tat of $131.6 million, from which deductions of $144.3 million have been made.
facts.F8: The plaintiff contends that five of the seven items which make up the $144.3 million deductions are unarguably wrong.
facts.F9: Approximately $12 million of the $18 million in dispute turned on the issue of whether or not payments were made in cash.

claim: The plaintiff alleged that the defendant’s negligence caused her back injuries on 9/8/2002 and 13/8/2002 and consequently caused her depression.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff alleged that the defendant’s negligence caused her back injuries on 9/8/2002 and 13/8/2002 and consequently caused her depression.
parties: Defendant: GEM GROUP ASIA LIMITED (山姆亞洲有限公司)

facts.F1: The defendant was the Hong Kong representative office of a United States company, which contracts with various manufacturers of bags for export to the United States.
facts.F2: In April 2001, the plaintiff was employed by the defendant as a receptionist. In addition to her duty as a receptionist, the plaintiff was assigned other duties from time to time.
facts.F3: One of these duties was packing and wrapping sample bags into boxes for shipment.
facts.F4: In July 2002, the defendant was moving its operation to Shenzhen, China and started to lay-off its staff in Hong Kong.
facts.F5: On or about August 2002, the plaintiff suffered minor injury to her back while packing sample bags into UPS boxes for shipment to the defendant’s Shenzhen office.
facts.F6: The plaintiff attended the A&E Department of United Christian Hospital after office hours on 13/8/2002 and was treated with analgesic after x-ray examination did not discover any abnormality and she was sent home with 5 days sick leave.
facts.F7: Between August 2002 and September 2002, the plaintiff attended her family physician Dr. Lam Kwok Wing for treatment on 8 occasions.
facts.F8: In 2002, the plaintiff was a healthy 28-year-old female at the time of the injury.
facts.F9: The plaintiff had previously performed the task of packing and lifting boxes without assistance.
facts.F10: The weight of the individual objects being lifted was within the ability of the plaintiff.
facts.F11: A colleague was available to help the plaintiff with the task if needed, but the plaintiff had never asked for assistance.
facts.F12: On 27/9/2002, the plaintiff fell while walking on the street and injured her left shoulder and the coccyx region, but the injury was minor in nature.
facts.F13: In November 2002, the plaintiff’s lower back pain got worst and she was admitted into St. Teresa Hospital for 5 days.
facts.F14: A MRI of the plaintiff’s lumbar spine showed normal findings. The pain continued and the plaintiff received 6 months of physiotherapy at the United Christian Hospital.
facts.F15: The plaintiff alleged the work-related injuries caused psychological problems and since 24/9/2003, she has been receiving treatment for depression from East Kowloon Psychiatric Centre.

requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims to be a victim of an email fraud resulting in USD520,000 being transferred out of its account with Silicon Valley Bank to unknown persons including Leabon Technology (HK) Ltd
parties: Defendant: ['Leabon Technology (HK) Limited', 'Bank of China (Hong Kong) Limited']

facts.F1: The plaintiff is a private Delaware LLC based in San Francisco.
facts.F2: The plaintiff’s accounting functions have been outsourced to Solutions On Call South LLC (SOCS) who has responsibility for keeping the plaintiff’s financial records and handling its bank accounts.
facts.F3: Email instructions for a remittance of USD520,000 were received by SOCS on 7 January 2021, which instructions were carried out but without first seeking a verbal confirmation from the plaintiff’s president, Mr Rosenthal, in breach of protocol.
facts.F4: SOCS received further email instructions for remittance of further funds to another bank account but as there were insufficient funds in the SV Bank account, SOCS contacted Mr Rosenthal and the fraud perpetrated on the Plaintiff came to light.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff took immediate action but the remittance had been processed and the matter was reported to the FBI and the Hong Kong Police Force.
facts.F6: The plaintiff obtained Norwich Pharmacal relief against the Bank and was able to confirm the identity of D1 as owner of D1’s account.
facts.F7: Bank documents reveal that USD519,972.30 (after deduction of the Bank’s fees from the Sum) remitted from the Plaintiff’s account with SV Bank on 7 January 2021 was paid into D1’s account.
facts.F8: A sealed copy of the originating summons, the supporting affidavit and the notice of appointment to hear the originating summons) were served by registered post at the registered address of D1 on 3 May 2021.
facts.F9: The Bank filed an acknowledgement of service and on 20 May 2021 stated that it takes a neutral stance in these proceedings.
facts.F10: The Balance remains in D1’s account.
facts.F11: The Sum was transferred from the Plaintiff’s account and can be traced into D1’s account.
facts.F12: The Bank is an innocent third party.

claim: The Plaintiff claims, inter alia, specific performance of the Agreement with all consequential and necessary directions pertaining thereto, and a declaration that the vehicles in question and the PSLs in respect thereof are held on constructive trust for the Plaintiff.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff claims, inter alia, specific performance of the Agreement with all consequential and necessary directions pertaining thereto, and a declaration that the vehicles in question and the PSLs in respect thereof are held on constructive trust for the Plaintiff.
parties: Defendant: LAI YAN TRANSPORT COMPANY LIMITED

facts.F1: The Plaintiff and the Defendant are parties to a provisional sale and purchase agreement titled "provisional sale and purchase agreement" ("\u4e09\u664b\u50be\u552e\u5408\u540d", hereafter referred to as "the Agreement") dated 1 June 2010.
facts.F2: Under the Agreement, Lee Wai Hung on behalf of the Defendant as the seller agreed to sell, and the Plaintiff as the purchaser agreed to purchase, three tour buses for a consideration of HK$3,000,000.
facts.F3: A PSL cannot be transferred as property, but the Transport Department would normally be prepared to grant an application to the purchaser of a commercial vehicle to "take up" a PSL issued in respect of the vehicle concurrently with the "renunciation" of the PSL by the seller of that vehicle as part and parcel of the sale transaction.
facts.F4: Upon signing the Agreement, the parties by their respective solicitors exchanged numerous letters initially with a view to coming to terms regarding the detailed implementation of the Agreement.
facts.F5: By a letter dated 17 February 2011, the Defendant's solicitors purported to terminate the Agreement for the Plaintiff's failure to fix a reasonable date for completion pursuant to the Agreement.
facts.F6: On the following day, the Defendant's solicitors sent to the Plaintiff's solicitors a cashier order in the sum of $500,000 being the return of the deposit paid under the Agreement by the Plaintiff.
facts.F7: Damages would be difficult to quantify where the contract is for the sale and purchase of a business to exploit the taxi plate, which was more than an ordinary article of commerce.
facts.F8: The contact was for the sale and purchase of a business to exploit the taxi plate.

claim: Damages for loss of expectation of life
requested_remedy: Damages for loss of expectation of life
parties: Plaintiff: LEUNG CHI YUEN and LEE WUI CHUN, the Administrators of the estate of LEUNG YAN CHUN, deceased
Defendant: TSANG SHUI CHING and LEE KA TIM

facts.F1: On October 23, a fatal accident occurred at approximately 8 o'clock in the evening on Nam Cheong Street, Kowloon.
facts.F2: A boy of 11 years' of age was riding a bicycle with two companions when he was struck and killed by the defendant's lorry as it overtook him.
facts.F3: The deceased's companion, a boy now aged 14 years, was riding at a distance of about two car spaces behind the deceased and noticed the approach of the lorry.
facts.F4: The companion lost control of his cycle and ran into a motor-cycle parked on the left-hand side.
facts.F5: The motor-cycle was parked between vehicles at right angles to the kerb, and the collision was minor, but it diverted the companion's attention.
facts.F6: The defendant was driving his lorry at an approximate speed of 10 m.p.h. when a shadow rushed out from between vehicles parked on his left-hand side.
facts.F7: The defendant braked immediately, swerved a little to his left, and felt the nearside rear wheel of his lorry bump over something.
facts.F8: None of the cycles carried a rear light despite the darkness.
facts.F9: Sunset on that day was 5.53 p.m., which supports the evidence of the constable that it was dark.
facts.F10: The constable made measurements of the road and the positions in which the lorry and the bicycle had finished, and prepared a sketch (Ex. 7).
facts.F11: The defendant did not see the three boys because he was not paying sufficient attention.
facts.F12: The defendant's course was not faulty, and he was well over on the offside of the carriageway.

facts.F2: The first petitioner and the respondent companies were incorporated for the purpose of real estate development.
facts.F3: The Wangs control 80% of the issued share capital of the respondents whilst the 1st and 2nd petitioners each hold 10%.

facts.F4: The Bankrupt lost a sum of approximately $79.5 million belonging to King Kong in a money-lending business in Macau, stocks and shares speculation, and investments in China.
facts.F5: The Bankrupt was unable to provide the Official Receiver and trustee in bankruptcy with detailed information and documentary evidence to support his losses.

facts.F9: The Bankrupt had relinquished all his interests in Ocean Palace to Yu Hua Loong.
facts.F10: The Official Receiver's continuing concern related to security trading activities only, and the Bankrupt had provided information relating to the securities trading account.
facts.F11: Yu Hua Loong had informed the Official Receiver of its intention to oppose the Bankrupt's application for discharge but had not made an application for leave to intervene.
facts.F12: Each adjournment is effectively a de facto postponement of the date of the Bankrupt's automatic discharge.

facts.F1: The claimant claimed repayment of two loans of HK$26,400 and HK$2,750 from the defendant.
facts.F2: The defendant did not dispute the second loan of HK$2,750 which was interest-free.
facts.F3: The defendant denied borrowing HK$26,400 from the claimant.
facts.F4: The defendant's case was that the claimant first lent her HK$5,000 in October 2010, and she did not repay until November 2011, with no interest charged until then.
facts.F5: From November 2011 onwards, interest at a monthly rate of 15% was charged on the HK$5,000.
facts.F6: By June 2012, the monthly interest of HK$750 had totalled HK$5,250.
facts.F7: In August 2011, the claimant lent the defendant a further sum of HK$1,880.
facts.F8: The total sum owed by the defendant to the claimant in June 2012 was HK$12,130 (HK$5,000 + HK$5,250 + HK$1,880).
facts.F9: The claimant charged the defendant monthly interest of HK$1,200 or about 10% on the sum of HK$12,130 from June 2012 to June 2013.
facts.F10: The total amount of interest as at June 2013 was HK$14,400.
facts.F11: The total sum of principal and interest owed by the defendant as at June 2013 was HK$26,530 (HK$12,130 + HK$14,400).
facts.F12: There is a difference of HK$130 between this sum and the sum of HK$26,400 claimed by the claimant.
facts.F13: The defendant repaid HK$5,000 to the claimant in August 2013.
facts.F14: The balance should be HK$24,280 (HK$26,530 + HK$2,750 (interest-free loan) – HK$5,000 (repayment)).
facts.F15: The claimant's claim is however at HK$24,200 (HK$26,400 + HK$2,750 (interest-free loan) – HK$5,000 (repayment) + HK$50).
facts.F16: The claimant charged the defendant a monthly interest of about 10% on the sum of HK$12,130 from June 2012 to June 2013.

facts.F1: Mr Yu Man was a client of CA Pacific Futures Limited (Futures) and C.A. Pacific Securities Limited (Securities) in January 1998.
facts.F2: Mr Yu traded in Hang Seng Index futures through Futures, and had signed a Client Agreement and opened an account with Securities, but did not buy or sell shares.
facts.F3: On 16 January 1998, Mr Yu contacted Mr Wan, a broker at Futures, to acquire shares in Sino Land as the price had dropped considerably.
facts.F4: Mr Wan told Mr Yu that Securities was being investigated by the Securities and Futures Commission and might be wound up, and suggested opening an account with Sun Hung Kai Securities (SHK) instead.
facts.F5: Mr Yu instructed Mr Wan to proceed to buy the shares for him, but to settle them later at a new account at SHK. However, he did not take steps to open a new account at SHK until several months later.

facts.F7: Mr Yu approached the liquidators and demanded the shares which had been credited to his account with Securities, but they have not done so due to questions caused by a shortfall in shares acquired by Securities for its clients.
facts.F8: Mr Yu had made Futures his agent for the purpose of instructing a stockbroker to acquire shares in Sino Land.
facts.F9: Mr Yu must have known that Futures could not acquire the shares by itself.
facts.F10: Mr Yu did become a client of Securities in respect of the acquisition of the Sino Land shares.

claim: The plaintiff bank claims that the defendant surety's guarantees are enforceable despite being given in contravention of the related party lending provisions of the Banking Ordinance 1964
requested_remedy: The plaintiff bank claims that the defendant surety's guarantees are enforceable despite being given in contravention of the related party lending provisions of the Banking Ordinance 1964

facts.F1: The plaintiff bank lent substantial sums of money to the principal debtors (Cyril Fung and associated companies) in contravention of the related party lending provisions of section 23 of the Banking Ordinance 1964
facts.F2: The defendant surety (Robert Fung) guaranteed the repayment of the loans to the plaintiff bank
facts.F3: The guarantees were given after 1st April 1976
facts.F4: The proceedings were commenced on 9th October 1986, after the commencement date (1st September 1986) of the Banking Ordinance 1986
facts.F5: Section 129 of the Banking Ordinance 1986 provides that contravention of any prohibition in the Ordinance on the entering into of any contract shall not render that contract unenforceable
facts.F6: The Banking (Amendment) Ordinance 1987 clarified section 129(1) by adding the words 'or in any Ordinance repealed by this Ordinance'
facts.F7: The legislature had demonstrated that contravention of the related party lending provisions contained in the Banking Ordinance 1986, or of the Ordinance which it repealed and replaced, is not to render contracts of guarantee unenforceable
facts.F8: The legislative history of the statutory provisions includes the Banking Ordinance 1948, Banking Bill 1964, Banking Ordinance 1964, and Banking Ordinance 1986

claim: The plaintiff seeks an interim prohibitory interlocutory injunction to restrain the defendant from acting in breach of a contract of employment by working for Lidl Hong Kong Ltd until after 31 August 2016.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff seeks an interim prohibitory interlocutory injunction to restrain the defendant from acting in breach of a contract of employment by working for Lidl Hong Kong Ltd until after 31 August 2016.
parties: Plaintiff: CEI Conrad Electronic International (HK) Limited

facts.F1: The plaintiff is the sole sourcing arm of the Conrad Electronic Group, a leading global retailer of electronics and technology.
facts.F2: The defendant was employed by the plaintiff as a merchandising manager on 16 September 2013.
facts.F3: The defendant was primarily responsible for liaising with suppliers and sourcing products, but also had a range of other duties including some connection with product design.
facts.F4: The contract of employment contained non-competition and confidentiality clauses, specifically paragraphs 8 and 9.
facts.F5: Paragraph 8 prohibited the defendant from working for any organization that is active in the business areas or similar areas as the Company or any subsidiary company for a period of six months after termination of the contract.
facts.F6: Paragraph 9 required the defendant to maintain absolute secrecy about all legal and factual matters pertaining to the Company and its business activities, particularly business and manufacturing secrets, suppliers' and customers' data and internal information.
facts.F7: The defendant tendered his resignation on 1 February 2016 and was put on gardening leave until 29 February 2016.
facts.F8: The defendant was seen to be working for Lidl Hong Kong on 10 March 2016, which he does not dispute.
facts.F9: The plaintiff took out an inter partes summons on 15 April 2016 for breach of contract under paragraphs 8 and 9 of the Contract to restrain the defendant from working at Lidl and to restrain him from disclosing confidential information.
facts.F10: At the inter partes hearing before Lok J on 22 April 2016, the defendant maintained he had already voluntarily terminated his employment with Lidl on 5 April 2016.
facts.F11: The matter was resolved by an undertaking from the defendant to inform the plaintiff of any potential new employment, which he did on 6 May 2016 indicating his intention to re-join Lidl on 17 May 2016.
facts.F12: The two clauses in question will expire on 31 August 2016, well before the action can be tried.
facts.F13: Restraint of Trade clauses are prima facie unenforceable, save where the legitimate interests of the employer are reasonably required to be protected and the public interest is served thereby.
facts.F14: The only dispute is as to the extent of the undertaking offered by the defendant.

parties: Defendant: Vianini S.P.A. High Island Water Scheme Reservoir, Hong Kong

facts.F1: The applicant was employed by the respondent as an odd job worker in the Stone Crushing Section at the High Island Water Scheme Reservoir.
facts.F2: The applicant was instructed to move an electric motor that was out of order on the day of the accident, February 5, 1974.
facts.F3: The applicant, with the help of a colleague, Mr. Chan Chun, was lowering the motor from a platform when he strained his lower back and buttock.
facts.F4: The applicant stopped work for a few minutes but later resumed, not regarding the injury as serious. He did not report the incident to his foreman.
facts.F5: The applicant felt pain in his back that evening, which continued the next day, and he did not return to work.
facts.F6: The applicant received various medical treatments, including admission to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital from May 2 to June 1, 1974, and continued to receive treatment as an out-patient.
facts.F7: The applicant's workers' record card shows that he was absent from work from February 6 to 12, 1974, and on sick leave from February 13 to 23, 1974.
facts.F8: The applicant did not return to work with the respondent after February 5, 1974.
facts.F9: The applicant did not obtain any employment until November 1975, when he commenced working as a newsvendor.
facts.F10: The respondent's accident report book contains no entry of an accident having been suffered by the applicant at work during February 1974.
facts.F11: The labour department was informed of the applicant's claim, but the date of the accident was initially recorded incorrectly as February 16, 1974.
facts.F12: The respondent was aware of the applicant's absence from work, but not that it was attributable to the accident.
facts.F13: The applicant had severe pain after the accident and believed that the accident had been reported, leading to a delay in his formal notice.
facts.F14: The applicant received medical evidence from Dr. Ho and Dr. Wedderburn.

parties: Plaintiff: a dental surgeon practising in Hong Kong
Defendant: a limited company dealing in commodities in Japanese Exchanges in Japan

facts.F1: The plaintiff opened an account with the defendant company on the 7th of June last year, for the purpose of trading in commodities in the Japanese Exchanges.
facts.F2: A sum of $10,000 was deposited with the defendant company which would enable the plaintiff to trade up to ten times the deposits currently with the defendant company.
facts.F3: The procedure for trading was that verbal instructions to buy or to sell any commodity in the Japanese Exchanges would be given to Brownie Fan, alias FAN Kar-man, who would then place the order within the defendant company.
facts.F4: The order would be sent to the Tokyo office by telex or by long distance telephone call and, upon confirmation, the defendant company would send a written confirmatory advice to the plaintiff.
facts.F5: Between the 8th of June and the end of June last year, the plaintiff made a profit of $6,990 and deposited a total of $110,505.15 as Marginal Deposits with the defendant.
facts.F6: On or about the 1st of July, the plaintiff instructed Mr. FAN to purchase forty-five units of red beans, but Mr. FAN instead sold forty-five units of white beans for the plaintiff.
facts.F7: The plaintiff did not receive a confirmatory advice for the purchase of red beans and was instead sent a confirmatory advice of sale of white beans.
facts.F8: On the 4th of July, the plaintiff received further unauthorised dealings in other commodities and complained to Mr. Peter CHAN, the Manager of the defendant company.
facts.F9: On the 5th of July, the plaintiff signed two documents in blank, exhibits 29 and 30, at the request of Mr. FAN, which he believed were necessary to clear up the confusion.
facts.F10: On the 8th of July, the plaintiff received another unauthorised dealing and made a further complaint to Mr. FAN, who confirmed that forty-five units of red beans had been sold.
facts.F11: The next following days, Mr. FAN disappeared, and the plaintiff had to contact Mr. William LAI, the Section Manager of the defendant company, to investigate the matter.
facts.F12: On the 17th of July, the plaintiff met Mr. FAN and recorded their conversation using a tape-recorder, in which Mr. FAN admitted to having made an error in executing the plaintiff's instructions.
facts.F13: The plaintiff's account was eventually closed on the 19th of July, and a Payment Instruction in the form of exhibit 30 was signed.
facts.F14: The defendant company paid the plaintiff a credit balance of $5,411.15, which was the only amount left in the plaintiff's account.
facts.F15: The defendant company had no authority to act for the plaintiff from the 5th of July onwards.
facts.F16: The plaintiff had instructed Mr. FAN to acquire forty-five units of red beans on the 1st of July and to sell them on the 8th of July, and should have accumulated a further profit of $49,680.

requested_remedy: The claim related to an accident on 23rd July 2011 on a construction site in the course of employment and the applicant took out his application for compensation pursuant to the Employees’ Compensation Ordinance Cap.282
parties: Defendant: CHEUNG YUK KWAN trading as CONCEPT PAINTING COMPANY and LUCKY GLORY ENGINEERING LIMITED

facts.F1: The applicant entered into a continuous employment contract with the 1st Respondent since 1997 up till the accident on 23rd July 2011.
facts.F2: The applicant was required to work on public holiday, there were times he was required to work more than 26 days a month and there were times he worked less than 26 days a month, on average he worked for 26 days a month prior the accident, and his daily rate was HK$700, his monthly income on average being HK$18,200.
facts.F3: The applicant made application for compensation pursuant to Section 7 of the Ordinance. During the accident, the applicant fell from a height landing on his back and suffered immediate paralysis of his lower limbs after the injury.
facts.F4: The applicant needed assistance in the activities of daily living due to the paralysis and stiffness of his spine.
facts.F5: Dr Chan, the neurologist, is in the opinion that most recovery of neurological functions after severe spinal injuries occurs within the first 12 months of the accident.
facts.F6: By now more than 20 months have elapsed since the applicant’s injury, further improvement in his neurological functions is not expected.
facts.F7: Dr. Chin, specialist in orthopaedics and traumatology, is in the opinion that the applicant’s current status is compatible with a well-maintained paraplegic patient.
facts.F8: With total loss of motion of both lower limbs, the applicant will be paralyzed for the rest of his life.
facts.F9: The impairment of the whole person is 63%. The loss of earning capacity based on the schedule in the Ordinance is 100%.
facts.F10: The applicant’s wife applied for leave and provided daily care in his hygiene, exercise, feeding etc. Since 23rd June 2012 the applicant has been cared for by his wife and also a domestic helper employed for his care and attention.
facts.F11: The Ordinance distinguishes between temporary and permanent incapacity.
facts.F12: A temporary incapacity can be total or partial and the periodical payment was supposed to be made at the same day as the wages.
facts.F13: The purpose of the Ordinance is to provide for the payment of compensation to employees who are injured in the course of their employment.
facts.F14: After receiving periodical payments for 24 months, the employee will be deemed to have suffered permanent incapacity so that the provisions of sections 7 or 9 will apply to him.

claim: damages for breach of contract
requested_remedy: damages for breach of contract

facts.F1: The plaintiff Mr Wong Leung Wing was the sole proprietor of Express Printing and Stationery Supplies from 1983 until 1991.
facts.F2: From 1983 until 1988, the plaintiff carried out a number of printing contracts for the defendant in Hong Kong.
facts.F3: On the 15th August 1985, the plaintiff entered into a contract for one year with the defendant to print cancellation bulletins.
facts.F4: The contract was renewed on the 15th May 1986 for two years and again for a further period of two years on the 15th November 1988, expiring on the 31st December 1990.
facts.F5: When the contract with the plaintiff was renewed in November 1988, Mr Fellman, a Vice-President of the defendant, was responsible for obtaining quotations for the printing of the cancellation bulletins.
facts.F6: Mr Antony Fung was employed by the defendant as a manager under Mr Fellman and liaised with Mr Wong in connection with the requirements of the defendant for the printing of the cancellation bulletins.
facts.F7: On the 22nd August 1988, Mr Wong wrote to the defendant with regard to a renewal of the contract and requested a revision of the previous pricing arrangement on the grounds of an increase in mailing costs and additional handling charges.
facts.F8: It is alleged by the defendant that the grounds for the increase were spurious and were made as a result of a collusive agreement between Mr Wong and Mr Fung.
facts.F9: Mr Fung left the employ of the defendant in March 1989.

claim: The plaintiff seeks specific performance of a sale and purchase agreement and damages.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff seeks specific performance of a sale and purchase agreement and damages.
parties: Defendant: Fung Sun Kwan Bernard (馮燊均)

facts.F1: The Memorandum of Agreement for the sale of New Kowloon Marine Lot No. 21 was signed between the plaintiff and defendant on 19 November 2004.
facts.F2: The Property has a long and complex history of acquisition, surrender, and reclamation.
facts.F3: The Vendor had obtained a sum of HK$31.5 million as provisional compensation from the Government under the Foreshore and Sea-Bed (Reclamations) Ordinance.
facts.F4: The Vendor claimed a further payment of HK$7.7 million under the Final Compensation Agreement and a contractual right to a re-grant of the Former Slipway at nominal premium.
facts.F5: The Purchaser's solicitors requisitioned for a statutory declaration due to a discrepancy in the name of the grantee under the Conditions of Sale and the name of the Vendor on his Hong Kong Identity Card.
facts.F6: This requisition led to a series of answers and counter-requisitions regarding the re-grant of the Former Slipway and its terms.
facts.F7: Despite repeated reminders, the Vendor failed to timely respond to the Purchaser's requisitions, leading the Purchaser to issue an Originating Summons on 25 January 2005.
facts.F8: The Vendor's title in respect of the Former Slipway and the fourth portion was extinguished under section 10(1)(a) of the Foreshore and Sea-Bed (Reclamations) Ordinance.
facts.F9: The compensation under the Final Compensation Agreement was in respect of the loss of two parcels of rights: one in respect of the rights in relation to the Former Slipway and the fourth portion, and another in respect of those relating to the rest of the Property.
facts.F10: The Vendor had no title to the Former Slipway, and the payment of rates and Government rent did not constitute an acknowledgement of title.
facts.F11: The Government could extract revenue from a new grant of the Former Slipway, and its inaction against the Vendor was due to the Vendor's personal right to a re-grant at nominal premium.
facts.F12: The Former Slipway was intended to be included in the Property to be sold and purchased, not reduced to just below two-thirds.

requested_remedy: The plaintiffs claimed to be the respective beneficial owner of Section D and Section E since 21 September 1992 and 17 February 1992, respectively, and alleged that the defendant has been a trespasser in wrongful occupation of the land since a date unknown to them.
parties: Plaintiff: Wan Kai Wah and Wan Kai Kwong

facts.F1: The dispute concerns Section D and Section E of Lot 218 in Demarcation District No.185, Shatin, New Territories.
facts.F2: The defendant alleged that he has been in adverse possession of both Section D and Section E since 1959.
facts.F3: The two actions were consolidated on 23 April 1996.
facts.F4: The trial was set down on 17 June 2002, but the plaintiffs did not appear.
facts.F5: The defendant gave evidence and called two factual witnesses, Mr Leung Chi Hung and Madam Poon Wai Sin, and one expert, Mr Leung Shou Chun.
facts.F6: The defendant rented a stone house at No.24 (also known as No.24C) of Ha Wo Che Village and operated a grocery store called 'LEUNG KEE' in 1959.
facts.F7: The defendant took over possession of Section D and Section E, levelled the rocky ground, and began to erect various wooden structures thereon.
facts.F8: The defendant repaired and renovated the structures from time to time and turned the vacant portion of the land into a garden.
facts.F9: The defendant has seven children, and the family address was stated as No.24 of Ha Wo Che Village in their birth certificates.
facts.F10: The Store was re-numbered from No.24 (or No.24C) to No.88, and the House was re-numbered from No.24 (or No.24C) to No.79 in the 1980s.
facts.F11: Acts of possession done on parts of land to which a possessory title is sought may be evidence of possession of the whole.
facts.F12: The land in question is open land, and physical control is normally impracticable, and what is a sufficient degree of sole possession and user must be measured according to an objective standard.

facts.F10: The Memorandum did not include an inventory of the house contents.
facts.F11: The plaintiff would not strip the house bare of all contents, including fitted wardrobes and kitchen cabinets.
facts.F12: The Memorandum came into being about 20 February 1992 and not backdated to the time of completion.
facts.F13: The defendant was given the keys to the house some time in March, after the signing of the Sale and Purchase Agreement.

parties: Defendant: ['United Top Properties Limited', 'Yong Ho Hing Co., Limited', 'XT IMPORT AND EXPORT LIMITED', 'KONGKONG GROUP CO., LIMITED', 'Zl Trade Limited', 'Jin Hongsheng Trading Co., Limited', 'Daily Star (HK) Trading Co Limited', 'HK TJ Limited', 'Diall Limited', 'Axxeum Trading Limited', 'Sino Union Inc Limited', 'Bank of China (Hong Kong) LIMITED', 'Standard Chartered Bank']

facts.F1: The Plaintiff is a company incorporated in California, USA.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff is engaged in the export, import, and distribution of Asian food products in the USA.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff maintained and maintains a bank account at Wells Fargo Bank, NA.
facts.F4: Mr. Darly Gormley, the Chief Executive Officer of the Plaintiff, was the registered holder and user of an email account.
facts.F5: An imposter posing as Mr. Susaki emailed Mr. Gormley using a fake email account.
facts.F6: The email requested Mr. Gormley's assistance in a 'confidential acquisition'.
facts.F7: Mr. Gormley was directed to work with the Second Imposter to make further payments to other purported shareholders involved in the Fake Acquisition.

facts.F9: The Second Imposter emailed the Plaintiff, requesting that it wire funds to various defendants' accounts in Hong Kong.
facts.F10: Mr. Gormley, without knowing that the First Imposter and the Second Imposter were not Mr. Susaki and Mr. David Hirschman, instructed Mr. Tom Kawaguchi, the Chief Financial Officer of the Plaintiff to wire the funds.
facts.F11: The funds were wired from the Plaintiff's Bank Account to the defendants' accounts.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff claims it discovered the fraud on December 6, 2019, when Atsuhiko Kimura, the Chief Financial Officer of the Parent Company, exchanged emails with Mr. Gormley.
facts.F13: Mr. Susaki informed Mr. Kimura that he was not aware of the Fake Acquisition or any of the wire transfers of the First, Second, Third or Fourth Sum.
facts.F14: The Plaintiff informed Wells Fargo, Standard Chartered Bank, and Bank of China of the fraud and filed a police report.
facts.F15: The Plaintiff initiated a recall of the four wire transfers with Wells Fargo.
facts.F16: The Hong Kong Police informed the Plaintiff of the transfer of the funds out of the defendants' accounts.

facts.F1: The plaintiff is a subsidiary company of Amcor Limited, an Australian company, and is a major cigarette packaging company.
facts.F2: The defendant was the Chairman and founder of the Vision Grande Group of Companies (VG Group) which is also in the cigarette packaging business.
facts.F3: The defendant's company, Vision Grande Group Holdings Limited (VGGHL), changed its name to AMVIG Holdings Limited (AMVIG) on 1 November 2006.
facts.F4: The defendant was involved in the cigarette packaging business in the PRC since the 1980s.
facts.F5: The defendant had discussions with the plaintiff in 2004 concerning an investment in VGGHL.

facts.F8: The undertaking was in the form of a Deed of Undertaking which included a profits guarantee, a covenant not to compete, an appointment undertaking, and a right of first refusal.

facts.F12: The defendant raised arguments regarding the implied terms and conditions contained in the undertaking.

claim: damages for an injury sustained in the course of her employment as a waitress
requested_remedy: damages for an injury sustained in the course of her employment as a waitress
parties: Defendant: Group Yield International Development Limited Trading as Federal Restaurant

facts.F1: The accident occurred at about 11:00 p.m. on 11 September 2005 in the course of the plaintiff's duties as a waitress in the 'Federal Restaurant'.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was in the process of returning a glass turntable into its storage cabinet when the accident occurred.
facts.F3: The glass turntable was 30 inches in diameter, 3/4 inches thick and weighed 25 lbs.
facts.F4: The storage cabinet was purpose-built to store approximately 25 glass turntables in a vertical position.
facts.F5: There were rubber mats in front of the cabinet designed to assist in the rolling of a turntable into a slot inside the cabinet.
facts.F6: The plaintiff had considerable experience as a waitress and had manoeuvred and stored similar turntables in her previous employment.
facts.F7: A joint medical report was prepared by Dr Lau Hoi Kuen and Dr Chan Sai Keung, which agreed that the plaintiff had suffered a soft tissue injury to the lower back consistent with the circumstance of the accident.
facts.F8: The plaintiff had pre-existing degenerative changes in her lower spine, which were probably exacerbated on 11 September 2005.

claim: claims an amount of $135,976 under a dishonoured cheque
requested_remedy: claims an amount of $135,976 under a dishonoured cheque

facts.F1: The Defendant was a contractor of Tim Lee Construction Company Limited for the major refurbishment work in San Hui Playground, Tuen Mun Heung Sze Wui Road, Tuen Mun, New Territories.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff supplied building materials to the Defendant for the said project.
facts.F3: The Defendant issued the cheque in issue, which was dated 15 March 2005, to the Plaintiff to settle two of the Plaintiff's invoices both dated 5 January 2005.
facts.F4: The cheque was dishonoured upon presentation for payment.
facts.F5: The Defendant had made two contracts with the Plaintiff for the supply of building materials for the said project: one for the supply of steel pergolas and the other for the supply of stainless steel products.
facts.F6: The Defendant complains of late delivery and poor workmanship of the goods in issue, and the Defendant has suffered loss as a result of the Plaintiff's breach of the contract for the supply of the steel pergolas.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff and the Defendant agreed to finalise the accounts under both contracts on or about 7 February 2005.
facts.F8: The parties agreed that the sum payable under both contracts were $131,216.46 for the contract of steel pergolas and $4,760 for the contract of stainless steel products.
facts.F9: The Defendant issued a cheque to the Plaintiff to settle the sums agreed under the finalised accounts, but subject to certain conditions.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff failed to deliver the mill certificates for the goods on 21 February 2005.
facts.F11: The parties met again on 24 February 2005 and agreed to vary the earlier agreement by extending both the deadline for providing the mill certificates and the payment date to 15 March 2005.
facts.F12: The Defendant issued a second cheque in the same amount to the Plaintiff, which is the subject matter of the present action, to replace the first cheque.
facts.F13: The Defendant claims that the second cheque was issued subject to the same conditions as those of the first cheque, save that the date for the delivery of the mill certificates be extended to 15 March 2005.
facts.F14: The delivery of a cheque is usually unconditional.
facts.F15: The second cheque was not issued subject to the same conditions as the first cheque.

claim: The plaintiff claims a debt of US$1 million from the defendants due to their failure to repay a loan.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims a debt of US$1 million from the defendants due to their failure to repay a loan.
parties: Defendant: DRAGONWOOD LIMITED, DATUK KHOO THAW CHOON, JOHN KHOO CHEO PING, TAH CHONG CHIN

facts.F1: In 1987, the plaintiff and the 1st defendant entered into a timber sale agreement.
facts.F2: Subsequent to that agreement, a loan agreement was entered into between the 1st defendant and the plaintiff, and supplemental letters of guarantee were provided by the 2nd, 3rd and 4th defendants to the plaintiff.
facts.F3: A sum of US$3 million was drawn on by the 1st defendant and the supplemental loan agreement was entered into in November 1987 between the plaintiff and all of the defendants.
facts.F4: Repayment was not made within the period required by the agreements and on 23rd August 1995, a statement of claim was issued.
facts.F5: In November 1995, certain meetings took place between the plaintiff and the 4th defendant in Malaysia, and attempts were made to reach a compromise for the payment of the outstanding sum.
facts.F6: On 13th December 1995, it is alleged by the appellants to this action, that a compromise agreement was reached.
facts.F7: A letter was sent by the plaintiff to the 2nd, 3rd and 4th defendants on 19th December 1995, purporting to set out the terms of the compromise.
facts.F8: On 20th December 1995, a first payment in the sum of US$100,000 or there about was paid by the 3rd defendant, who did acknowledge that a compromise existed, to the plaintiff.
facts.F9: This payment was confirmed by the plaintiff on 22nd December 1995.
facts.F10: On 2nd February 1996, the 2nd and 4th defendants still not having signed any document acknowledging that they were bound by any compromise, filed a defence to the Statement of Claim issued by the plaintiff.
facts.F11: On 8th February 1996, a reply was filed and on 20th February 1996, the 3rd defendant paid a second payment of US$100,000 or there about to the plaintiff who, on 27th February 1996, confirmed that payment.
facts.F12: Information available indicated that the loan was not subject to the Money Lenders Ordinance, distinguishing the case from Ng Shou Chun v. Hung Chun San.

facts.F2: The Accident occurred on 18 November 2016, when the Deceased was repairing a private car in the course of employment for a customer of the Respondent.
facts.F3: The Deceased was crushed by the car jack which toppled while he was lying underneath the chassis, resulting in fatal injuries.
facts.F4: The Respondent did not attend the trial and failed to provide any evidence to contradict the Applicant's account of the Accident.

facts.F8: The Deceased's monthly salary before the Accident was HK$21,000.
facts.F9: The value of the Respondent's provision of lodging to the Deceased was around 1/5 of the Deceased's monthly salary, i.e., HK$4,000.

claim: Challenging the so-called 'blanket policy' of the Director not to permit mandated refugees or screened-in torture claimants to work in Hong Kong, and seeking declaratory and other relief.

facts.F1: Five applicants, MA, GA, PA, FI, and JA, are mandated refugees or screened-in torture claimants who have been stranded in Hong Kong for a prolonged period of time with little prospect of resettlement or departure in the immediately foreseeable future.
facts.F2: The applicants are not permitted to work in Hong Kong under the Director's immigration policy.
facts.F3: The applicants have made requests to the Director for permission to work, but their requests have been refused or are still pending.

facts.F6: The applicants have been provided with assistance and subsistence support by the Government and other agencies, but they argue that this is not sufficient to meet their needs.
facts.F7: The Director has a discretion to permit mandated refugees or screened-in torture claimants to work in exceptional circumstances.
facts.F8: The Director must take into account the individual circumstances of each applicant when exercising his discretion.

requested_remedy: claims made by the plaintiff for breach of employment and non-disclosure agreements, infringement of copyright in its ’Mold Information Sheet’ and proposal drawing
parties: Defendant: Rishi Kumar Bhatnagar and Possehl Hong Kong Precision Machining Ltd.

facts.F1: Kras Asia Limited is a Hong Kong company and a subsidiary of Kras Corporation of Pennsylvania in the United States.
facts.F2: Kras Asia Limited designs, manufactures and sells precision manufacturing equipment for the semi-conductor industry.
facts.F3: The company uses individually designed and manufactured moulds for each customer in accordance with information supplied by the customer on a ’Mold Information Sheet’. 28 different versions are stored in the company’s computer.
facts.F4: After obtaining relevant customer information, proposal drawings are prepared by one of Kras Asia Limited's draughtsmen for customer consideration.
facts.F5: Rishi Kumar Bhatnagar was employed as Kras Asia Limited's production manager between 6th April 1981 and 15th June 1987.
facts.F6: Bhatnagar resigned after giving four months’ notice which expired on 15th October 1987.
facts.F7: Before he left the company, Bhatnagar was reminded of clauses 8 and 11 of the employment agreement by Kras Asia Limited's managing director, Mr Leet.
facts.F8: Bhatnagar signed a non-disclosure agreement, agreeing not to disclose confidential information and not to compete with Kras Asia Limited in the Colony of Hong Kong for a certain period.
facts.F9: After resigning, Bhatnagar began working as a consultant for Possehl Hong Kong Precision Machining Ltd., a competitor of Kras Asia Limited.
facts.F10: Kras Asia Limited suspected Bhatnagar of copying company documents and breaching the agreements.
facts.F11: Upon investigation, it was alleged that Bhatnagar had given confidential documents to the investigator including a 'Mold Information Sheet' and a proposal drawing.
facts.F12: Kras Asia Limited claimed that Possehl Hong Kong Precision Machining Ltd. had reproduced and used the company's documents without permission.
facts.F13: Bhatnagar and Possehl Hong Kong Precision Machining Ltd. denied copying the plaintiff's documents, claiming that the 'Mold Information Sheet' had been received from a customer in India and widely distributed.
facts.F14: Kras Asia Limited alleged that Bhatnagar had breached the employment and non-disclosure agreements and infringed the company's copyright.
facts.F15: An ex parte application for an Anton Piller order was made by Kras Asia Limited against the defendants.
facts.F16: The order was made by Mayo J. without full disclosure of material facts by Kras Asia Limited.
facts.F17: There was material non-disclosure of facts by Kras Asia Limited which influenced the result of the ex parte application.
facts.F18: The validity of Kras Asia Limited's claim for breach of agreements and copyright infringement cannot be assessed until a trial where findings of facts are made.

claim: Claims its value of $540,000 from the defendant management company for the stolen car
requested_remedy: Claims its value of $540,000 from the defendant management company for the stolen car
parties: Defendant: The management company of Scenic Villas

facts.F1: Mr Henry Ching's Toyota Lexus was stolen from the carpark of Scenic Villas on the night of 19 November 1991.
facts.F2: The thief or thieves entered the carpark in a stolen Honda, circumvented the sophisticated Lexus alarm system in less than 20 minutes, and departed in the Lexus.
facts.F3: The elderly caretaker, who was on duty that night, made two signed statements about the incident but has since disappeared.
facts.F4: Mr Ching is the general manager of the plaintiff, the Reebok Company Limited, and was provided with the car and an apartment at Scenic Villas as part of his employment.
facts.F5: Scenic Villas has one road access for vehicles and a night caretaker who operates the barrier arms with a button.
facts.F6: Around 1990/1991, there was a sudden and notorious upsurge of vehicle thefts in Hong Kong, with luxury model cars being targeted by thieves.
facts.F7: Scenic Villas carpark was no exception, with four cars stolen in just over one year, including Mr Ching's previous company car, a Toyota Crown.
facts.F8: The defendant management company had taken some security measures, including a patrolling system, beatbooks, and 'walkie-talkies' for caretakers.
facts.F9: The defendant had also recommended and obtained a quotation for a special carpark access control system, but it was not implemented due to an objection from one of the owners.
facts.F10: The caretaker had been instructed to record registration numbers, look at drivers' faces, and question them if appropriate.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's car was on a list of 10 high-risk or luxury models that the caretaker had been warned about.
facts.F12: The caretaker had raised the barrier and let the stolen Lexus drive away after the driver had given a flat number that matched the one on the Lexus' windscreen label.
facts.F13: The caretaker had later gone to Mr Ching's flat to 'double-check' and had reported the theft to the police immediately.
facts.F14: The supermarket within Scenic Villas is open to the public until late hours and has customers who are not residents, which affects the defendant's control over vehicles and their occupants.
facts.F15: The defendant had taken reasonable steps to address the risk of vehicle theft.
facts.F16: The caretaker's actions on the night of the theft were in line with the defendant's instructions and policies, except for a lapse that did not cause the loss of the car.

claim: declaration that the sum of HK$361,444.83 and interest accrued thereon were funds held on trust for the plaintiff and an order against DBS Bank (Hong Kong) Limited for the immediate release and transfer of the Sum to the plaintiff
requested_remedy: declaration that the sum of HK$361,444.83 and interest accrued thereon were funds held on trust for the plaintiff and an order against DBS Bank (Hong Kong) Limited for the immediate release and transfer of the Sum to the plaintiff

facts.F1: The defendant, SOE KIN FAI, committed a fraud against the plaintiff by means of false documents and induced the latter, a money lender, into believing that the defendant was authorized to obtain mortgage loans over a property owned by Wing Wo Lung Co Ltd (WWL).
facts.F2: As a result, the defendant obtained from the plaintiff a total of $22 million by way of two mortgage loans.
facts.F3: The sum of HK$361,444.83 (the Sum) which was part of the proceeds of the fraud, has remained in the account opened by the defendant with DBS Bank (Hong Kong) Limited (R) in the name of WWL.
facts.F4: WWL has confirmed that it has nothing to do with the fraud, the bank account opened in its name and the Sum.
facts.F5: The Police has been informed and they have no objection to the plaintiff taking legal action to seek the return of the Sum.
facts.F6: The defendant has been absent from the proceedings and his whereabouts are unknown.
facts.F7: R has expressed that they take a neutral stance in the matter and do not seek to be heard.
facts.F8: The application is thus uncontested.
facts.F9: The defendant holds the loans on constructive trust for the plaintiff.
facts.F10: WWL is not the real holder of the bank account and does not have any power, control or authority over the same.
facts.F11: Without a vesting order against R, the Sum would likely be left in 'limbo' in the bank account.
facts.F12: The balance of the Sum net of any bank charges payable to the respondent since 5 November 2015.

facts.F5: The food counter was managed by the plaintiff and had a total of 16 staff operating at the time.
facts.F6: Business at the food counter dropped in October 2001 due to competition from a nearby CRC supermarket.
facts.F7: The defendant started to lay off and reduce its staff at the food counter in December 2001 to reduce expenses.
facts.F8: The floor of the food counter was slippery due to the nature of the work, and the use of matting on the floor was not permitted by the supermarket management.
facts.F9: The defendant provided cheaper rubber boots to its staff instead of slip-resistant boots made in Japan due to the high cost.
facts.F10: The plaintiff had complained about the shaky and unstable condition of the ladder before the accident, but the defendant did not replace it.
facts.F11: The plaintiff was injured while taking stock in the storeroom of the food counter and was taken to the hospital for treatment.
facts.F12: The plaintiff's marriage broke up after the accident.

facts.F3: The applicants had a five-year lease for the subject premises, which commenced on 25th February 1992.

facts.F10: The market rental of the subject premises was used as a guide to determine goodwill due to lack of reliable profits records.
facts.F11: A discount rate of 9% was applied to calculate deferred reversionary interest.

claim: damages to his vehicle
requested_remedy: damages to his vehicle

facts.F1: On or about 10 pm on the evening of 23 December 1999, the Plaintiff’s vehicle was driven by his employee, Miss Koo, who was travelling on the second lane eastbound on Connaught Road Central.
facts.F2: At the same time, the Defendant was driving his rented taxi in the third lane going northbound on Pedder Street.
facts.F3: The two vehicles collided with each other.
facts.F4: Miss Koo’s evidence was that as she approached the intersection, the traffic light was red and she stopped. A minute later the light turned green.
facts.F5: She proceeded into the intersection and the Defendant’s taxi ran into her vehicle.
facts.F6: The Defendant’s version was that he had just picked up passengers going to the General Post Office. He turned from Queen’s Road Central into Pedder Street.
facts.F7: When he turned into Pedder Street, he saw there were five to six fire engines and ambulances on Pedder Street and Connaught Road blocking traffic.
facts.F8: There was a traffic jam such that the buses on the left first and the left second lane were blocked, but he saw that his light was green, so he proceeded into the intersection of Connaught and Pedder.
facts.F9: Because there was such traffic, he was travelling only at 20 kilometres an hour.
facts.F10: The letter from the Fire Services Department confirmed that on the evening in question, there was a “1 Alarm Fire”.
facts.F11: A “1 Alarm Fire” is the lowest rate of fire and it was highly unlikely that there were five to six fire engines that stopped on Connaught Place blocking all traffic on the left first and the left second lanes on Pedder Street.
facts.F12: The Defendant had picked up passengers just before the accident.
facts.F13: The Plaintiff’s employee, Miss Koo, correctly identified the traffic lights on the scene.

facts.F1: Giant Wizard Corporation is an overseas company which appears to carry on business in Hong Kong.
facts.F2: The petitioner, LI TIN SANG ADAM, claims that he is a shareholder in Giant Wizard Corporation.
facts.F3: The 1st to 4th Respondents are four brothers, members of the Poon family - Messrs Poon Bun-chak, Poon Kai-chak, Poon Kei-chak and Poon Kwan-chak respectively.

claim: The plaintiff seeks an interlocutory injunction to restrain the defendant from implementing the resolution to expel him as a member and to remove him as a director, executive director, and deputy administrator of the social section of the defendant, pending trial.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff seeks an interlocutory injunction to restrain the defendant from implementing the resolution to expel him as a member and to remove him as a director, executive director, and deputy administrator of the social section of the defendant, pending trial.

facts.F1: The defendant is a large organization with many members who are all natives of Chungshan.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was one of its 99 Directors and the Deputy Administrator of the Social Section.
facts.F3: In 2009, the plaintiff purchased red wine for board meetings and New Year celebrations and was reimbursed $49,400 based on 4 'blank invoices'.
facts.F4: Fellow clansmen suspected that the wine could be purchased for less and asked the plaintiff for information about the source and price of the wine.
facts.F5: The plaintiff responded that he had purchased the wine from a friend whose nightclub business was closing down and that the price was the amount he had reclaimed.
facts.F6: The defendant's board requested further particulars and evidence, which the plaintiff failed to provide.
facts.F7: A report was made to the ICAC, but no action was taken due to a lack of evidence.
facts.F8: The 12th meeting in September 2010 confirmed the board's resolution to suspend the plaintiff, which had been passed almost a year earlier.
facts.F9: The 13th meeting raised the issue again, and a lawyer, Mr. Ho Kwan Yiu, spoke and said he needed time to consider the evidence and would submit a report to everyone in the next meeting.
facts.F10: At the 14th meeting, Mr. Ho did not attend, and the Vice-Chairman, Mr. Kan Chik Hong, mentioned that Mr. Ho's opinion was to follow the mechanism laid out in Article VII of the Articles of Association.
facts.F11: The plaintiff was expelled under Article VII, which states that a member can be expelled for willfully committing a breach of the Association's Articles or byelaws, or for an act of gross misconduct likely to be injurious to the Association.
facts.F12: The voting was by ballot on pre-typed voting forms, with 46 members voting (43 in favor, 2 against, and 1 abstention).
facts.F13: The plaintiff complains that the resolution was not on the agenda, he had no prior notification, and he had no opportunity to prepare to defend himself.
facts.F14: There are forthcoming elections in June 2011.

claim: The plaintiff claims against the defendant damages, interest, and costs
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims against the defendant damages, interest, and costs
parties: Defendant: The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited

facts.F1: The plaintiff, Mr. Gurdas, was the founder and a 50% shareholder and a director of Esquire (Electronics) Ltd (Esquire), a banking customer of the defendant.
facts.F2: In October 1981, the defendant provided 100% finance to enable Esquire to purchase a property known as Li Fung House in Tsim Sha Tsui at the price of $180 million.
facts.F3: The Esquire group agreed to a restructuring of its loans with the defendant, who imposed a condition that Esquire would have to sell its properties by the end of 1982 to repay a portion of the loans.
facts.F4: In about August 1982, Esquire received an offer from a third party, BASF China Ltd, to purchase the property at 10/F Wing On Plaza (Wing On property) for $60 million, but the defendant's manager, Mr. Ian Donaldson, told Esquire not to accept the offer as the defendant wanted to purchase the Wing On property for itself.
facts.F5: The defendant failed to purchase the Wing On property, and Esquire was eventually forced to sell it in December 1986 for only $36 million.
facts.F6: On 22 February 1984, the plaintiff and the other 50% shareholder of Esquire, Mr. Arjan Choithramani, attended a meeting with the defendant and its solicitors, during which the plaintiff was presented with a Restructuring Agreement prepared by the defendant's solicitors.
facts.F7: The plaintiff signed the Restructuring Agreement on behalf of Esquire and other companies in the group and also on his own behalf as a shareholder and guarantor.
facts.F8: The Restructuring Agreement contained false information, stating that the amount of the defendant's Property Portion of the Esquire group's indebtedness was $182.1 million as at 13 September 1983, when it was in fact only $152 million.
facts.F9: The plaintiff did not have knowledge of the false figure until many years later, and the defendant's fraudulent action was a primary cause of the plaintiff's bankruptcy.
facts.F10: The plaintiff was made a bankrupt on two occasions, first on 30 December 1996, and then again on 9 March 2015.
facts.F11: On each occasion, the Official Receiver became the plaintiff's trustee in bankruptcy, and the plaintiff's pre-existing property, including his things in action, became vested in the Official Receiver.
facts.F12: The plaintiff discovered the alleged falsity of the figure at the latest by early 2006.
facts.F13: The plaintiff had allegedly suffered loss due to the insertion of the false figure in the Restructuring Agreement.
facts.F14: The statement of claim did not establish a discernible causal link between the alleged loss and the insertion of the false figure.

lawsuit_type: An application for an order to strike out and dismiss the action

facts.F1: The Plaintiff entered into a provisional agreement of sale with the Defendants to purchase the property for $1,630,000.00 on 22nd September 1997.

facts.F7: No challenge was made to the assignment or to the subsequent three assignments of the property, and all parties have acted in good faith.

claim: The price of goods sold and delivered.
requested_remedy: The price of goods sold and delivered.
parties: Defendant: Win Line Knitting Factory Limited

facts.F1: The plaintiff was a limited company incorporated on 4 April 2005, engaged in the knitting business.
facts.F2: The defendant was one of its customers.
facts.F3: Prior to the incorporation of the plaintiff, one Mr. Lau Ying Kwok (Lau) traded as a sole proprietorship called Yee Fat Trading Company (YFT).
facts.F4: YFT had dealings with the defendant since about 2003, contracting out the processing and/or packaging steps in the manufacture of garments to YFT.
facts.F5: The defendant did place a substantial number of orders with YFT, and a running account was established between them.
facts.F6: The defendant would at times make pre-payments to YFT for the orders given to alleviate YFT’s cash flow problems.
facts.F7: In about 2004, the plaintiff failed to meet the delivery deadline for 4 of the defendant’s orders, resulting in the defendant having to ship the goods by air, thereby incurring additional cost.
facts.F8: The plaintiff was incorporated in 2005 to carry on the same business as YFT because YFT was in financial difficulties.
facts.F9: Upon incorporation, the plaintiff had 4 shareholders, with Lau holding the biggest single block of shares in the proportion of 50% of the total shareholding.
facts.F10: The defendant placed its orders with the plaintiff instead of YFT, although there were still some orders which went to YFT.
facts.F11: Around Chinese New Year of 2006, the plaintiff delivered a statement of account, which was then the subject of negotiation, until it was settled (subject to the present action) on about 18 May 2006.
facts.F12: The defendant set off the airfreight charges incurred as a result of YFT’s delay.
facts.F13: On 15 June 2005, the plaintiff sent a letter to the defendant stating that YFT’s business had been transferred to the plaintiff.
facts.F14: Hsieh and Luk testified in support of the defendant’s version of events.

facts.F1: The Government of Hong Kong provided a downpayment loan to Mr. Choi, a civil servant, under the Home Financing Scheme (the Scheme) to purchase a residential property.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was a 57-year-old self-employed night shift taxi driver who was injured in an accident on 4 June 1994.
facts.F2: The accident occurred when the defendants' vehicle ran into the back of the plaintiff's taxi, pushing it forward and causing the plaintiff to be run over by his own taxi.
facts.F3: The plaintiff suffered multiple injuries, including a fractured right pelvis, a deep laceration to his right thigh, and a compression injury to the nerve of his left wrist.
facts.F4: The plaintiff was hospitalised in Princess Margaret Hospital from 4 to 9 June 1994, and was then transferred to Caritas Medical Centre, where he was discharged on 21 June 1994.
facts.F5: In March 1995, the plaintiff was re-admitted to Princess Margaret Hospital for two operations, one on his knee and the other for decompression of the ulna nerve at his wrist.
facts.F6: The plaintiff claimed that he had been driving taxis for 12 hours a shift, 26 days a month, and that his monthly income was around $14,300.
facts.F7: The defence disputed this, citing a letter from the Motor Transport General Union Taxi Driver Branch which suggested that the median income for taxi drivers was lower.
facts.F8: The plaintiff presented evidence from another witness, Mr Liu Kan, who stated that his current earnings as a night shift taxi driver were around $675 per shift, or $17,550 per month.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was employed by the 1st defendant as a general construction site labourer.
facts.F2: The 1st defendant had subcontracted slope work on the landward side of the South Lantau Road from the main contractor, the 2nd defendant.

claim: claims specific performance of the Provisional Agreement and damages in lieu of or in addition to specific performance
requested_remedy: claims specific performance of the Provisional Agreement and damages in lieu of or in addition to specific performance

facts.F1: The Plaintiff purchased a flat known as Flat D, Pak Yuen Garden Mansion, fifth floor, together with a car-parking space, at Tai Hang Lane, Tai Mang Road, Hong Kong, from the Defendant Company by a contract described as a Provisional Agreement dated the 9th June, 1970.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff's solicitors wrote to the Defendant Company's solicitors on the 11th June 1970, and on eight subsequent occasions, asking for the draft Agreement.
facts.F3: The Defendant Company sent notice regularly to the Plaintiff demanding payments of the instalments in accordance with the Provisional Agreement, with the first notice dated 26th November 1970.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff made only one payment of $3,000 deposit, and failed to pay any of the instalments due to being advised by his solicitors not to pay until there was a reply to the requests made by his solicitors.
facts.F5: The Defendant Company informed the Plaintiff in May 1971 that the suit premises had been sold to a third party due to the Plaintiff's failure to pay any of the instalments, but offered to return the deposit.
facts.F6: The Occupation Permit for the suit premises was issued on the 15th August 1972.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff registered the writ of summons of this action as lis pendens against the flat in question.
facts.F8: The Defendant Company agreed to sell to one K.Y.K. Co. Ltd. the suit premises for $152,000 payable within seven days of the issue of the Occupation Permit on the 5th October 1971.
facts.F9: The current market value of the suit premises is about $320,000 according to the evidence of a chartered surveyor called by the Plaintiff.
facts.F10: The Defendant Company failed to furnish the draft Agreement to the Plaintiff.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff's failure to pay the instalments was not justified by the Defendant Company's failure to furnish the draft Agreement.

claim: declaration of entitlement to the grant of administration of the Deceased’s estate
requested_remedy: declaration of entitlement to the grant of administration of the Deceased’s estate

facts.F1: The parties contest for the right to administration of the estate of late Madam Luk Kim Ying, deceased.
facts.F2: The Deceased was born on 15 November 1915 and was a single woman at the time of her death.
facts.F3: The plaintiff, Lily, claims to be the adopted daughter of the Deceased in Hong Kong.
facts.F4: The 1st defendant, Cheung, claims to be the surviving lawful husband of the Deceased.
facts.F5: The 2nd defendant, Luk, claims to be the adopted daughter of the Deceased in the Mainland.
facts.F6: Lily was born in Hong Kong on 5 April 1951 and was handed over to the Deceased for raising soon after birth.
facts.F7: In 1956, Lily was made a ward under the custody of Cheung Wing Tak.
facts.F8: The Deceased entered into a registered marriage with Chao Cheung Yuk in Hong Kong in 1957.
facts.F9: Luk was born in the Mainland on 18 May 1963 and was adopted by the Deceased in Jiangsu in 1984.
facts.F10: Luk moved to Hong Kong on a one-way permit in 1986 and resided with the Deceased until she got married.
facts.F11: The Deceased owned various landed properties in Hong Kong, some of which were co-owned with Luk.
facts.F12: The Deceased was suffering from mental incapacity in 2001 and the Guardianship Board appointed Luk as her guardian.
facts.F13: The Deceased passed away intestate on 15 March 2006.
facts.F14: Cheung applied for grant of administration in respect of the Deceased’s estate in 2007, claiming to be the surviving lawful husband.
facts.F15: Lily’s evidence of adoption is hearsay and lacks corroborative value.
facts.F16: There were inconsistencies in Cheung’s statements regarding his marriage.
facts.F17: Cheung has mental incapacity.
facts.F18: The authenticity of Cheung’s marriage certificate is in dispute.
facts.F19: The Notary Certificate issued in Mainland is a common form of formal proof of adoption arrangement.
facts.F20: Luk’s adoption meets the requirements of de facto adoption under Mainland law.

facts.F2: The wife is ethnically Chinese and the husband is Belgian.
facts.F3: The parties' marriage was dissolved in Belgium in March 2010.

facts.F9: Counsel made submissions relevant to the case.
facts.F10: A consent summons was filed on 10 November 2021.

facts.F8: The parties did not contemplate what would happen regarding the defendant's occupation if the transactions were not completed.
facts.F9: The plaintiff retained the notice to quit, as evidenced by its inclusion in the sale agreement.
facts.F10: The provision in the extension agreements that Main Lion and Madam Wan would be responsible for arrears of rental.
