facts.F2: As the First Plaintiff proceeded around a right-hand bend on the flyover, his way was blocked by stationary traffic, and he braked.
facts.F3: The Third Party braked behind him, but his car slid into the Plaintiff's vehicle, causing minor damage.
facts.F4: The parties left their vehicles and inspected the damage.
facts.F5: After the original collision, the vehicles were moved to the extreme left-hand side of the flyover to leave room for other traffic to pass.
facts.F6: The Defendant drove his vehicle around the same corner of the flyover and came upon the two stationary cars and the group of people standing by them.
facts.F7: The Defendant applied his brakes, but lost control of his vehicle and slid into the group of people, injuring the Plaintiffs.
facts.F8: Photographs and a sketch plan of the flyover were produced in evidence, depicting the position of the vehicles and the location of the accident.
facts.F9: The Defendant's vehicle had impaired braking efficiency.
facts.F10: The Defendant failed to maintain his vehicle properly.

claim: claims for the misdelivery of 5 shipments of goods
requested_remedy: claims for the misdelivery of 5 shipments of goods
parties: Defendant: The owners of the ships or vessels Murter, Brij, and Al Salimiah

facts.F1: The Plaintiff Glory Products Co. Ltd. entered into an agreement with Wing Tung Wei (China) Ltd. (WTW), a freight forwarder, for the transportation of garments from China to Venezuela.
facts.F2: WTW issued Talent Bills, a type of bill of lading, to the Plaintiff, which were then used by the Plaintiff to obtain payment from the Buyer, Acetex International SA.
facts.F3: Unbeknownst to the Plaintiff, WTW, through its shipping department 'Talent Express Line', arranged with Hong Kong Maritime Co. Ltd., the Hong Kong agent of CAVN, for the issuance of CAVN Bills, a separate type of bill of lading, for the same shipments.
facts.F4: The CAVN Bills listed WTW as the shipper and Amaya, the notify party in the Talent Bills, as the consignee.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff had no knowledge of the CAVN Bills and did not authorise WTW to enter into a contract with CAVN.
facts.F6: The CAVN Bills were not provided to the Plaintiff and were instead kept in the drawer of WTW's office.
facts.F7: Upon arrival in Venezuela, the goods were delivered to the Venezuelan Customs, who then released the goods to Oran, the customs agent of Amaya, without requiring the production of the CAVN Bills.
facts.F8: The Plaintiff eventually discovered the existence of the CAVN Bills and commenced proceedings against the Defendants, claiming misdelivery of the goods.
facts.F9: Raymond Kwok was the former Assistant General Manager of WTW.
facts.F10: The Venezuelan Customs released the goods to Oran, the customs agent of Amaya, without requiring the production of the CAVN Bills.

facts.F1: On 22nd September 1968, the plaintiff was a passenger in a car driven by the 1st defendant when it had an accident on Deep Water Bay Road.
facts.F2: The plaintiff sustained injuries, including abrasions to his left forearm, bleeding from his left ear, and blood clots on both nostrils, with the left half of his face paralyzed due to a fracture at the base of the skull.
facts.F3: The plaintiff was hospitalized at Queen Mary Hospital until his discharge on 16th October 1968, with his condition described as quite good except for the facial palsy.
facts.F4: The plaintiff's injuries resulted in permanent paralysis of the left side of his face, affecting his eye, ear, mouth, and facial muscles.
facts.F5: The plaintiff had to undergo medical treatment and would require further surgery to close his left eye and improve his facial features.
facts.F6: The plaintiff was a professional musician before the accident, with total earnings of around $1,200 - $1,500 per month.
facts.F7: After the accident, the plaintiff could not continue playing the guitar professionally due to his hearing defect and now works for his father for $500 per month.
facts.F8: The plaintiff's father provides him with extra money when needed.
facts.F9: The plaintiff intends to pursue his career as a musician if it were not for the accident.
facts.F10: The accident significantly reduced the plaintiff's earning capacity.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's future prospects as a musician were uncertain.
facts.F12: The vicissitudes of life would impact the plaintiff's future career and earnings.

requested_remedy: The applicants sought to impugn the decisions made by the Director and the Secretary for Justice to remove banners and placards from FLG demonstration locations, confiscate demonstration banners and placards and portable frames, and continue to remove banners and placards from FLG demonstration locations on the purported ground that their display was in breach of Section 104A of the Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance.
parties: Plaintiff: 徐慧敏 (CHEE FEI MING) and HUNG SHUI FUNG
Defendant: DIRECTOR OF FOOD AND ENVIRONMENTAL HYGIENE and SECRETARY FOR JUSTICE

facts.F1: The applicants, Falun Gong practitioners, staged static demonstrations at various locations in public places, displaying publicity materials without obtaining the required permission from the Director of Food and Environmental Hygiene.
facts.F2: The applicants claimed that their demonstrations were peaceful and did not obstruct the public or cause any nuisance, and that the Director's decision to remove their publicity materials was an unlawful restriction on their freedoms of demonstration, assembly, and speech.
facts.F3: The respondents, the Director of Food and Environmental Hygiene and the Secretary for Justice, contended that the applicants' displays of publicity materials without permission were in contravention of Section 104A of the Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance, and that the Director's decision to remove the materials was lawful and reasonable.
facts.F4: The Director had delegated his functions and powers under Section 104A to three specified categories of officers of the Lands Department, who had adopted a Management Scheme for the Display of Roadside Non-commercial Publicity Materials Implementation Guidelines for processing applications for permission to display such materials on public roadsides.
facts.F5: The applicants had not applied for permission under the Management Scheme, and the Director had not given his prior permission for the display of the publicity materials.
facts.F6: The applicants relied on their constitutional rights to freedom of speech, assembly, and demonstration under Article 27 of the Basic Law and Articles 16 and 17 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights.
facts.F7: There was no clear and unambiguous representation by the Director that he would not enforce Section 104A of the Ordinance against the applicants.

claim: The plaintiff is claiming damages for injuries sustained from being knocked down by a motorcycle in July 1975.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff is claiming damages for injuries sustained from being knocked down by a motorcycle in July 1975.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was fifty-seven years of age and worked as a waitress in a small restaurant at the time of the accident.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was detained in hospital for some nine months after the accident.
facts.F3: The plaintiff spent three months with one or both legs in traction and most of the remainder with the right leg in plaster.
facts.F4: The plaintiff received treatment and instruction in physiotherapy in the last three weeks of her hospital stay.
facts.F5: A medical report dated July 1976 indicated that the first three items of injury mentioned above have left no permanent disability.
facts.F6: The medical report also showed that there was considerable restriction in the movements of the right arm and both legs; shortening of both legs, and to different degrees; wastage of various muscles; several small scars, one of which had been remedied to some extent by a skin graft; and a substantial loss of grip strength in the right arm.
facts.F7: The plaintiff walked with a shuffling gait, could do so only slowly and for about one hour at a time and had difficulty in climbing steps.
facts.F8: The plaintiff was unfit for any form of work which involved standing or walking and was unable to lift heavy weights.
facts.F9: The doctor assessed her impairment as 15 per cent of the whole woman.
facts.F10: The plaintiff started work again for her previous employer on the 1st January that year, doing much lighter work at the reduced salary of $400 per month.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's husband spent $5,000 on providing extra nourishment to her during her recovery, but this was not recoverable as the plaintiff did not incur the expense herself.
facts.F12: The assessment of general damages was based on the plaintiff's pain and suffering, loss of amenities, and loss of future earnings.
facts.F13: The special damages were based on the plaintiff's loss of past earnings, travelling expenses, and other expenses directly related to her recovery from the injury, but not including expenses incurred by her husband.

facts.F9: The Director of Marine took into account relevant factors, including safety considerations, and acted with caution when making decisions on the change in permitted hours of duty.

Defendant: YUENG MAN LOONG MAXLY, YEUNG MAN FUNG, LO WAI YIN, YEUNG TUNG SHING, GOLD PLEASURE INDUSTRIAL COMPANY LIMITED (1st to 5th Respondents)

facts.F1: The petitioners, BEATRICE TSANG SAU HING and LUANA TSANG SAU KUEN, were the directors of GOLD PLEASURE INDUSTRIAL COMPANY LIMITED.
facts.F2: The provisional liquidators were appointed over the companies.
facts.F3: The petitioners sought an order to inspect documents related to a joint-venture company, owned by the Company, which operated manufacturing facilities in China.
facts.F4: The documents were said to be relevant to certain issues which arise in the winding-up petition.
facts.F5: The provisional liquidators agreed to make available records of the joint venture which were actually in their possession in Hong Kong for inspection by the petitioners.
facts.F6: The Chinese joint venture partner was unwilling to afford inspection of the documents to the petitioners at all.
facts.F7: The petitioners sought to restore the application by summons dated 27 December 2006.
facts.F8: The petitioners sought leave to amend the summons so as to make it an application under RHC Order 24, rules 3 and 7 as well.
facts.F9: The provisional liquidators did not object to the course being taken and undertook to cause the Company to comply with its obligations of discovery in the circumstances of this case.
facts.F10: The order for discovery was not served on the Company and the Company did not make discovery.
facts.F11: The company had redevelopment potential for the property in question.
facts.F12: The provisional liquidators had entered into a conditional agreement for the sale and purchase of the property of Sunville.

facts.F12: The sisters did not take any steps to achieve the purpose of providing for their nephews and nieces

facts.F7: The defendant, Tong Kee, denied any breach of its duty of care and claimed that Rahman was contributorially negligent.
facts.F8: The plaintiff's injury was reasonably foreseeable.
facts.F9: The plaintiff had pre-existing degenerative changes in his lower back.

claim: The Plaintiff (Purchaser) seeks a declaration that, because of a repudiatory breach of the agreement of sale by the Defendant (Vendor), it was entitled to rescind the contract and seek damages.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff (Purchaser) seeks a declaration that, because of a repudiatory breach of the agreement of sale by the Defendant (Vendor), it was entitled to rescind the contract and seek damages.

facts.F1: On 5th November 1997, the Vendor agreed to sell and the Purchaser agreed to purchase a residential apartment in Kowloon for a price of HK$7,000,000.
facts.F2: Clause 2 of the provisional agreement stated that the purchase price shall be paid by the Purchaser to the Vendor in the manner as follows: (a) Initial deposit shall be paid upon signing of this agreement in the sum of HK$300,000, (b) Upon signing of the Formal Agreement for Sale and Purchase on or before 18th November 1997 further deposit shall be paid in the sum of HK$750,000.
facts.F3: The provisional agreement contained the usual escape clauses and clause 8 provided that the vendor shall compensate the purchaser with a refund of the initial deposit and liquidated damages if the vendor fails to complete the sale.
facts.F4: On 13th November 1997, the Vendor's solicitors forwarded a draft of the formal agreement for sale and purchase to the Purchaser's solicitors.
facts.F5: The Purchaser's solicitors obtained their client's signature to the formal agreement, had it attested and then returned it to the Vendor's solicitors together with their cheque for the sum of $750,000 being the further deposit due.
facts.F6: The signed formal agreement and cheque were delivered under cover of a letter dated 18th November 1997 stating that the said cheque is sent subject to the Vendor's firm's undertaking to return to the Purchaser within the next 3 days from the date thereof the original of the said Agreement duly signed by the Vendor and attested by the Vendor's solicitors.
facts.F7: The Vendor's authorised representative was under the impression that time was not of the essence as he was in Macau on 18th November 1997 and, for business reasons, was apparently unable to return to Hong Kong to sign the agreement until a week later; that is, on 24th November 1997.
facts.F8: Prior to 24th November 1997, the Purchaser's solicitors had been pressing for a resolution of matters and, when it was discovered on 22nd November that the Vendor had still not signed, notice was sent accepting the Vendor's 'wrongful repudiation' of the provisional agreement and demanding 'compensation' in terms of clause 8 thereof.
facts.F9: The provisional agreement did not contain any written provision that time was of the essence.
facts.F10: The Vendor's failure to sign the formal agreement on or before 18th November 1997 did not activate the trigger mechanism that obliged the Purchaser to pay a further deposit.

facts.F3: In early 2006, the plaintiff was looking for capital for the continuation and expansion of the business of Taiyuan Sanxing.
facts.F4: The 1st defendant is and was the controlling shareholder, chairman and chief executive of the 2nd defendant, a company listed in the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEx).
facts.F5: In about April 2006, the 1st defendant visited the plaintiff and inspected the operation of Taiyuan Sanxing with a view to a joint venture.

facts.F13: The 1st defendant failed to procure the listing of the JV Co within the said 18 months from the beginning of the joint venture, and failed to procure the injection of capital at RMB200 million to RMB500 million.
facts.F14: The 1st Representation was a statement of fact and not an opinion or intention of the 1st defendant.
facts.F15: There was no disclosure by the sole shareholder and director of the 5th defendant regarding the source of the US$3 million loan.

parties: Defendant: The 1st Defendant and The 2nd Defendant

facts.F1: The accident occurred on 12th March 1976 when the Plaintiff was crossing Kwun Tong Road, Kowloon from south to north and the vehicle driven by the 1st Defendant was travelling from east to west
facts.F2: The material stretch of Kwun Tong Road is divided by a railing into two parts with 3 lanes on each side for traffic travelling in opposite directions
facts.F3: The Plaintiff was crossing Kwun Tong Road on an uncontrolled stud crossing which traversed the whole of Kwun Tong Road with a gap for the crossing in the dividing railing
facts.F4: The Plaintiff was knocked down in the third lane, i.e. after he had crossed two-thirds of the westbound carriageway
facts.F5: The Plaintiff was with a group of 20 odd pedestrians waiting to cross
facts.F6: There were many vehicles on the road
facts.F7: After all vehicles had stopped the Plaintiff followed the other pedestrians to cross
facts.F8: There were 14 to 15 persons in front of him, the closest being about 2 feet in front of him, and some pedestrians followed him
facts.F9: When the Plaintiff reached the third lane he lost consciousness and did not feel the collision nor did he see the Defendant's vehicle
facts.F10: The Plaintiff recovered consciousness in hospital
facts.F11: A statement made by the Plaintiff in hospital on 7th April 1976 (26 days later) to a police officer investigating the accident stated that he was standing on the pavement ready to cross the road but that he could not remember anything after that
facts.F12: There was no mention of the vehicles being stationary nor of a group of pedestrians crossing with him in the hospital statement
facts.F13: The Plaintiff claimed to have suffered a fracture of his forehead which caused injury to his brain, but his claim of serious head injury is not supported by the medical report dated 5th November 1976 from the United Christian Hospital
facts.F14: The Plaintiff was conscious and oriented when he was admitted, that he had retrograde amnesia in that he could not remember what happened at the accident, and that there was no medical evidence of brain damage
facts.F15: The 1st Defendant was familiar with Kwun Tong Road near the vicinity of the accident
facts.F16: The 1st Defendant knew of the railing dividing the road and the existence of the stud crossing
facts.F17: The 1st Defendant was travelling in the third lane at about 28 miles per hour with a moving lorry on his left about 4 or 5 feet ahead of him when he saw the Plaintiff cross the front of the goods vehicle about 10 feet from his vehicle
facts.F18: The 1st Defendant immediately applied the emergency brake but nevertheless the left front of his vehicle knocked the Plaintiff down
facts.F19: The Plaintiff put himself in jeopardy
facts.F20: A a contributory negligence of 50% is attributed to the Plaintiff

claim: opposition to the registration of the BORSALINI mark under the Trade Marks Ordinance, Cap. 43
requested_remedy: opposition to the registration of the BORSALINI mark under the Trade Marks Ordinance, Cap. 43
parties: Defendant: Wong Wai Sum, trading as Chi Hang Company

facts.F1: The appellant was established in 1857 in Italy as a manufacturer and vendor of headgear under the trade mark BORSALINO, the very rare surname of its founder.
facts.F2: BORSALINO acquired a world-wide reputation in the 1970s and early 1980s for clothing, perfumery, and leather goods.
facts.F3: The appellant's mark BORSALINO (in capital and script form) has been registered in Hong Kong in respect of clothing and perfumery.
facts.F4: The respondent, Wong Wai Sum, trading as Chi Hang Company, was not familiar with English and could pronounce English words by looking at their spelling.
facts.F5: Wong was not familiar with the mark BORSALINO when he invented the mark BORSALINI in discussions with his colleagues.
facts.F6: The respondent's colleagues assisted him with the correct spelling of the BORSALINI mark.
facts.F7: Wong did not know that BORSALINO was an Italian surname when he started selling leather wallets and handbags with the BORSALINI mark in the summer of 1983.
facts.F8: Wong's sales were primarily exports to Japan and Taiwan, only a small proportion being distributed to Hong Kong retailers (mainly leather goods speciality shops).
facts.F9: Leather goods marked BORSALINI accounted for some 70% of Wong's export sales.
facts.F10: There have been no complaints of confusion between the marks BORSALINO and BORSALINI.
facts.F11: Wong Wai Sum has since died and proceedings were carried on against his widow, Leung Hoi Yung, by an order of Liu J. on 19th October 1992.
facts.F12: The level of public inconvenience is a significant factor when determining whether to exercise discretion under section 22 of the Trade Marks Ordinance
facts.F13: The association of a trade mark with the goods of a 'fashion house' may create public inconvenience if a similar mark is registered in respect of similar goods
facts.F14: The BORSALINO mark has a broad reputation globally and in Hong Kong.

lawsuit_type: appeal against the decision of the Registrar of Trade Marks

requested_remedy: The Plaintiff was seeking US$600,000 and loss of profit in the sum of HK$20,000 from the Defendant for breaches of two oral agreements to provide currency exchange and remittance services.
parties: Plaintiff: Tai Shing Lee Victor (戴勝利) trading as Lucky Reminbi Exchange Foreign Currency Co
Defendant: Wu Ka Yu Jennie (胡嘉瑜)

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was a foreign currency exchange operator trading under the name of Lucky Reminbi Exchange Foreign Currency Co.
facts.F2: Ms O Sau Kuen, Fanny was the wife of the Plaintiff and at the material time was a staff of Lucky.
facts.F3: The Defendant was also a foreign currency exchange operator.
facts.F4: The Defendant claims she used to be the licensee of 圓通兌換找換店 and dealt with fellow currency exchange operators, including the Plaintiff, in the name of 圓通 when providing money exchange/remittance services to customers.
facts.F5: After April 2017, the Defendant became the staff of Joint Profit Inc Limited 駿利行有限公司 and dealt with fellow currency operators, including the Plaintiff, as the agent/staff of Joint Profit.
facts.F6: This Action arose out of two foreign exchange and remittance transactions between Lucky and the Defendant which took place in July 2017.
facts.F7: The first agreement was reached on 25 July 2017 between Ms O on behalf of the Plaintiff and the Defendant, for the Plaintiff to procure RMB2,776,000 to be deposited into the PRC ABC Account and the Defendant to procure US$400,000 to be deposited into the Action Thrive HSBC Account.
facts.F8: The second agreement was reached on 26 July 2017 between Ms O on behalf of the Plaintiff and the Defendant, for the Plaintiff to procure RMB2,845,400 into the PRC ABC Account and the Defendant to procure US$200,000 into the Action Thrive HSBC Account and US$200,000 into the You BOC Account.
facts.F9: On 28 July 2017, Ms O informed the Defendant that the Plaintiff’s client had not received the US$200,000 supposedly deposited into the You BOC Account.
facts.F10: On 31 July 2017, the Plaintiff was informed that the sum of US$600,000 had not been deposited into the Action Thrive HSBC Account.
facts.F11: It was discovered that the bank deposit slips sent by the Defendant to the Plaintiff were forged documents prepared by a fraudster, Wong.
facts.F12: Wong had been known to the Defendant for years and deposited a cheque into the relevant bank account to create the impression that money had been deposited into it, but the cheque was subsequently dishonoured.
facts.F13: The Defendant was a person of substantial means.
facts.F14: The Defendant had given HK$1.5 million to Ms O when the latter had cash flow problems.

requested_remedy: damages under the Fatal Accidents Ordinance and the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance
parties: Defendant: 1st Defendant: motor-cyclist, 2nd Defendant: motor-cycle owner

facts.F1: On 30th December, 1974, Madam NG Kam-yuk was attempting to cross Tai Po Road with her baby daughter and young son, and met with an accident with a motor-cycle ridden by the 1st Defendant.
facts.F2: The motor-cycle belonged to the 2nd Defendant.
facts.F3: The deceased was admitted into the Kwong Wah Hospital with no injuries other than those to her skull.
facts.F4: The 1st Defendant was travelling at 27/28 miles an hour and was 25 feet behind a taxi.
facts.F5: The 1st Defendant saw the taxi in front drive past the stud-crossing and ought to have anticipated that pedestrians would use the crossing.
facts.F6: The 1st Defendant failed to exercise due care and was too close to the centre railing for comfort.
facts.F7: The deceased stepped onto the path of the motor-cycle without prior warning, but had agility impaired by the children in her charge.
facts.F8: A motor-cycle is not a silent contraption and the sound would have been sufficient warning had the deceased exercised due care.
facts.F9: The deceased's funeral expenses totalled $1,620.
facts.F10: Since the death of the deceased, the Plaintiff paid $500 a month for the care and attention of his children, and later $650 a month.
facts.F11: The degree of negligence on the part of the deceased was assessed at 40% and the degree of blame on the part of the motor-cyclist at 60%.
facts.F12: The lack of evidence in rebuttal of the Plaintiff's testimony regarding the expenses for the care and attention of his children justified accepting his evidence.

facts.F1: The Defendant is a public company, Mr. John Chan is the Defendant's Managing Director, and also the Director and sole beneficial owner of Angklong Limited, which is a controlling shareholder of the Defendant.
facts.F2: In September 1994, Angklong had a margin account facility with the Plaintiff.
facts.F3: By the end of 1996, the Defendant was indebted to Angklong in the sum of $108,630,000.00 as a shareholder's loan.
facts.F4: In or about January 1998, Angklong owed the Plaintiff the sum of $54,302,841.54.
facts.F5: On 22 January 1998, a meeting of the Board of Directors of the Defendant resolved to enter into a loan agreement with the Plaintiff for a loan facility of $25 million.
facts.F6: The Loan Agreement was executed by John Chan on 26 January 1998 and was forwarded to the Plaintiff for execution.
facts.F7: Copies of the Defendant's Memorandum of Association and New Bye-laws and the Minutes of the Meeting of the Directors on 22 January were sent to the Plaintiff together with the Agreement.
facts.F8: The Loan Agreement was executed by Henry Fung and Benson Lo on behalf of the Plaintiff.
facts.F9: The Defendant gave notice to the Plaintiff on 26 January 1998 that it intended to draw the sum of $25 million under the Loan Agreement on the following day.
facts.F10: On 27 January 1998, the Plaintiff credited the sum of $25 million to Angklong's account and on 12 February 1998, debited the Defendant's account with the same amount.
facts.F11: There is no documentary evidence to suggest that the sum of $25 million was ever credited into the Defendant's bank account.
facts.F12: On 4 March 1998, shares in the Defendant were suspended from trading.
facts.F13: The Plaintiff issued proceedings against Angklong Limited on 11 March 1998 to recover the sum of $30,396,741.45.
facts.F14: On 5 March 1998, the Plaintiff declared that the loan facility to the Defendant had terminated and demanded repayment of $25,310,445.21.
facts.F15: The present proceedings against the Defendant were instituted on 14 March 1998.
facts.F16: On 3 August 1998, Angklong paid the Plaintiff the sum of $10 million.
facts.F17: The Defendant made admissions in their letters dated 10 March 1998 and 15 September 1998, effectively admitting their indebtedness to the Plaintiff.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff rented the Ground Floor and the basement of Full Win Commercial Centre, No. 573 Nathan Road, from the Defendants as landlord, for the period from 15 August 2000 to 14 August 2003, at a monthly rent of $130,000.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff yielded up the Premises to the Defendant on 14 August 2003.
facts.F3: The Defendant deducted a sum of $280,729 from the deposit, and only returned to the Plaintiff on 11 September 2003 the balance of the deposit in the sum of $251,003.
facts.F4: When the Plaintiff surrendered the Premises to the Defendant, the following items of works had been done: (1) Alterations and/or additions to fire service installations of Defendants in the Premises including 50 heat detectors, 50 remote controlled lights, 1 set of fire alarm, 108 fire sprinklers and 1 set of fire hose (the Fire Services Work); (2) Demolition of 2 toilets, i.e. the toilet for the disabled (with water closet and wash basin) and the male toilet (with water closet, wash basin and male lavatory), removal of wash basins in the female toilet and installation of another water closet thereon; (3) Raised flooring by concrete of 6 inches thick embedded with water and drainage pipes on the area coloured pink on Exhibit D1; (4) Demolition of 2 walls (including 2 doors) next to the staircase leading from the Ground Floor portion to the Basement portion of the Premises.
facts.F5: The cost of repairing and reinstating the fire services installations is $27,000. The cost of repairing and reinstating 3 toilets and 2 walls next to the staircase is $103,700. The cost of reinstating the floor is $58,000. The loss of use and occupation of the Premises required for the execution of the reinstatement works rental for 20 days at $92,029, based on estimated market rental of $110,000, and air-conditioning charges and management fees at $28,044 per month.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff delivered the Premises with only 3 partitions, each of which had a water closet, after demolishing 2 smaller toilets and converting the wash basins area in the larger toilet into another partition with a water closet.
facts.F7: The Premises should have been delivered by the Plaintiff in a bare shell condition, meaning unfurnished and undecorated, as per the meaning of 'bare' in the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary.
facts.F8: Only the Fire Services Work which cost $27,000 was carried out as reinstatement work by the Defendant.
facts.F9: The direct losses and damages sustained or incurred by the Defendant due to the Plaintiff's breach of the Lease amount to $68,413.20.

facts.F4: On 11 March 2006, Mr. Lim signed a provisional sale and purchase agreement (the agreement) drafted by the Plaintiff.
facts.F5: The agreement left the name, address, and ID card number of the purchaser blank.
facts.F6: Mr. Lim was requested to sign the receipt clause on the right bottom part of the draft agreement even though the purchaser's identity and cheque number of the deposit were also left blank.
facts.F7: No deposit was paid to Mr. Lim until a cheque was handed over to him on 13 March 2006 together with a copy of the agreement after the purchaser placed his signature on the agreement.
facts.F8: The purchaser signed the provisional sale and purchase agreement on the evening of 12 March 2006.
facts.F9: The purchaser was one Ko Sik Ka, who Mr. Lim suspected was Kelvin Ko, the owner of unit 11C.
facts.F10: Mr. Lim had instructed Kenneth he did not wish to sell to Mr. Kelvin Ko.
facts.F11: Kenneth told Mr. Lim the purchaser was not the owner of unit 11C.
facts.F12: Mr. Lim claimed Kenneth had misrepresented to him the purchaser was not the owner of unit 11C.
facts.F13: The Plaintiff claimed it had acted with full propriety and denied Kenneth had misrepresented to Mr. Lim the purchaser was not the owner of unit 11C.
facts.F14: Kenneth should have ascertained the full name and identity of the purchaser before approaching the vendor to sign the provisional sale and purchase agreement.
facts.F15: Kenneth had clearly induced Mr. Lim to sign an open offer to an unknown purchaser without receiving any consideration.
facts.F16: Payment of a deposit would usually accompany the offer and given to the vendor when the vendor signed the provisional agreement.
facts.F17: It is usual practice for the purchaser to sign the provisional sale and purchase agreement first to give the vendor the choice of accepting or rejecting the offer.

facts.F1: The case arises from an application for an interlocutory injunction by the plaintiff (P), the owner of a Montessori school, to restrain one of its former teachers (D) from working for P's competitor in Discovery Bay.

facts.F3: The plaintiff and defendant entered into an employment agreement on or about 22nd March 2021, which contained a non-compete clause (Clauses 5.6 and 7) that restricted D from working for any Montessori schools or learning centres in certain areas for 1 year after the termination of her employment with P.

facts.F7: The parties consented to the withdrawal of the Summons upon undertakings given by D, with costs reserved.

facts.F9: The relationship between a school and its students and parents is not analogous to the relationship between a commercial entity and its clients.

facts.F8: The parties were unable to agree on the costs of and incidental to the cause of the 2nd petition.
facts.F9: The decision to dispose of the 1st petition was a joint decision.
facts.F10: The parties had reached an agreement on the proper course to be taken.
facts.F11: The 'event' of the 1st petition was that the marriage had broken down irretrievably.

parties: Defendant: Max Share Limited and China Resources (Holdings) Company Limited

facts.F1: Max Share Limited was formed in 1986 with two hundred thousand shares of $1 each, of which 49% were allotted to Ng Yat Chi and 51% were allotted to three individuals, Kei Kwong Chuen, Bao Feng, and Wang Hong Ling, as nominees for a company called Strong Progress Ltd.
facts.F2: Strong Progress was a wholly-owned subsidiary of China Resources (Holdings) Ltd, which was in turn owned by the state.
facts.F3: Ng Yat Chi and Kei Kwong Chuen played a major role in the management of the Company, with Ng as the Managing Director and Kei as the Chairman of the board of directors.
facts.F4: The Company suffered substantial losses, while various companies controlled by Ng regularly derived profits from entering into transactions with the Company and its subsidiaries.
facts.F5: In 1988-9, Madam Zhu You Lan became the chairman of China Resources (Holdings) in Hong Kong, and in July 1990, Mr Zhou Chuan Ru was appointed to supervise the Company's business.
facts.F6: In November 1990, Ng Yat Chi agreed to transfer his shares to Strong Progress, but the agreement was subsequently terminated.
facts.F7: The Company increased its share capital by 250 times in May 1992, diluting Ng's shareholding from 49% to 0.4%.
facts.F8: Ng Yat Chi was adjudicated bankrupt in August 1992 and his shares in the Company were acquired by Mr Bing Choy.
facts.F9: Ng Yat Chi and China Resources (Holdings) Ltd had a personal relationship, mutual confidence, and the agreement that both would participate in the conduct of the business.
facts.F10: The Company's accounts did not present a true and fair view of its transactions and financial position, but this was not due to any intention to conceal information from Ng Yat Chi.
facts.F11: The increase in share capital was for the purpose of diluting Ng's shareholding.
facts.F12: Ng Yat Chi had accepted that he would no longer participate in the management of the Company after the meeting of 1 June 1991.

requested_remedy: The applicant claims that the impugned provisions are in breach of Articles 25 and 26 of the Basic Law and Articles 21(b) and 22 of the Bill of Rights for being discriminatory against certain candidates (such as the applicant) on the grounds of their political views and the status of non-association with other political parties.

facts.F1: The applicant, Chau Tsun Kiu, stood for election in the Kowloon West Geographical Constituency in 2012.
facts.F2: He was a member of People Power, a political party, and had a political stand known as 'radical democracy'.

facts.F1: The plaintiff and the defendant are brothers and sons of the Deceased.
facts.F2: In or about 1985, the parties' parents purchased Section C and Section RP of Lot 959 in DD 118 (the 'Land') and they moved into the same around the 1990's.
facts.F3: A house was constructed on the Land wherein the parties' parents lived in one section and the plaintiff and his family lived in the other.
facts.F4: The plaintiff and his family moved out of the Land sometime in the mid-90's and the defendant and his family moved onto the Land sometime in 2012.

facts.F9: The Deceased passed away on 26 January 2014 and unbeknownst to the plaintiff, the defendant obtained the grant of probate (the 'Grant') in respect of the Estate on 9 April 2015.
facts.F10: There has been no distribution of the Estate whatsoever, whether according to the Will or otherwise, despite the fact that the Deceased passed away in 2014 and the Grant was obtained in 2015.

facts.F3: The BVI companies hold the entire share capital of two Hong Kong companies, Ever Rich (Group) Ltd and Ever Rich Printing Manufacturing Company Ltd.
facts.F4: The Hong Kong companies are the main assets of the BVI companies.
facts.F5: The Petitioner alleges that prior to the incorporation of the BVI companies in about 1996, he and the Respondents were equal shareholders in the Hong Kong companies, which were run by them as a quasi-partnership.
facts.F6: The Petitioner claims that the BVI companies were incorporated at the suggestion of the Respondents, who assured him that after their incorporation and the transfer to them of the Petitioner’s and the Respondents' shareholdings of the Hong Kong companies, all the companies would continue to be run on the same basis.
facts.F7: The Petitioner alleges that the relationship between the Respondents and himself broke down towards the end of 2001.
facts.F8: The Petitioner alleges that at a time when it was proposed that Ever Rich (Group) Ltd should be listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, the proposed financial advisers for the listing application, Messrs Deloitte, discovered irregularities and inconsistencies in its financial records.
facts.F9: The Petitioner alleges that there followed between December 2001 and March 2002 a series of steps which had the effect of excluding him from the management of the Hong Kong and BVI companies, culminating on 7 March 2002 with the passing of resolutions removing him as a director of the BVI companies.
facts.F10: On 8 March 2002, the Petitioner issued proceedings against the Respondents, the Hong Kong companies, and the BVI companies, seeking orders requiring them to reinstate him as a director of the BVI companies and to restore him to the management of the Hong Kong companies.
facts.F11: On 17 July 2002, the Respondents were appointed as additional directors of the Hong Kong companies.
facts.F12: On 25 October 2002, the Petitioner took out his application for the appointment of provisional liquidators in respect of the BVI companies.
facts.F13: The Respondents, as representatives of the BVI companies, made declarations of solvency in respect of the Hong Kong companies on 29 October 2002, and passed special resolutions for the voluntary winding up of the Hong Kong companies on 4 November 2002.
facts.F14: Messrs Lai Kar Yan Derek and Darach E Haughey, partners of Deloitte, were appointed liquidators of the Hong Kong companies.
facts.F15: The liquidators of the Hong Kong companies would be aware of the Petitions and the outstanding action, and the allegations made in them, and would have to look into these matters and take such action as they may think appropriate.
facts.F16: The costs of appointing a provisional liquidator would be increased if someone other than Messrs Lai and Haughey were to be appointed.

facts.F11: The Plaintiff's solicitors accepted the terms offered by the Defendant's solicitors on 7th July.

facts.F2: Zheng is a Mainland resident and a shareholder and director of Grand Pride.

claim: claims damages for personal injury resulting from chemical burns to the scalp caused by the 2nd defendant's employee, Barbie
requested_remedy: claims damages for personal injury resulting from chemical burns to the scalp caused by the 2nd defendant's employee, Barbie
parties: Defendant: LAM WING SHAN trading as NATURAL HAIR TREATMENT CENTRE and NATURAL HAIR TREATMENT CENTRE CO. LIMITED

facts.F1: The plaintiff claims that he was a customer at the 2nd defendant's shop and that on 19 November 2002 his hair was dyed by an employee named Barbie
facts.F2: The plaintiff alleges that he suffered chemical burns to his scalp as a result of the hair dyeing process
facts.F3: The 2nd defendant admits that it operated the shop and employed a person named Barbie, but denies that the plaintiff visited the shop for hair dyeing on 19 November 2002
facts.F4: The 2nd defendant denies that Barbie applied an inappropriate or incorrectly diluted bleach solution, and claims that the plaintiff failed to inform the employee of any allergy or sensitivity to bleach
facts.F5: The plaintiff claims that he was unaware of any allergy or sensitivity and received no advice to test the solution before applying it
facts.F6: The 2nd defendant's shop was open 24 hours a day and was offering a promotional offer where customers could have products applied free of charge by the shop staff
facts.F7: The plaintiff went to the shop with his colleague, Miss Ho, and chose the colours and started to have his hair washed before Miss Ho left
facts.F8: The plaintiff had his hair bleached and dyed, and felt pain and discomfort during and after the process
facts.F9: The plaintiff complained to the employee, Barbie, three times during the process, but she told him to endure it
facts.F10: After the process, the plaintiff went home and washed his hair five times to get rid of the dye marks on his skin, only to find that they were burn wounds stained with dye
facts.F11: The plaintiff went back to the shop and met with the manager, Mr. Alex Chan, who said that the bleach concentration did not need to be so strong
facts.F12: The plaintiff was taken to the Sky One Clinic by Ms Lam and Mr Chan, where he saw a doctor and complained about Barbie's service
facts.F13: The doctor referred the plaintiff to a dermatologist, Dr. Peter Cheung, who diagnosed severe contact dermatitis, most probably caused by strong irritants applied locally
facts.F14: The plaintiff has produced photographs taken by his colleague showing the redness and scab formation on his scalp
facts.F15: The 2nd defendant's representatives changed their stance on the plaintiff's claim once they had a basis for their defence
facts.F16: The plaintiff believed Barbie's assurances and did not want to go home with his hair discoloured

claim: compensation under sections 9, 10 and 10A of the Employees' Compensation Ordinance (Cap 282)
requested_remedy: compensation under sections 9, 10 and 10A of the Employees' Compensation Ordinance (Cap 282)
parties: Defendant: Hon Man Environmental Trading Company Limited

facts.F1: The Applicant, Brar Lakhvir Singh, applied for compensation under the Employees' Compensation Ordinance for an alleged accident on 13th September 2008 while working at Hon Man Environmental Trading Company Limited.
facts.F2: The Respondent challenged the Applicant's claim, stating that the Applicant did not have an accident on 13th September 2008.
facts.F3: The Applicant commenced working for the Respondent on 8th September 2008 with a monthly salary of HK$9,000 and a monthly food allowance of HK$700.
facts.F4: The Applicant's main duty was to operate the compressor machine.
facts.F5: On 13th September 2008, at about 8:10 am, the Applicant's boss asked him to operate the machine again.
facts.F6: At about 10:00 am, while the Applicant was using his right hand to push the plastic scrap into the collection chamber, a Chinese worker who was deaf and dumb touched the machine.
facts.F7: The material part in the Applicant's witness statement described the accident as follows: 'At about 10:00 am, I had filled the collection chamber with plastic scrap and I was using my right hand to push back the plastic scrap into the collection chamber. As I was doing so the other Chinese worker with disability came and without giving me any indication switched on the compressor machine and the compressing board started to move downwards.'
facts.F8: The Applicant's version of the accident was inconsistent with his original claim.
facts.F9: The Respondent's evidence showed that there was no accident on 13th September 2008.
facts.F10: The Applicant took 2 hours of rest after the alleged accident and then cleaned up the place and left at about 7:00 pm.
facts.F11: On 14th September 2008, the Applicant resumed duty as usual with a bandage around his right hand.
facts.F12: The Applicant was told by RW1 that there was no more work for him and he would call him again for work later.
facts.F13: The Applicant then approached RW2, who told him that there was nothing she could do.
facts.F14: The Applicant went to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital (QEH) Accident and Emergency Department on 16th September 2008 for consultation.
facts.F15: Upon examination, there was tenderness over the right wrist, but X-rays showed no bony fracture.
facts.F16: Sick leaves were given for 16th to 19th September 2008.
facts.F17: The Applicant repeatedly attended QEH A & E for treatment and was given sick leaves from time to time until 7th November 2008.
facts.F18: On or about 10th November 2008, the Applicant changed to Yau Ma Tei Jockey Club General Out-patient clinic for treatment and was given sick leaves from time to time until 21st May 2009.
facts.F19: As at the date of the Applicant's statement dated 11th May 2009, he still had pain over his right hand and wrist and he could hardly lift up heavy objects above 5 kg in weight.
facts.F20: The Applicant spent $4,000 on medical expenses.
facts.F21: Dr. Wong's opinion stated that the Applicant's condition was quite static since the first consultation and that he did not have any serious objective pathology.

claim: The plaintiff claims against the defendant for the loss and damage suffered being the value of the goods that Davco had failed to pay in the sum of US$84,240.00. It is alleged by the plaintiff that it had a contract of carriage with the defendant as contained in or evidenced by the cargo receipts and that the defendant had acted in breach of contract in releasing the goods to Davco without the authorisation or consent of the plaintiff or of the consignee in the cargo receipts. Further, it is alleged by the plaintiff that the defendant had acted in breach of its duty as a bailee for reward. Further or in the alternative, the plaintiff claims against the defendant in conversion.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims against the defendant for the loss and damage suffered being the value of the goods that Davco had failed to pay in the sum of US$84,240.00. It is alleged by the plaintiff that it had a contract of carriage with the defendant as contained in or evidenced by the cargo receipts and that the defendant had acted in breach of contract in releasing the goods to Davco without the authorisation or consent of the plaintiff or of the consignee in the cargo receipts. Further, it is alleged by the plaintiff that the defendant had acted in breach of its duty as a bailee for reward. Further or in the alternative, the plaintiff claims against the defendant in conversion.

facts.F1: The plaintiff sold candle holders to Davco Silver Limited in the United States in mid 1999.
facts.F2: The goods were sold on the term of FOB Xingang.
facts.F3: The defendant issued two Forwarder’s Cargo Receipts to the plaintiff, acknowledging that the goods were received by the defendant in apparent good order and condition and that the goods were to be shipped by the vessel as stated in the cargo receipts and on the terms and conditions set out therein.
facts.F4: The plaintiff failed to obtain payment for the goods from Davco under the two letters of credit provided by Davco.
facts.F5: Notwithstanding this, the goods were released to Davco without production of any of the cargo receipts.
facts.F6: The defendant is a freight forwarder.
facts.F7: The plaintiff claims that it had a contract of carriage with the defendant as contained in or evidenced by the cargo receipts.
facts.F8: The defendant contends that it had acted for Davco as the latter’s freight forwarder.
facts.F9: Alternatively, the defendant contends that the plaintiff had acted as the agent of Davco in giving instructions to the defendant to act as the forwarder for the goods.
facts.F10: The plaintiff alleges that the defendant had acted in breach of contract in releasing the goods to Davco without the authorisation or consent of the plaintiff or of the consignee in the cargo receipts.
facts.F11: The plaintiff also alleges that the defendant had acted in breach of its duty as a bailee for reward.
facts.F12: The plaintiff further alleges that the defendant had failed to provide proper details in the two bills of lading in that Davco was wrongly named in the bills of lading as the consignee, contrary to the plaintiff’s instructions.
facts.F13: There is a dispute as to fact in this matter.
facts.F14: The plaintiff had caused the goods to be placed on board the vessels at the loading port.
facts.F15: The plaintiff had arranged with Davco to reserve the right of disposal.
facts.F16: The condition imposed by the seller is to be ascertained to determine whether the seller has indicated his intention to retain a right of disposal.
facts.F17: The seller takes or deals with a shipping document by indicating the manner that the seller imposes a condition.
facts.F18: The form of the shipping document is considered in determining the seller's intention to retain a right of disposal.

claim: RSL seeks declaratory reliefs in relation to the use of a landed property known as the Remaining Portion of Lot No. 714 in Demarcation District 450, Yiu Wing Street, Kwai Chung, New Territories (the Lot), in particular, the use of a columbarium within a Taoist temple erected on the Lot.
requested_remedy: RSL seeks declaratory reliefs in relation to the use of a landed property known as the Remaining Portion of Lot No. 714 in Demarcation District 450, Yiu Wing Street, Kwai Chung, New Territories (the Lot), in particular, the use of a columbarium within a Taoist temple erected on the Lot.

facts.F1: RSL is a Hong Kong company incorporated in September 2007, with 6 corporate shareholders, all but one of them incorporated in the BVI, and one in Macau.
facts.F2: The Lot was acquired by RSL on 3 December 2007 at a cost of HK$116 million, without a mortgage.
facts.F3: RSL submitted building plans for redevelopment as a 'Taoism Place cum meditation rooms' in June 2008.
facts.F4: RSL's representatives were asked about columbarium use in September 2008 and replied negatively in October 2008.
facts.F5: In December 2009, RSL confirmed plans to establish and operate a columbarium on the Lot.
facts.F6: A Taoist temple, Hong Dao Tang (HDT), was erected on the Lot in January 2010, with approximately 26,000 niches for ashes.
facts.F7: The Government has classified HDT as non-compliant with planning requirements under Part B of the Information on Private Columbarium.
facts.F8: The Lot is governed by the terms of New Grant No. 3306, which includes General Condition No. 15 (GC 15) and clause 7(5), both prohibiting human remains on the Lot without consent.
facts.F9: GC 15 and clause 7(5) are relied upon by the Government to prohibit the storage of ashes on the Lot.
facts.F10: Cremation was a known practice in Hong Kong in 1953.
facts.F11: The definition of 'religious institution' and 'columbarium' in the OZP was used for interpretation in this case.
facts.F12: A factual matrix of 1953 was examined to understand the context and purpose of GC 15.

claim: The Plaintiff claims damages for loss suffered as a result of a breach of duty of care by the Defendant.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff claims damages for loss suffered as a result of a breach of duty of care by the Defendant.
parties: Defendant: KIM YI PROPERTY AGENCY LIMITED

facts.F1: In 2007, the Plaintiff, through an introduction by the Defendant, entered into a tenancy agreement (“the Tenancy Agreement”) with Most Choice Investment Limited (“the Landlord”) for a term of 2 years for Shop No.1, Ground Floor, 124-126 Wan Chai Road, Hong Kong (“the shop”), at a monthly rent of $23,800, commencing on 1 October 2007.
facts.F2: The Defendant acted as agent for both the Plaintiff and the Landlord.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff received from the Buildings Department a building order dated 6 December 2007 (“the Building Order”), addressed to the Landlord, to demolish a structure or structures erected on the external wall at the front of the shop.
facts.F4: The location of the unauthorised structure(s) was indicated on an attached plan, as an area hatched black – a rectangular area in front of the shop.
facts.F5: It is the Plaintiff's case that the Building Order related to (1) a structure ('the signboard structure') which extended from the external wall of the building, erected over the front of the shop, whose purpose was to support the installation of a neon light signboard, and (2) a rectangular platform which extended from the floor of the shop at the front on to the pavement, which formed an extension of the floor of the shop ('the floor extension')
facts.F6: After the Plaintiff learned about the Building Order, the Plaintiff contacted the Landlord through the Defendant, and certain negotiations took place between the Plaintiff and the Landlord over the tenancy, which did not result in any agreement.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff then stopped paying rent and vacated the premises after they used up the rental deposit.
facts.F8: Mr Yiu Yau Pik gave evidence for the Plaintiff, stating that he was the manager of the Plaintiff in August 2007, and he was looking for suitable premises for opening a shop for the sale of mobile telephones in Wanchai.
facts.F9: He contacted Miss Ng Sau Ling of the Defendant and accompanied her to view the shop, where he asked her about the floor extension, and she replied that there was no problem with it.
facts.F10: Mr Benson Wong Sai Ning, a building surveyor, gave expert evidence on behalf of the Plaintiff, stating that in his opinion, both the bulkhead and the floor extension would have been unauthorised structures, as they did not form part of the approved building plans for the building.
facts.F11: Miss Ng gave contradictory evidence, stating that she never heard Yiu ask her about the floor extension, and that she did not give the answer Yiu said she gave.
facts.F12: There was no written contract between the Plaintiff and the Defendant.
facts.F13: The Plaintiff did not plead the scope of service agreed between the Plaintiff and the Defendant.
facts.F14: The Defendant, as an estate agent acting for a vendor (including a landlord), was not required to provide the Plaintiff with prescribed information about the property as it was non-residential.

claim: The plaintiff alleged that the bus moved without warning as he was alighting, causing him to fall and sustain injuries.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff alleged that the bus moved without warning as he was alighting, causing him to fall and sustain injuries.
parties: Defendant: Unspecified (China Motor Bus and its driver)

facts.F1: On 11th May 1979, the plaintiff was a passenger on a China Motor Bus that stopped at a bus-stop outside a branch of Overseas Trust Bank.
facts.F2: The plaintiff claimed that as he was about to step off the bus, it moved without warning, causing him to fall and sustain a hip joint fracture.
facts.F3: The plaintiff was taken to the Tang Shiu Kin Hospital and later transferred to the Tung Wah Hospital, where he was diagnosed with tuberculosis as a result of silicosis.
facts.F4: The plaintiff spent 46 days in hospital and attended as an outpatient at the Sai Ying Pun Jockey Club Clinic.
facts.F5: He used two crutches for 3 months and has been using one crutch since then.
facts.F6: The plaintiff's medical reports indicated a 16% impairment of his right leg and 6% impairment of the Whole Man.
facts.F7: The plaintiff's right leg is half an inch shorter than his left, and he experiences pain in his right hip and right knee 4/5 times a day.
facts.F8: The plaintiff's employer testified that he would have worked for a year and a half had he not met with the accident, and would have earned $100-160 per day.
facts.F9: The plaintiff's medical condition was complicated by his pre-existing tuberculosis and silicosis.
facts.F10: There were four passengers behind the plaintiff when he alighted the bus.
facts.F11: The plaintiff was not the last passenger to alight the bus.
facts.F12: An independent witness, Mr. Chu, testified in favor of the driver's account of the incident.
facts.F13: A driver testified that the bus had not moved after it had stopped at the bus-stop.

facts.F1: The alleged accident occurred on the morning of 24 August 2009 inside the parking area of Sheung Wing House, Upper Ngau Tau Kok Estate.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was employed as a Senior Police Constable by the Hong Kong Police Force and was attached to the Sau Mau Ping District Headquarter Squad 1.
facts.F3: The 1st defendant was responsible for the management of the Upper Ngau Tau Kok Estate, including the place of the alleged accident.
facts.F4: The 2nd defendant was the property management company providing property management services to the Upper Ngau Tau Kok Estate, including the place of the alleged accident.
facts.F5: On the morning of the alleged accident, the plaintiff was on duty and walking across the parking area to the Upper Ngau Tau Kok Temporary Police Station with his colleague.
facts.F6: A plan of the area was produced, showing the path that the plaintiff and his colleague would take to reach the Temporary Police Station.
facts.F7: Photographs were taken of the location, showing a drain covered by a long continuous metal grille.
facts.F8: There were boards placed on the kerb of the pavement to enable wheeled carts to access the pavement from the road surface.
facts.F9: The edges of the boards looked frayed and worse from wear and tear, but the surfaces remained smooth.
facts.F10: There were piles of sand at the end of the car park, and construction work was being carried out at the estate.
facts.F11: A CCTV recording showed the events of the alleged accident, including the plaintiff walking towards the pavement, stepping on one of the boards, and falling forward.
facts.F12: The plaintiff did not get up after falling and was later taken to the hospital.
facts.F13: The plaintiff gave a statement to the police on 15 January 2010, stating that he stepped onto something on the kerb and fell, and had not lost consciousness.
facts.F14: The plaintiff's left foot did not slip on the board, but rather his right foot gave way as he was stepping forward.
facts.F15: The plaintiff had back problems and issues with his superiors, which raised suspicion about the accidental nature of his fall.

facts.F2: The Plaintiffs agreed to purchase the flats for the same price as Country Wide's purchase price from Overture Co. Ltd., plus a 'position queuing fee' of $160,000 for each flat.
facts.F3: Country Wide failed to pay the balance of the purchase price on the due date (February 26, 1991) and the interest on the overdue balance.
facts.F4: The Plaintiffs and Country Wide entered into provisional sale and purchase agreements on March 11, 1991, with completion to take place on March 12, 1991.
facts.F5: However, on March 12, 1991, the developer, Overture Co. Ltd., refused to allow the change of names unless the balance of the purchase price and the accrued interest were paid.
facts.F6: On March 13, 1991, Country Wide sold the same flats to Tam Ho Yin and Tsui Yim Chu (the second and third Defendants) with completion due on March 23, 1991.
facts.F7: The Plaintiffs registered their provisional agreements at the Land Office on March 16, 1991, after learning about the sale to Tam and Tsui.
facts.F8: Tam and Tsui had already taken possession of the flats and made significant financial commitments.

claim: claims made by the plaintiff under the Fatal Accidents Ordinance and Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance
requested_remedy: claims made by the plaintiff under the Fatal Accidents Ordinance and Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance
parties: Plaintiff: Chan Lan Hing's widower, administrator of the estate of Chan Lan (or Lin) Hing

facts.F1: Chan Lan Hing was killed in a road accident on 11th July 1969 while travelling as a passenger in a car driven by Lo Cheung Hung, deceased.
facts.F2: The accident was caused by the negligence of Lo Cheung Hung, deceased.
facts.F3: The plaintiff is the widower of Chan Lan Hing and the administrator of her estate.
facts.F4: The plaintiff and the deceased had three children, Tam Chi Ho, Tam Chi Wai, and Tam Chi Man, who were aged 14, 11, and 4.5 years old respectively at the time of the accident.
facts.F5: The deceased was 35 years old at the time of her death.
facts.F6: The plaintiff worked as a taxi driver and earned around $1,000 per month, but this was not sufficient to support the family.
facts.F7: The deceased occasionally worked at a garment factory and contributed around $300 per month to the family expenses.
facts.F8: After the deceased's death, the plaintiff gave up his full-time taxi driving job to look after the children and started working part-time as a taxi driver and a dentist's technician, earning around $600 per month.
facts.F9: The plaintiff employed someone to look after the youngest child for 13 months, but had to stop due to financial difficulties.
facts.F10: The deceased made clothes for her children and managed the household, so the plaintiff did not need to employ any household help while she was alive.
facts.F11: The plaintiff claimed funeral expenses of $1,687, but was only awarded $1,723 after deductions.
facts.F12: The number of dependents in the family was reduced by one after the deceased's death.
facts.F13: The dependants would receive a lump sum when the children came of age.
facts.F14: The plaintiff had the possibility of remarrying in the future.

facts.F9: MO Fat, who was cycling behind the plaintiffs, corroborated the second plaintiff's account of the accident.

claim: The plaintiff seeks to tax bills issued by the defendant to the plaintiff.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff seeks to tax bills issued by the defendant to the plaintiff.
parties: Plaintiff: plaintiff (name not mentioned in the judgment)
Defendant: defendant (name not mentioned in the judgment), a firm of solicitors

facts.F1: The plaintiff was the sole shareholder and a creditor of a company called Pioneer Iron & Steel Group Company (PSG) incorporated in the British Virgin Islands.
facts.F2: PSG had been placed into voluntary liquidation since late June 2010.
facts.F3: The defendant was a firm of solicitors practicing in Hong Kong which ceased practice on 1 March 2012 upon its merger with another firm of solicitors.
facts.F4: Prior to October 2010, Messrs Deacons acted for the plaintiff in respect of the PSG Matter.
facts.F5: On 30 September 2010, the plaintiff met Ms Cindy Wong, a consultant of the defendant, to discuss whether the defendant could provide assistance to the plaintiff in the PSG Matter.
facts.F6: On 6 October 2010, Ms Wong sent a copy of the defendant's retainer letter (Retainer Letter) to the plaintiff.
facts.F7: The plaintiff signed and returned the Retainer Letter to the defendant on 8 October 2010 without amendment.
facts.F8: By a bill numbered B2010K0242 dated 29 November 2010 (1st Bill), the defendant charged the plaintiff $3,900,000 as its profit costs and $1,358,373 as disbursements for the period from 28 September 2010 to 6 November 2010.
facts.F9: By a bill numbered B2011D0610 dated 29 April 2011 (2nd Bill), the defendant charged the plaintiff $5,129,973.50 as disbursements.
facts.F10: By a bill numbered B2011E0098 dated 16 May 2011 (3rd Bill), the defendant charged the plaintiff $2,200,000 as its profit costs (Agreed Costs) and $1,438,304 as disbursements covering the period from 7 November 2010 to 16 May 2011.
facts.F11: Miss Wong left the defendant's employment on 18 May 2011
facts.F12: On 24 June 2011, the defendant wrote to Tang & So (T&S), the then solicitors acting for the plaintiff, alleging that there were balance fees payable by the plaintiff to the defendant.
facts.F13: The defendant said that such fees had been written off by Miss Wong without authority.
facts.F14: On 29 December 2011, the plaintiff received a bill numbered B2011E0098(A) dated 17 June 2011 (4th Bill) from the defendant charging the plaintiff additional profit costs in the sum of $7,959,975 (Additional Costs) for the period from 7 November 2010 to 16 May 2011 (i.e. the same period as covered by the 3rd Bill).
facts.F15: On 27 January 2012, the plaintiff commenced these proceedings seeking an order to refer the 1st to 4th Bills to taxation.
facts.F16: The plaintiff filed six affirmations in these proceedings.
facts.F17: Substantial costs had been incurred by the parties for the trial of the Preliminary Issues.

claim: claims for arrears of salary and expenses
requested_remedy: claims for arrears of salary and expenses
parties: Defendant: Regent Ken International Limited and MS International Investments Limited

facts.F1: The plaintiff claims he entered into a contract of employment with the 2nd defendant, MS International Investments Limited, or the 1st defendant, Regent Ken International Limited, or both, as a management consultant.
facts.F2: The defendants claim that the plaintiff was employed by Shenzhen Sundarb Glass Company, a mainland firm controlled by Mr LIONG.
facts.F3: The plaintiff relies on a letter dated 10 January 1995, which sets out payments due for January, February, March, and April 1995.
facts.F4: Mr LIONG agrees that he received the letter and wrote on it his signature and the date, 10 January 1995, and bracketed a number of figures, which were variations to some extent of the figures on the original letter.
facts.F5: The plaintiff was paid for a period of time, but the payments started to slip, and by September 1995, there was a significant deficit or arrears in respect of the money due to him under contract.
facts.F6: The plaintiff rendered accounts to Regent Ken, which bore the address of the company in Hong Kong, but the accounts were handed to Mr LIONG or somebody in his employment in Shenzhen.
facts.F7: The plaintiff worked for Regent Ken International Limited, who took upon the obligation of paying him for his work, and invoices and statements of account were rendered to Regent Ken.
facts.F8: The plaintiff gave notice of termination of employment to Mr LIONG on 3 March 1996, stating that the amount due to him was HK$139,329.
facts.F9: Mr LIONG denied seeing any statements of account or invoices referred to by the plaintiff, and claimed that Mr Christensen owed money to Sundarb.
facts.F10: The written contract was with the 2nd defendant, MS International Investments Limited, but there was an oral variation which substituted Regent Ken International Limited as the employer of the plaintiff.
facts.F11: Regent Ken International Limited took upon the obligation of paying the plaintiff for his work through some loose arrangement between the two companies as to who actually employed the plaintiff.
facts.F12: The plaintiff and the defendants were in a dispute over whether the plaintiff was employed by Regent Ken International Limited, MS International Investments Limited, or both.

claim: The plaintiff submits that the word 'pigeon' does not include racing pigeons, because a racing pigeon is not poultry.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff submits that the word 'pigeon' does not include racing pigeons, because a racing pigeon is not poultry.
parties: Plaintiff: Hong Kong Racing Pigeon Association

facts.F1: The members of the plaintiff engage in the sport of racing pigeons, which involves pigeons flying long distances, sometimes over 1000 kilometres to China and other countries.
facts.F2: The racing pigeons are expensive, with pedigree birds costing up to HK$20,000.00 and unhatched eggs costing about $1,000.00 each.
facts.F3: The racing pigeons are generally kept in well-maintained lofts and in good conditions.
facts.F4: A number of the birds get lost on the long-distance races and some are killed, therefore it is necessary for the members to keep a substantial number of racing pigeons.
facts.F5: The problem which has arisen in this case is that by virtue of the Waste Disposal Ordinance, Cap. 354, the keeping of pigeons in certain urban areas is restricted.
facts.F6: Section 15 of the Waste Disposal Ordinance provides that no person shall keep 'livestock' at any premises in a 'livestock prohibition areas' (which generally covers the urban areas).
facts.F7: A contravention of Section 15 is an offence.
facts.F8: The word 'livestock' is defined in Section 2 as meaning 'pigs or poultry', and the word 'poultry' means 'chickens, ducks, geese, pigeons and quail'.
facts.F9: The legislative debate on the Waste Disposal Ordinance shows that the purpose of the Ordinance was to restrict large farming operations taking place in the urban areas and which provided food for the people of Hong Kong.
facts.F10: Racing pigeons are not kept for food.
facts.F11: Other legislation in Hong Kong, such as the Public Health (Animals and Birds) Ordinance, utilizes the same definition of 'poultry'.
facts.F12: The intention of the legislature was to restrict large farming operations taking place in the urban areas which provided food for the people of Hong Kong.

claim: recovery of possession of domestic premises due to reasonable requirement for her own occupation
requested_remedy: recovery of possession of domestic premises due to reasonable requirement for her own occupation

facts.F1: The premises were let to the Defendant for a term of 2 years, commencing on January 1st 1978, at a monthly rental of $630.
facts.F2: The tenancy agreement contains a clause appearing to give the Defendant an option to continue the tenancy at the end of the agreed term, but the Defendant failed to give the required written notice.
facts.F3: The tenancy expired on December 31, 1979 by effluxion of time.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff seeks to recover the premises on the ground that she requires them for her own occupation.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff gave oral notice of her intention to recover the premises to the Defendant on several occasions, but did not provide written notice.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff has lived with her aunt and a former 'clansman's' widow since August or September 1979 due to ill health and the termination of her employment as an amah.
facts.F7: The Defendant lives in the premises with her mother and younger sister, and intended to get married in March 1980.
facts.F8: The Defendant was unable to find alternative accommodation within their means.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff had close to 12 months' notice of the Defendant's intention to recover the premises.
facts.F10: The Defendant had enough time to find alternative accommodation but was unable to do so within their means.

facts.F2: The applicants engaged the services of Public Communication Strategic Consultancy Limited (PCSC) to run their election campaign.
facts.F3: Each applicant appointed their own election agent and election expense agent, with 3 of them being employees of PCSC.

claim: Damages against all five defendants for conspiracy to deceive or to defraud the Plaintiff, damages against each of them for negligence, damages against the 1st and 2nd Defendants for fraudulent misrepresentation, damages for breach of contract against the 2nd Defendant
requested_remedy: Damages against all five defendants for conspiracy to deceive or to defraud the Plaintiff, damages against each of them for negligence, damages against the 1st and 2nd Defendants for fraudulent misrepresentation, damages for breach of contract against the 2nd Defendant
parties: Plaintiff: The Plaintiff (a company incorporated in New Zealand)

Defendant: 1st Defendant, 2nd Defendant, 3rd Defendant (a corporation incorporated in Panama), 4th Defendant (a foreign corporation carrying on business in Hong Kong), and 5th Defendant (the president of the 3rd Defendant company and a director and manager of the 4th Defendant)

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was in the market for a few hundred tonnes of paraffin wax in early 1979.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff was a regular buyer from China, but at that time China was not in a position to supply, and it directed its attention to an associated company in Singapore managed by Jimmy Ong.
facts.F3: Mr. Ong contacted a Mr. Lui, who introduced him to the 1st Defendant in Singapore.
facts.F4: The 1st Defendant offered to sell 350 tonnes of China paraffin wax semi-refined at US$580 per tonne C. & F. New Zealand.
facts.F5: The offer was orally accepted by the Plaintiff through its Singapore associates.
facts.F6: A letter of credit was opened in favour of Trisonda (Pte) Ltd. in Singapore.
facts.F7: The 1st Defendant did not have the goods to sell and made excuses about increase in prices and freight rates.
facts.F8: The 1st Defendant introduced the 2nd Defendant, who claimed to have a partner who could ship the goods from Hong Kong.
facts.F9: A new letter of credit was opened in favour of Sandler Textiles in Hong Kong.
facts.F10: The 2nd Defendant negotiated the letter of credit with fraudulent documents.
facts.F11: The shipment was purported to have been made on board a motor vessel called the Tonga, but the Tonga was never in Hong Kong.
facts.F12: The 3rd, 4th, and 5th Defendants were involved in the conspiracy, with the 5th Defendant issuing a false bill of lading.
facts.F13: The defendants' actions were overt acts of conspiracy.
facts.F14: The Plaintiff would have been in a different position if the representations had not been made.

claim: The return of a sum of money paid as initial deposit for the purchase of a property and/or damages for breach of contract, and/or for misrepresentation
requested_remedy: The return of a sum of money paid as initial deposit for the purchase of a property and/or damages for breach of contract, and/or for misrepresentation

facts.F1: The registered owner of a property in Repulse Bay entered into a Provisional Sale and Purchase Agreement ('the 1st Provisional Sale and Purchase Agreement') to sell the property to the Defendant on 2 November 1997.
facts.F2: The purchase price was $22m.  The agreement was delivered on 8 January 1998 for registration at the Land Registry.
facts.F3: It had not been registered by the Land Registry by 19 March 1998.
facts.F4: In early March 1998, the Plaintiff became interested in the property and instructed its agent to conduct a land search which showed the date, the parties and the consideration in respect of the 1st Provisional Sale and Purchase Agreement.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff assumed that the 1st Provisional Sale and Purchase, like most provisional agreements, contained 'escape clauses' whereby the parties are given 'an option to back out'.
facts.F6: The Purchaser signed a Provisional Sale and Purchase Agreement ('the 2nd Provisional Sale and Purchase Agreement') offering to purchase the property for $20.58m on 7 March 1998.
facts.F7: The escape clauses in this agreement were deleted and the Purchaser drew a cheque for $700,000 as initial deposit.
facts.F8: On 12 March 1998, the Purchaser's solicitors told the Purchaser that the Confirmor's solicitors had said that no formal Agreement had yet been signed between the registered owner and the Confirmor.
facts.F9: On 14 March 1998, the Purchaser's solicitors wrote to the Confirmor's solicitors asking for the 1st Provisional Sale and Purchase Agreement 'as soon as possible'.
facts.F10: On 16 March 1998, the Purchaser's solicitors wrote a letter asserting the existence of the contract and propounding rights under it.
facts.F11: The Purchaser did not rescind, nor was it intending or considering rescission of, the 2nd Provisional Sale and Purchase Agreement on the ground of misrepresentation.
facts.F12: On 16 March 1998, the Purchaser's solicitors wrote a letter which led to the Purchaser's issue of the writ.
facts.F13: The letter of 16 March 1998 was an unequivocal election by the Purchaser to affirm the contract.
facts.F14: There are no serious material factual disputes in the present case.
facts.F15: The Confirmor did not have any obligation to deduce title at that stage.

lawsuit_type: Application for summary judgment on Counterclaim and to strike out the Plaintiff’s claim

claim: The plaintiff claims for the return of HK$27,000 and disputes the alleged losses and liability for the variation margin calls.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims for the return of HK$27,000 and disputes the alleged losses and liability for the variation margin calls.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was told by YIM Ming about his profit position on 28th October, 1978.
facts.F2: The plaintiff told YIM Ming that he wished to terminate his account and withdraw HK$27,000 on 29th October, 1978.
facts.F3: YIM Ming requested a written notice, and the plaintiff wrote a document in Chinese at YIM Ming's dictation on 30th October, 1978.
facts.F4: YIM Ming told the plaintiff that the document was an informal notice and promised to provide a formal notice form the next day, but failed to do so.
facts.F5: The plaintiff made attempts to contact YIM Ming from 31st October, 1978, but was unsuccessful.
facts.F6: The plaintiff saw his solicitors on 8th November, 1978, and they sent a letter to the defendant on 10th November, 1978, demanding the return of HK$27,000.
facts.F7: The defendant's manager, LAU Mei-kan, gave evidence that the defendant could have closed the plaintiff's account on 3rd November, 1978, due to non-payment of the variation margin call, but did not take action.
facts.F8: A customer could close their account by giving oral or written notice to the defendant's agent.
facts.F9: YIM Ming was not called to give evidence.
facts.F10: The plaintiff did not enter into any further transactions after giving notice on 30th October, 1978.

parties: Plaintiff: ['Wong Chi-wai, Dominic (1st plaintiff)', "N/A (2nd plaintiff suing by mother and next friend, Wong Chi-wai, Dominic's crumbling information on the second victim does not provide any data on the name of the second plaintiff)"]

facts.F1: On 22 April 1998, the 1st and 2nd plaintiffs were attacked by a pack of dogs while walking up the staircase in a residential building at No. 29 Tai Ha Street, Tai Wo Hau in Tsuen Wan, New Territories.
facts.F2: The 1st plaintiff was running an errand with the 2nd plaintiff and her elder sister when the attack occurred.
facts.F3: The defendant, Chu Shiu-chuen, was the owner of the dogs and was eventually summoned and convicted of various offences related to the incident.
facts.F4: Both plaintiffs were sent to the Accident & Emergency Department of Yan Chai Hospital for treatment.
facts.F5: The 1st plaintiff sustained multiple abrasions, laceration wounds, and puncture scars over both upper and lower limbs, as well as post-traumatic stress disorder and a phobia of dogs.
facts.F6: The 2nd plaintiff, who was 4 years old at the time of the attack, suffered three laceration wounds over both thighs and multiple minor bite and scratch marks over her thighs and left arm.
facts.F7: The incident had a profound psychological impact on both plaintiffs, with the 1st plaintiff becoming tense, worried, and suffering from depressive mood, and the 2nd plaintiff developing a phobia of dogs.
facts.F8: Both plaintiffs received medical treatment and were prescribed analgesics, antibiotics, and anti-rabies vaccinations.
facts.F9: The 1st plaintiff underwent psychiatric counselling and treatment, and Dr. Peter Ho Pang-nin diagnosed her with post-traumatic stress disorder and a phobia of dogs.
facts.F10: Dr. Ian Nicholson, a plastic surgeon, assessed the 1st plaintiff's permanent cosmetic disability at 5%.
facts.F11: The 1st plaintiff's loss of earnings and earning capacity was linked to her phobia of dogs and desire to avoid employment with dogs.
facts.F12: The defendant was absent and did not participate in the proceedings.
facts.F13: The plaintiffs' claims were largely unopposed.
