facts.F1: On the 28th of February 1982, the 1st Defendant was driving a coach back to Tuen Mun from Lok Ma Chau with a party of children who had been out on a day’s excursion.
facts.F2: The coach was owned by the 2nd Defendant who was also the 1st Defendant’s employer.

facts.F6: The coach was proceeding along a straight stretch of the road possibly a little in excess of the speed limit of 40 miles per hour.
facts.F7: The coach was travelling in the fast or outer lane, and in that lane there was other traffic about 2 coach lengths ahead of it.
facts.F8: In the inner lane, there was a vehicle about 10 to 20 feet ahead and between that vehicle and the coach there was a blue car travelling a little faster than the coach.
facts.F9: Suddenly, that blue car, which did not subsequently stop and has not been traced, cut into the fast lane some 6 to 8 feet ahead of the coach.
facts.F10: The 1st Defendant reacted to it by braking and swerving a little to his right.
facts.F11: The coach then skidded across the central reservation, colliding with the public light bus.
facts.F12: The evidence led by the Defendants does not establish that the gap between the blue car and the vehicle ahead of it in the inner lane was being closed.
facts.F13: The distances testified to by various witnesses must be regarded as very approximate.
facts.F14: The road conditions were wet and slippery.
facts.F15: Inconsiderate drivers frequently cut lanes on the road.
facts.F16: Public light buses stop on the inner lane to pick up and drop passengers.

claim: The Applicant seeks an Order of Certiorari quashing the Decision and an Order of mandamus requiring the Authority to approve or reconsider the plans which were submitted.
requested_remedy: The Applicant seeks an Order of Certiorari quashing the Decision and an Order of mandamus requiring the Authority to approve or reconsider the plans which were submitted.

facts.F1: The Applicant submitted building plans to the Building Authority for approval for the redevelopment of Nos. 15 & 17 Sands Street, Hong Kong.
facts.F2: The plans proposed a 26-storey domestic building, but the Building Authority refused to give its approval on the ground that the carrying out of the works shown thereon would result in a building differing in height from the building previously existing on the same site.
facts.F3: The Building Authority's decision was contained in a letter dated 28th November 1991.
facts.F4: The Authority's main objection to the plans was that the density of development contemplated was excessive due to limited vehicular access to the site.
facts.F5: The Applicant argued that the Authority had exceeded its powers by taking into account fire and other safety requirements which were not matters for consideration under section 16(1)(g) of the Buildings Ordinance.
facts.F6: The Applicant also argued that the Authority had usurped the functions or powers of the Director of Fire Services and the Town Planning Board.
facts.F7: The Applicant obtained evidence from the Fire Services Department, which certified that the plans were acceptable subject to certain conditions, and that the Department had considered the surrounding circumstances, including the lack of vehicular access to the site.
facts.F8: The Authority's decision was based on a policy decision promulgated in a circular in 1974, which stated that no buildings higher than existing buildings would be approved where access was limited.
facts.F9: Section 16(1)(g) of the Buildings Ordinance gave the Authority wide discretions to consider factors such as the safety of people in and around a building.
facts.F10: Each body, including the Building Authority, the Director of Fire Services and the Town Planning Board, had a different perspective and role in the process.

facts.F1: The plaintiff and the first defendant engaged in a joint venture to operate a merchant vessel called Quarry Bay trading between ports in the Far East and the Middle East over a period of eight months
facts.F2: The basis of the venture was that they would share the profits realised from freight charges levied in respect of goods shipped between these ports
facts.F3: On January 14, 1977, they entered into a charter-party agreement with a firm known as Narcissus to charter the Quarry Bay for an eight-month period
facts.F4: On the same date, they also entered into an agreement between each other setting out their mutual obligations and liabilities as to the operation and management of the vessel and the manner in which the freight earnings would be shared between them
facts.F5: Clauses 2 and 3 of the agreement between the plaintiff and the first defendant were submitted as evidence
facts.F6: The vessel proceeded to Taiwan and took on a cargo which earned a payment in freight of about US$155,000 after which she left Kaoshiung, Taiwan on January 26 for Pusan in South Korea to receive further cargo
facts.F7: Between January 26 and February 7, the plaintiff became increasingly concerned that as yet no money had been deposited in the joint account in accordance with Clause 2 of the agreement
facts.F8: Between February 1 and 7, a series of telex messages passed between the parties and their agents in Taiwan, Korea, and Hong Kong concerning the absence of such payments
facts.F9: In one of these communications, the plaintiff was informed that a partial remittance amounting to US$48,000 was to be paid into a certain bank account at the Banque Nationale De Paris in Hong Kong
facts.F10: The plaintiff was not aware who owned the account, leading to the second, third, and fourth defendants being brought in as parties to the original application for interim relief
facts.F11: The account belonged to the second defendant, leading to the proceedings against the third and fourth defendants being discontinued on March 11, 1977
facts.F12: Since no result favourable to the plaintiff had come about as a result of these exchanges, the application for interim injunctions was made on February 25

PERN, BRETAGNE, THE ATTORNEY GENERAL

facts.F1: The Trustee of the Will of Wu Chan Alice Martha seeks to vary the trusts created by her Will dated 13 August 1974 and two Codicils dated 13 March 1975 and 27 October 1976.
facts.F2: The beneficial interests under the trusts are vested in the 1st and 2nd Defendants (the settled legacy), and the 3rd, 4th, 5th Defendants and the Attorney General (the Residuary Estate) for the benefit of Hong Kong charities.
facts.F3: The Will provides for the automatic appointment of an Emergency Trustee if Hong Kong ceases to be part of the British Commonwealth, which would result in the Trust being managed in Canada and subject to Canadian tax laws.
facts.F4: The Testatrix suffered from ill health and senile dementia from the mid-80s and did not alter the provisions of her Will after the Sino-British Agreement in 1984.
facts.F5: The Attorney General represents the unascertained beneficiaries under paras.(i) and (iv) of Clause 8(c) and supports the proposed variation.
facts.F6: The proposed variation avoids the fiscal disadvantages and administrative difficulties that would arise if the Trust were to be managed in Canada.
facts.F7: The Testatrix’s intention was to benefit Hong Kong charities, as evidenced by the Will as a whole.

facts.F1: The Plaintiffs were the vendors of the property, namely Flat H on 22nd floor, Block 31 of Laguna City, Kowloon (the Property) and the Defendant was the purchaser under an Agreement for Sale and Purchase dated 2nd March 1998 (the Agreement, Exh. P4).
facts.F2: The Defendant had, pursuant to the Agreement, paid deposit and part-payment for the total sum of HK$508,000.00.
facts.F3: The Defendant had failed to pay the balance of the purchaser price for the sum of HK$4,572,000.00 on the date of completion on 16th June 1998.
facts.F4: The Plaintiffs had, on 17th June 1998, through their solicitors given notice to the solicitors acting for the Defendant to terminate the Agreement.

facts.F7: On 13 July 1998, through Centaline, the new purchasers were introduced to the Plaintiffs and they had signed the agreement for the sale of the Property to the new purchasers for the price of HK$3,600,000.00 (see Exh.P7).

claim: Declaration that the contract dated 9 September 2006 is voidable due to misrepresentations made by the defendants and damages to be assessed
requested_remedy: Declaration that the contract dated 9 September 2006 is voidable due to misrepresentations made by the defendants and damages to be assessed
parties: Plaintiff: K & M JEWELLERY COMPANY LIMITED
Defendant: COLOUR SILVER TECHNOLOGY COMPANY LIMITED and PANG SIU CHUNG

facts.F1: The plaintiff, K & M Jewellery Company Limited, is a Hong Kong company that manufactures, trades, and distributes low and middle-priced karat gold jewellery.
facts.F2: The 1st defendant, Colour Silver Technology Company Limited, is a Hong Kong company that manufactures, trades, and distributes chemicals for electroformed and electroplating jewellery pieces.
facts.F3: The 2nd defendant, Pang Siu Chung, is the director and shareholder of the 1st defendant and was involved in the development of electroforming techniques.
facts.F4: The plaintiff and the 1st defendant entered into a contract on 9 September 2006, which included an agreement to purchase chemicals from the 1st defendant for the production of electroformed jewellery.
facts.F5: The contract also included a clause that the validity of the contract was founded on the successful application of a US patent for a new electroforming technique.
facts.F6: The new technique was allegedly invented by Pang Siu Chung and was the subject of the misrepresentations made by the defendants.
facts.F7: The plaintiff relied on these representations in entering into the contract and purchasing the chemicals from the 1st defendant.
facts.F8: However, the plaintiff subsequently discovered that the new technique was not commercially viable for mass production and that the representations made by the defendants were untrue.
facts.F9: Tong Kwok Kwong, the managing director of the plaintiff, relied on the representations made by Pang in entering into the contract.
facts.F10: Chong Lung Sam, an expert in chemistry, testified that the new technique was not commercially viable for mass production due to two significant defects.
facts.F11: Pang owed a duty of care to the plaintiff in advising and recommending the new technique and failed in this duty by failing to inform the plaintiff of the defects in the new technique.
facts.F12: The issue of the writ in HC Action No. 2467 of 2006 on 9 November 2006 validly rescinded the contract.

requested_remedy: Damages against the first and second defendants for breach of contract, damages against the third defendant for conspiracy, and a decree of specific performance of the service agreement
parties: Plaintiff: The plaintiffs (part of a partnership including the first defendant)
Defendant: First, Second and Third defendants

facts.F1: The plaintiffs and the first defendant were partners in a business venture.
facts.F2: The first defendant refused to bring an action as a plaintiff, so the plaintiffs joined him as a defendant.
facts.F3: The third defendant, a company, owned a property called Diamond House.
facts.F4: The third defendant employed the first and second defendants as managers of Diamond House for seven years under an agreement dated December 30th.
facts.F5: The agreement between the third defendant and the first and second defendants provided for the managers to run the boarding house as if it were their own, with profits and losses split accordingly.
facts.F6: The agreement also guaranteed the third defendant $5,000 per month and specified that the first and second defendants were not sublessees or licensees of the third defendant.
facts.F7: The plaintiffs, along with the first defendant, entered into a service agreement with the first and second defendants on January 19th, 1968, to finance the management of Diamond House.
facts.F8: The agreement stated that profits would be shared among the members of the partnership after the first and second defendants paid the third defendant $5,000 per month.
facts.F9: The arrangement was set to last for seven years, and all parties signed the agreement, except the third defendant.
facts.F10: The plaintiffs claim damages against the first and second defendants for breach of the service agreement and against the third defendant for conspiracy.
facts.F11: The plaintiffs also sought a decree of specific performance of the service agreement.
facts.F12: The plaintiffs accepted the first defendant's resignation.
facts.F13: The second defendant was not employed as a manager of Diamond House.
facts.F14: The third defendant reassumed management of Diamond House when the first defendant resigned.
facts.F15: The third defendant never parted with possession of the premises.

claim: claims for compensation pursuant to the Employees’ Compensation Ordinance
requested_remedy: claims for compensation pursuant to the Employees’ Compensation Ordinance
parties: Defendant: Pine Logistics Company Limited (加林美物流有限公司)

facts.F1: Pine Logistics was a subcontractor of container hauling services at Container Terminal No.9, Tsing Yi, New Territories
facts.F2: The applicant (Hui) started working for Pine Logistics as a container tractor driver in July 2007
facts.F3: On 7 September 2007, while he was in the course of work, a traffic accident happened and he was injured
facts.F4: Hui was provided some safety training records of the container terminal to sign
facts.F5: He was informed of the terms of his work and pay
facts.F6: He was asked to sign a written service agreement
facts.F7: Hui was also asked whether he had a mandatory provident fund account
facts.F8: As requested, Hui also gave HK$840, as Hui understood, for the purpose of the company arranging insurance for him
facts.F9: Pine Logistics employed captains to liaise with the drivers needed
facts.F10: The captains would contact the drivers to come to work and it would be up to the drivers to decide whether to take the job
facts.F11: Pine Logistics provided all the container tractors that the drivers drove
facts.F12: The fuel came from a supplier nominated by its main contractor
facts.F13: The drivers had to follow the instructions sent to them via their pagers during work
facts.F14: The demand for container hauling service by its main contractor varied substantially daily
facts.F15: It was therefore flexible and cost-effective to engage the drivers as self-employed
facts.F16: However, the arrangement was changed in June 2008, and all the drivers of Pine Logistics have ceased to work as self-employed but are now contracted as employees
facts.F17: There was a lack of real bargaining between Pine Logistics and the drivers in the service agreements
facts.F18: The service agreements were already prepared and dictated by Pine Logistics

claim: The Applicant sought a declaratory order that the 1994 increase and/or the 1995 increase were void ab initio and of no effect. They were in breach of the mandatory provisions implied into the DMC by Section 34E of the Building Management Ordinance, Cap.344 (BMO), and Paragraph 1 of the Seventh Schedule of the same Ordinance. They were also inconsistent with the provisions of Clause D3 of Section V of the DMC. The Applicant also asked for a declaratory order for the proper calculation, apportionment and determination of the monthly management fees payable by the Applicant for the Ground floor and Third floor.
requested_remedy: The Applicant sought a declaratory order that the 1994 increase and/or the 1995 increase were void ab initio and of no effect. They were in breach of the mandatory provisions implied into the DMC by Section 34E of the Building Management Ordinance, Cap.344 (BMO), and Paragraph 1 of the Seventh Schedule of the same Ordinance. They were also inconsistent with the provisions of Clause D3 of Section V of the DMC. The Applicant also asked for a declaratory order for the proper calculation, apportionment and determination of the monthly management fees payable by the Applicant for the Ground floor and Third floor.
parties: Defendant: Retail Warehouses Limited, Wofoo Property Management Limited

facts.F1: The Applicant has been the owner of the Ground floor and Third floor of the Watson Building since 10th May 1985.
facts.F2: The first Respondent (R1) was the registered owner of the whole of the Building until 17th March 1982, when it assigned the 13th floor of the Building to a second owner.
facts.F3: A Deed of Mutual Covenant (DMC) was executed and registered in the Tsuen Wan New Territories Land Registry under Memorial Number 248727 and later re-registered under Memorial Number 267737.
facts.F4: Under the DMC, R1 was appointed to be the first manager of the Building for a term of seven years from 17th March 1982, and thereafter until the termination of the appointment.
facts.F5: There are a total of 402,475 undivided shares in the building, with the Ground floor allotted 75,000 shares and the Third floor allotted 30,631 shares.
facts.F6: There is no incorporation of owners, nor is there an owners’ committee.
facts.F7: The second Respondent (R2) took over the management of the Building, although there was no formal documentary evidence to that effect.
facts.F8: The Applicant accepts that R2 is the de facto manager.
facts.F9: R1 and R2 have common directors and shareholders.
facts.F10: On 27th March 1997, R1 sold off all its remaining interest in the Building to Grace Magic Limited.
facts.F11: The Applicant was under the impression that previous increases in management fees were on account of inflation.
facts.F12: On 1st October 1994, the monthly management fees for the Ground floor were increased to $6,000 from $4,922.28, and that for the Third floor was increased to $11,400 from $9,424.88 (the 1994 increase).
facts.F13: On 1st December 1995, the management fees for the Ground floor were increased to $37,500 per month, and that for the Third floor was increased to $15,315.50 (the 1995 increase).
facts.F14: The Applicant protested against the 1995 increase by a letter dated 18th December 1995 addressed to R2.
facts.F15: The Applicant demanded to see the accounts relating to the Building’s expenses, and statements of income and expenditure, under Section V Section H of the DMC.
facts.F16: None of the procedures required under the BMO for increase of management fees had been followed.
facts.F17: The Respondents produced certain accounts, including audited financial statements, bank statements, and management fee receipts.
facts.F18: The auditors’ report stated that a proper system of internal accounting control had not been in place for the periods in question.
facts.F19: The 1993 rate was set as the baseline for payment of management fees until the proper determination of the fees under the provisions of the Seventh Schedule of the Building Management Ordinance.

claim: The plaintiff claimed on a cheque dated 11 September 1997 in the sum of $193,340.00 drawn by the Defendant but countermanded by the Defendant
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed on a cheque dated 11 September 1997 in the sum of $193,340.00 drawn by the Defendant but countermanded by the Defendant
parties: Defendant: SHUN TAT PLASTIC ELECTRONIC FACTORY LIMITED

facts.F1: The Defendant placed a purchase order with the Plaintiff to supply 40,000 electronic integrated circuits (ICs) and 20,000 liquid crystal display units (LCDs) on 5 August 1997
facts.F2: A deposit of 30% of the purchase price was paid by the Defendant and the balance was payable cash on delivery
facts.F3: Each Tamagochi required both an IC and a LCD and the Defendant would have had to purchase another 20,000 LCDs from another source
facts.F4: The Plaintiff delivered 1,000 chicken model ICs and 1,000 LCDs on 21 August for a trial production
facts.F5: The Plaintiff invoiced the Defendant in respect of the balance of chicken model ICs (19,000) and LCDs (19,000) on 21 August
facts.F6: The Defendant did not reply to the Plaintiff's enquiry about the payment of the invoice and it appeared that the Defendant was making excuses for not taking delivery
facts.F7: On 5 September, the Plaintiff faxed the Defendant demanding it take delivery by 8 September, or the Plaintiff would make alternative arrangements for the goods
facts.F8: The Defendant replied that due to their production arrangements, they wished to collect the sets of IC in two lots, 10,000 each for the two models, to be sent on Tuesday 9 September
facts.F9: The Plaintiff received a further message from the Defendant confirming that it would take delivery of 19,000 not before Wednesday 10 September, and require half each, 9,000 chicken and 10,000 dinosaur
facts.F10: On 8 September, the Plaintiff faxed the Defendant an invoice in respect of 9,000 chicken model ICs, 10,000 dinosaur model ICs and 10,000 LCDs
facts.F11: The goods were delivered to the Defendant on 10 September, and the Defendant gave the Plaintiff a cheque for $193,340.00, dated 11 September 1997, in payment of the invoice
facts.F12: The cheque was returned due to insufficient funds due to a stop payment order made by the Defendant
facts.F13: The Defendant claimed that its customer cancelled its order and the Defendant suffered a loss as a result of the Plaintiff's breach of agreement
facts.F14: The Defendant's associate company, Catic Electronic Ltd had contracted to supply 38,000 manufactured Tamagochi to a US customer, Kin Image Inc of Los Angeles
facts.F15: The Defendant's accounts department would have drawn a cheque for such a large sum without confirmation from those dealing with the transaction that the goods supplied were in accordance with the contract
facts.F16: There were memos sent on 22 August and 11 September from the Defendant that were suspicious and probably not genuine

facts.F1: The 2nd Plaintiff, SUN YAT-SEN UNIVERSITY, set up a Food Engineering Research Centre (FERC) in 1991.
facts.F2: In 1995, the State Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China issued a document converting the centre into an institute called '國家教委食品工程研究中心' (Food Engineering Research Centre of State Education Ministry).
facts.F3: The 1st Plaintiff was established in 1993 as a joint venture between the 2nd Plaintiff, Science and Technology Development Centre of the State Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China, and Liu Xin.
facts.F4: The 1st Plaintiff manufactured and marketed lingzhi spore powder capsules, which were initially sold under the brand name Hometown Food.
facts.F5: In 1998, the 2nd Plaintiff negotiated with Mr. Cheng to distribute the products, but the negotiations fell through.
facts.F6: In January and February 1999, the parties negotiated an agreement for the 1st Defendant to act as the distributor of the lingzhi spore powder produced by the 1st Plaintiff.
facts.F7: The agreement was executed in writing between FERC, the 1st Plaintiff, and the 1st Defendant.
facts.F8: The 1st Defendant marketed the lingzhi spore powder in Hong Kong under the brand name ENHANVOL 盈康活.
facts.F9: The 1st Defendant also marketed a lingzhi tea product under the brand name ENHANTEA 盈康茶.
facts.F10: In November 2002, the 1st Defendant marketed products manufactured by other suppliers under the ENHANVOL and 盈康活 brand names.
facts.F11: The Plaintiffs published a public declaration in several Chinese newspapers on December 4, 2002, announcing that they had ceased supply to the 1st Defendant and appointed a new distributor.
facts.F12: The 1st Defendant continued to use the names ENHANVOL and 盈康活 after the termination of the agreements.

claim: damages for the death of Lam Sze Ching, Lam Shuk Ying and Fong Yin Ha are the administratrices of the estate of Lam Sze Ching.
requested_remedy: damages for the death of Lam Sze Ching, Lam Shuk Ying and Fong Yin Ha are the administratrices of the estate of Lam Sze Ching.
parties: Plaintiff: Yu Shuk Ying and Fong Yin Ha
Defendant: Proficiency Industrial Products Limited, Ip Kwai Ming, China Motor Bus Company Limited, and Lam Kwok Ming, China Motor Bus Company Limited (Third Party)

facts.F1: The deceased, Lam Sze Ching, was the sole proprietor of the Maintain Ease (Hong Kong) Company, a cleaning company.
facts.F2: In the early hours of the morning of 24 October 1994, the deceased was performing cleaning works for the Hang Seng Bank Ltd at the external wall of the Hang Seng Bank Building in Connaught Road Central.
facts.F3: The deceased had hired a special purpose truck with a folding crane from the 1st defendant, Proficiency Industrial Products Limited, for the cleaning works.
facts.F4: The 2nd defendant, Ip Kwai Ming, was employed by the 1st defendant to drive the truck and operate the crane.
facts.F5: At about 5:15 am, a double decker bus owned by the 3rd defendant, China Motor Bus Company Limited, and driven by its employee, the 4th defendant, Lam Kwok Ming, hit the jib cabin, throwing the deceased and the 2nd defendant onto the ground.
facts.F6: The deceased died later the same morning from the injuries he received as a result of the fall.
facts.F7: There was no dispute that the truck was parked on the pavement with its crane extended over the second lane of the westbound carriageway of Connaught Road Central without any hazard lights on, and no part of Connaught Road Central was closed or blocked off by cones or warning lights.
facts.F8: The road was not closed off by cones or warning lights when the accident occurred.
facts.F9: The deceased had suggested not blocking off the road as part of the cleaning works.
facts.F10: The deceased did not ensure that the necessary safety precautions were taken during the cleaning works
facts.F11: The deceased earned an income and had expenses that were considered when calculating damages.
facts.F12: The parties agreed on a multiplier for damages calculation.

claim: damages for non acceptance of 2,084.50MT of the Steel Bars
requested_remedy: damages for non acceptance of 2,084.50MT of the Steel Bars

facts.F1: The sales contract No. NSS404 was entered into between the plaintiff and the defendant on 27 June 2011 for the purchase of 3,500MT (+/-3%) of BS4449/1988 Grade 460 and/or HKCS2:1995 high tensile deformed steel bars of various sizes
facts.F2: The last delivery that the defendant had accepted was the delivery of 300.789MT of the Steel Bars on 4 October 2012
facts.F3: Payment was only made on 30 November 2012, 26 days after the payment due date
facts.F4: The defendant repudiated the sales contract on 11 October 2012, and the plaintiff accepted the repudiation on 16 October 2012
facts.F5: The plaintiff commenced proceedings by the issue of the Writ to claim damages for non-acceptance of 2,084.50MT of the Steel Bars
facts.F6: The Hong Kong market for deformed steel bars is a global market with imports from various countries
facts.F7: The participants involved in the actual sale process of deformed steel bars in Hong Kong can be divided into four levels: manufacturers, agents for steel mills or importers, stockists, and construction companies or engineering contractors
facts.F8: The plaintiff was engaged in the business of supplying steel products, including rebars, and the sales contract with the defendant was the plaintiff's only outstanding contract that had not been fully performed
facts.F9: The defendant had purchased the Steel Bars for the construction of reinforced concrete box culverts at the north apron area of the Kai Tai Airport development, but the construction of the box culverts was omitted due to a variation order dated 2 December 2011
facts.F10: Stockists in general do not, and cannot purchase in one go and warehouse all the rebars required to be supplied under all their contracts at hand
facts.F11: The market price of the Steel Bars on or about 31 October 2012 required a discount of 10% to reflect both the bargaining factor and the discount to attract a buyer to take immediate delivery of more than 2,000MT of rebars

facts.F4: The defendant, Gao, and Tan were also directors of the plaintiff in the periods 24-10-1991 to 28-9-1993.

facts.F23: The sub-sale and purchase agreement between Mr Soon and Sun Fung Limited was signed on 27 May 2003.
facts.F24: However the assignment to Sun Fung Limited was dated 22 June 1993.
facts.F25: The plaintiff never has any interest in the land.
facts.F26: The plaintiff incurred a $3,600,000 loan from Excellent Fine on about 28 May 1993.
facts.F27: The loan was paid to Saleswin Enterprises Limited on 28 May 1993.
facts.F28: On the same day, a sum of $3,650,000 was received by the plaintiff from Saleswin Enterprises Limited.
facts.F29: Part of the money ($2,250,000) was described as repayment by the defendant of the $2,250,000 advancement, but was in truth no repayment by the defendant.

facts.F1: Sale and purchase of  the entire shareholding in a Hong Kong incorporated company known as Galaxy Garment Limited.
facts.F2: Mr. Kuthoor sold 10,000,000 shares in Galaxy to Vagas Lane for HK$10,000,000 in cash.
facts.F3: Mr. Kuthoor also sold one share in Paris Sky to Vagas Lane for HK$130,000,000 with HK$90,000,000 in cash and an allotment of shares equivalent of HK$40,000,000.
facts.F4: Vagas Lane became the sole owner of the entire issued share capital of Galaxy, and Mr. Kuthoor resigned as sole director of both Galaxy and Paris Sky after completion of the sale and purchase.
facts.F5: Galaxy had outstanding mortgage loan of HK$75,987,258.90 to Lei Shing Hong Credit Ltd at the time of completion of the sale and purchase.
facts.F6: Ms. Tsoi asked for a loan of HK$10,000,000 for a term of one year from FA Finance, and a three-month interest-free loan of HK$7,000,000 was agreed.
facts.F7: Ms. Tsoi signed no loan agreement with FA Finance, and the loan was deposited into her bank account based on a false representation.
facts.F8: Ms. Tsoi denied asking for a personal loan from FA Finance and claimed that the HK$7,000,000 was a payment by Vagas Lane for its promise to pay HK$10,000,000 to Mr. Kuthoor and Ms. Tsoi.
facts.F9: Mr. Kuthoor was declared bankrupt, and the Official Receiver did not adopt his actions or assign the right of action to him.
facts.F10: Mr. Kuthoor no longer had standing to pursue his counterclaim in the Breach of Warranties Action and his claim in the HK$10 Million Claim Action.
facts.F11: Ms. Tsoi has not provided sufficient evidence to prove the 1st and 2nd Alleged Oral Agreements.

facts.F1: The plaintiff and defendant entered into an Agreement for Sale and Purchase on 2 January 1997 for the sale of two equal undivided 210th parts or shares of and in Kowloon Inland Lot No.10319 and the erections and buildings thereon known as Yick Man Building, Nos.5-19 Ha Heung Road, together with the sole and exclusive right and privilege to hold, use, occupy and enjoy all that Flat C on the 2nd floor and flat roof of the Building.
facts.F2: The Lot is rectangular in shape and is one of a number of lots that have a frontage on Ha Heung Road.
facts.F3: The Building was erected in 1976 and consists of 13 storeys.
facts.F4: Flat C is on the side and has a frontage over the lane, while Flats A and B have frontages on Ha Heung Road.
facts.F5: Portions of Flats A and B protrude beyond the boundary of the Lot by some 10 feet, but the protrusions do not project over the road, only the pavement.

facts.F7: The Vendor’s solicitors responded that the issue of the Letter of Compliance Memorial No.264970 and the issue of the Occupation Permit No.K92/76 implied consent to build over Crown Land, but the Plaintiff’s solicitors disagreed and insisted on having documentary proof of waiver or consent.
facts.F8: The Vendor’s solicitors later argued that the Government must be deemed to have abandoned its rights on the ground that the Building had been in existence for over 20 years and the Government had taken no enforcement action since 1976.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff conceded that the Defendant had good title to the property.
facts.F10: Flat C is habitually occupied.

facts.F1: The Petitioner and the 1st Respondent own 50% of Gottinghen Trading Limited and Pacific Overseas Investment Limited.
facts.F2: The companies are incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and Samoa respectively.
facts.F3: Gottinghen was acquired in 1998 by the Petitioner to provide a platform to receive customers’ orders and to sub-contract her own extra orders.
facts.F4: The 1st Respondent increased Waysung’s capital and obtained an export license in 2002, allowing Waysung to export finished garments directly to Gottinghen.
facts.F5: The Petitioner met the 1st Respondent in Shanghai and became the 1st Respondent’s partner in 2003.
facts.F6: In 2006, the Petitioner suggested that Gottinghen be used to control foreign exchange risks and to invest in securities.
facts.F7: The Petitioner and the 1st Respondent acquired Pacific Overseas Investment Limited in May 2007 to apply for shares in initial public offerings.
facts.F8: The relationship between the Petitioner and the 1st Respondent rapidly deteriorated from 2007 onwards.
facts.F9: Gottinghen currently holds equities worth HK$7,201,376.80 and cash worth HK$24,440,329.57 in Hong Kong, as well as US$500,000 in an account with Credit Suisse in Singapore.
facts.F10: Pacific has assets consisting solely of HK$31,953.10 in cash in an account with DBS in Hong Kong.
facts.F11: The Petitioner served both Petitions on the 1st Respondent within 6 weeks before the hearing.

parties: Defendant: The 2nd respondent and the company (1st respondent)

facts.F1: The applicant deposes that she is both a member and director of the company, whilst the only other member or director is the 2nd respondent.
facts.F2: The applicant claims she holds 350,000 shares of the company, and the second respondent claims she holds 100,000 shares.
facts.F3: The company's latest annual return confirms these figures.
facts.F4: The origin of the dispute lies in the 2nd respondent's refusal to allow the applicant to see the company's books of account.
facts.F5: The applicant apparently did not have any managerial involvement in the company.
facts.F6: The applicant requisitioned the directors to convene a general meeting of the company to consider a resolution for the appointment of an additional director.
facts.F7: The 2nd respondent declined to attend the board meeting, which was dissolved for failure of the required quorum of two directors.
facts.F8: As the general meeting had not been called, the applicant as the requisitionist convened an extraordinary general meeting under S.113 of the Ordinance.
facts.F9: The 2nd respondent declined to attend, and the general meeting could not take place for lack of a quorum.
facts.F10: The 2nd respondent denied the applicant's title to the shares founding the application, claiming that the initial shareholdings were intended to be equally divided among herself, the applicant, and one LAM Tin-sang.
facts.F11: The 2nd respondent further claimed that when Lam retired from the business he was supposed to transfer his shares to her, but they were mistakenly recorded as being transferred to the applicant.
facts.F12: The 2nd respondent said that she had an agreement with the applicant for the sale of all the applicant's shares to her for $400,000, but there was no formal transfer of the shares.
facts.F13: The 2nd respondent contended that the company was in a state of deadlock and proposed to wind it up.
facts.F14: The applicant and the 2nd respondent were former friends.
facts.F15: The 2nd respondent presented a case for specific performance of the alleged agreement for purchasing the applicant's shares, coupled with an application under S.100 of the Companies Ordinance for rectification of the register of shareholders.

facts.F2: The mortgage loan was HK$4.9 million to be repaid by instalments.

facts.F4: Pursuant to the Legal Charge and the relevant facilities letters, the overdraft formed part of the secured indebtedness of the Legal Charge.
facts.F5: Since April 1998, the defendants defaulted in repaying the monthly mortgage instalments under the Legal Charge.
facts.F6: The plaintiff sold the mortgaged property in October 1999 and applied the net sale proceeds to settle the outstanding indebtedness in the mortgage account in full and the overdraft account partially.
facts.F7: As at 10 November 1999, the net debit balance in the overdraft account was HK$4,928,056.35.
facts.F8: The plaintiff incurred a sum of HK$106,500.00 as estate agent’s fees for the sale of the mortgaged property and debited the defendants’ overdraft account with the same on 15 November 1999.
facts.F9: The total outstanding in the overdraft account on 30 November 1999 amounted to HK$5,034,556.35 with interest in the sum of HK$68,428.75.
facts.F10: In the statement on the overdraft account dated 13 October 2001, the plaintiff sent to the defendants, it was stated that a sum of HK$6,195,063.47 was credited into the overdraft account, resulting in a nil balance.
facts.F11: Seven years later, the plaintiff commenced the present action against the defendants for the said sum of HK$5,034,556.35.
facts.F12: The representation in the Statement was an internal writing-off and was sent to the defendants by mistake.

claim: The Plaintiff is claiming for the sum of $175,000.00 due under an agreement dated 7 February 1998.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff is claiming for the sum of $175,000.00 due under an agreement dated 7 February 1998.
parties: Defendant: WONG YING HUNG (1st Defendant), WONG LAI WA (2nd Defendant), WONG LAI YING (3rd Defendant), CHAN CHI KIN (4th Defendant)

facts.F1: The Plaintiff and the Defendants were partners of a partnership called Yan Wing Chinese Restaurant.
facts.F2: The partnership commenced business on 21 August 1997.
facts.F3: The partners filed the necessary particulars of the partnership with the business registration office, but the 4th Defendant's name did not appear as a partner in the business registration record.
facts.F4: The Restaurant was operated at Shop No. 1 and Shop No. 2A of Great Wall Building under 2 tenancy agreements.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff and the 1st Defendant signed the tenancy agreements on behalf of the partnership.
facts.F6: The partnership also had the use of Shop 102 on the first floor of the same building for storage purpose.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff and each of the other partners contributed the sum of $200,000.00 for the business.
facts.F8: The business was not good and the partnership was losing money.
facts.F9: The partners met on 7 February 1998 to discuss the Plaintiff's withdrawal from the partnership.
facts.F10: It was agreed that the Plaintiff should withdraw and be paid a sum of $175,000.00.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff signed an agreement in Chinese recording his agreement to withdraw from the partnership.
facts.F12: The material part of the agreement provided for the Plaintiff's withdrawal, removal of his name from the tenancy agreements, and non-involvement in the business.
facts.F13: The agreement was signed by all 5 partners and each also put his fingerprint on the document.
facts.F14: The Plaintiff packed up all his belongings and left the business after the agreement was signed.
facts.F15: The Plaintiff never took part in the business again.
facts.F16: The Plaintiff contacted the landlord or its agent to transfer the tenancy of Shop 102 to the 1st Defendant, but was told that it would be necessary to have the 1st Defendant participate in the transfer.
facts.F17: The Plaintiff contacted the 1st Defendant, but he was busy and told the Plaintiff that he would deal with the matter later.
facts.F18: The 2nd Defendant informed the Plaintiff that the Defendants would arrange to instruct solicitors to have the name on the 2 Shops 1 and 2A tenancy agreements changed on 7 April 1998 and the payment of the $175,000.00 would be made then.
facts.F19: The Plaintiff received a phone call from the 2nd Defendant on 7 April 1998 to settle the matter.
facts.F20: The Plaintiff met with the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Defendants at the Restaurant on 8 April 1998 to collect his money.
facts.F21: The Defendants offered the Plaintiff the sum of $91,250.00 only and told him that the change of name procedure could be done at the solicitors' office on another day.
facts.F22: The Plaintiff refused to accept the offer.
facts.F23: On 7 April 1998, the removal of the Plaintiff's name from the tenancy agreements was planned to be handled by solicitors.
facts.F24: The Defendants arranged to instruct solicitors to change the names on 7 April 1998, implying a plan for the solicitors to handle the removal of the Plaintiff's name.

claim: To appoint a provisional liquidator for Texxan Industries Limited and Chino Industries Limited due to allegations of bias and conflict of interest by the joint liquidators
requested_remedy: To appoint a provisional liquidator for Texxan Industries Limited and Chino Industries Limited due to allegations of bias and conflict of interest by the joint liquidators
parties: Defendant: CM Nacson and EM McMillan (joint liquidators)

facts.F1: The companies Texxan Industries Limited (Texxan) and Chino Industries Limited (Chino) were incorporated on 27th March 1981.
facts.F2: In June 1988, the companies became wholly owned by Texxan Consolidated Limited, a Bermuda company beneficially owned by the petitioner and the Yue Xiu group.
facts.F3: The Yue Xiu group claims that Texxan is indebted to them for $157,000,000 and Chino for $95,000,000.
facts.F4: The petitioner claims a sum of $836,000 from Texxan and $136,000 from Chino.
facts.F5: The companies are alleged to be insolvent and unable to pay their debts.
facts.F6: Statutory declarations were made by the Yue Xiu directors on 7th March 1990, stating that the companies could not continue in business and should be wound up under section 228A of the Companies Ordinance.
facts.F7: The Yue Xiu directors appointed MR Nacson and EM McMillan as joint provisional liquidators on 8th March 1990.
facts.F8: The joint liquidators were appointed as joint liquidators by a majority in value of the alleged aggregate value of debts of the Yue Xiu companies and its supporters at the first meeting of creditors on 3rd April 1990.
facts.F9: The petitioner alleges that the joint liquidators are not unbiased nor independent due to the involvement of their firms with the Yue Xiu group.
facts.F10: The petitioner claims that the joint liquidators have assisted the Yue Xiu group in various ways, including procuring payments from trade debtors and investigating trade debts.
facts.F11: The joint liquidators deny these allegations and argue that they have acted impartially.
facts.F12: A test for bias was considered in R. v. Liverpool City Justices Ex-parte Topping [1983]1 WLR 119, which is whether there is the appearance of bias rather than whether there is actual bias.
facts.F13: The balance of convenience may be influenced by the possibility of waste and duplication of efforts if a new provisional liquidator was appointed.

facts.F1: The plaintiffs and the defendants are blood brothers and indigenous villagers of the New Territories, and members of the same family.
facts.F2: They have been receiving rental income from various lots of land in the Yuen Long area which they rented from either the Tong or the Tso for subletting purposes.
facts.F3: The plaintiffs claim that the defendants wrongfully refused to acknowledge certain lots of land were partnership properties, and treated the same as their own.

facts.F8: The genuineness of the Jan 2013 letter was not disputed by the defendants.

facts.F10: The younger brothers told the police that they leased some land lots to Ms Lau's company, which is inconsistent with their case in this action.
facts.F11: Witnesses gave conflicting testimonies regarding the partnership.
facts.F12: Some witnesses had motives to deliberately give untruthful testimony.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff and Defendants entered into a Sale and Purchase Agreement dated 18th February 1981 for the property known as Flat A, 6th floor, Beverley Heights (Block B), Belair Garden, Shatin, New Territories at a price of $1,106,000.00.
facts.F2: The Defendants failed to accept the conveyance of the flat, and the Plaintiff took out proceedings on 14th April 1984 against them.
facts.F3: The completion date for the sale was 22nd February 1982 (i.e., within 14 days upon being notified by the Plaintiff of the issuance of the Temporary Occupation Permit of Stage I) pursuant to Clause 6(a) of the Agreement.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff gave notice of 'rescission' of the sale by a letter dated 15th November 1982.
facts.F5: The flat was subsequently sold for $663,228.00 under an assignment dated 15th July 1985.
facts.F6: Messrs. Jones Lang Wootton, the valuer of the Plaintiff, put the market value of the flat as at 6th August 1982 at $763,000.00.
facts.F7: The 1st Defendant's valuer, Messrs. A.G. Wilkinson, placed market values at $786,000.00 and $805,000.00 on the flat as at 6th August 1982 and 23rd August 1985 respectively.
facts.F8: P.W.2 assessed the value of the flat at $715,000.00 as at 3rd May 1985.
facts.F9: The market value of the flat in April 1982 was used in assessing damages as the difference between the original purchase price and the market value at that time.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff made part payments to the Defendants which were to be credited in assessing damages.
facts.F11: There were periods of delay by the Plaintiff for which interest was disallowed.

claim: The plaintiff's claims are based on three causes of action: (1) fraudulent misrepresentation, (2) Quistclose trust, and (3) breach of agreement.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff's claims are based on three causes of action: (1) fraudulent misrepresentation, (2) Quistclose trust, and (3) breach of agreement.
parties: Plaintiff: LEW KEE JACK (also known as JACK LEW and as JACKIE LEW)
Defendant: CHINA RAILWAY INVESTMENT (HK) LIMITED, ASIANOTICE INVESTMENTS LIMITED, CHINA RAILWAY CONSTRUCTION CORPORATION (HK) LIMITED, YIU FUNG

facts.F1: The plaintiff, Mr. Lew Kee Jack, is a Canadian Chinese who made a fortune in the restaurant business and later became an international investor.
facts.F2: The three defendants are part of the China Railway Construction Group. The main subsidiary in Hong Kong is the 3rd defendant, China Railway Construction Corporation (HK) Limited.
facts.F3: The 1st defendant, China Railway Investment (HK) Limited, is a fully-owned subsidiary of the 3rd defendant, and the 2nd defendant, Asianotice Investment Limited, a BVI company, is a shelf company that was specially created for the transaction.
facts.F4: In 2000, the telecom market was hot, and China Unicom Limited had just gone public in Hong Kong in June 2000.
facts.F5: The plaintiff learned that the China Railway Construction Group had 'founder' shares in United, which could be converted into China Unicom shares, and showed interest.
facts.F6: A meeting took place on June 30, 2000, where the plaintiff alleged an oral agreement was made with the 3rd defendant, as represented by Mr. Hao, to purchase United 'founder' shares.
facts.F7: The agreement included the representation and warranty that the United 'founder' shares would be convertible into China Unicom shares within two years, and if not, the money paid would be refunded.
facts.F8: Documents were created subsequent to the meeting, including a draft Chinese agreement, transfer acknowledgement, assurances, and warranties from the 1st defendant.
facts.F9: A second transaction took place for a larger block of 10 million United 'founder' shares at a slightly adjusted price of HK$10 per share plus commission.
facts.F10: The plaintiff made payments to the defendants totaling HK$137 million, HK$14 million, and HK$15 million, respectively.
facts.F11: The defendants later admitted they did not have any United 'founder' shares and that China Railway Construction Group was not a 'founder' shareholder.
facts.F12: Mr. Lew was invited to go to Beijing to meet with the head office but did not result in any solution.
facts.F13: Solicitors became involved, and correspondence showed that the plaintiff demanded payment from the defendants in March 2003, leading to rejection after delay.
facts.F14: There is a risk of dissipation of assets by the defendants.

lawsuit_type: Interlocutory application for a Mareva injunction

claim: The plaintiff claimed damages arising out of the alleged negligence of the 1st Defendant and the vicarious liability of the 2nd Defendant
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed damages arising out of the alleged negligence of the 1st Defendant and the vicarious liability of the 2nd Defendant

facts.F1: The 2nd Defendant was the owner of a Toyota saloon car (KC517) that was driven by the 1st Defendant for the 1st Defendant's own purpose
facts.F2: There was a crash between the Toyota and the BMW saloon car (KM5242) owned by the Plaintiff
facts.F3: At the time of the crash, there was a two-lane roundabout with a two-lane passageway going to the 12 o'clock position of Tuen Mun and a one-lane passageway going to Yuen Long through the roundabout
facts.F4: The Third Party (driver of the BMW) was driving on the slow lane of the 6 o'clock position through the roundabout intending to exit at the 3 o'clock position
facts.F5: The 1st Defendant was driving on the fast lane of the 6 o'clock position through the roundabout intending to exit at the 12 o'clock position
facts.F6: The two cars collided in the vicinity of the 12 o'clock position
facts.F7: The impact was between the right front corner of the BMW car and the left side body of the Toyota
facts.F8: The momentum caused both cars to swerve to another position before stopping altogether
facts.F9: The car entering the roundabout has to give way to the cars already in the roundabout
facts.F10: The Third Party stopped at the Give Way lines to observe the traffic before entering the roundabout
facts.F11: The 1st Defendant also stopped at the Give Way lines of the roundabout before entering
facts.F12: Both the Third Party and the 1st Defendant were driving at a speed of 40 kph
facts.F13: The Third Party was taking a longer route (being on the outer lane of the roundabout)
facts.F14: The 1st Defendant was taking a shorter route (being on the inner lane of the roundabout)
facts.F15: From the time the 1st Defendant reached the Give Way lines up to the point of collision, he had failed to keep any or any proper lookout or to have any sufficient regard for the traffic in the roundabout
facts.F16: The 1st Defendant failed to make sure that his entry into and exit from the roundabout would not affect or endanger the cars in the roundabout

claim: a declaration as to possessory title arising out of the allegedly adverse possession of a residential flat in Ho Man Tin, Kowloon
requested_remedy: a declaration as to possessory title arising out of the allegedly adverse possession of a residential flat in Ho Man Tin, Kowloon

facts.F1: The Premises were purchased in 1972 by two gentlemen, Lai Yu (“Lai Senior”) and Poon Wing Chung (“Poon Senior”) as business partners.
facts.F2: The purchase was made jointly but for reasons that are immaterial, the decision was taken to register the property in the name of the defendant.
facts.F3: Lai Senior and Poon Senior’s business relationship turned sour and the partnership was dissolved in 1976.
facts.F4: After the dissolution of the partnership, Lai Senior seemed to have felt he was cheated by Poon Senior and treated Poon Senior’s share of the property as being his, in compensation.
facts.F5: The defendant had understood the property to be owned by him legally and beneficially since 1976.
facts.F6: There were no formal written agreements for the occupation of the Premises by Poon Senior’s brother, Poon Yiu Chung (“PYC”), or Poon Yiu Chung's family.
facts.F7: PYC’s occupation of the Premises initially as a tenancy at will, with a rental agreed, later became rent-free.
facts.F8: The plaintiff had been resident in the Premises since 1997 and had lived there rent-free throughout, the defendant contended that this occupation was with his permission.
facts.F9: The plaintiff changed the locks and the doors to the Premises after moving in in 1997.
facts.F10: The plaintiff has paid for the maintenance of the Premises and of the common parts of the building, and has paid utility and management charges.
facts.F11: The defendant has paid government rent and rates but has not visited or lived in the Premises during this period.
facts.F12: The first contact between the plaintiff and the defendant was when the defendant commenced proceedings to recover possession of the Premises.
facts.F13: The relationship between the parties suggested that the defendant would not seek independent physical entry to the Premises.
facts.F14: The plaintiff’s acts were insufficient to show an intention to possess the Premises exclusively and adverse to the paper owner.
facts.F15: The defendant knowingly acquiesced in the occupation of the Premises by the plaintiff and his family up to the commencement of the proceedings.

requested_remedy: claims declarations as to beneficial ownership over the Property, to set aside the Transfer and for damages
parties: Defendant: Lee Tin Choi (also known as Li Tin Choi) and Lee Chan Lai Lin

facts.F1: The Plaintiff is the nephew of the Defendants.
facts.F2: The dispute is over beneficial ownership to a small house (the Property) erected as a result of an illegal development of small houses in the New Territories.
facts.F3: Under the development agreement, D1 provided land and the developer provided capital, ting fees and building costs.
facts.F4: The land was subdivided into 7 lots and assigned to 7 tings, including the Plaintiff and 2 sons of D1.
facts.F5: The tings applied for building licenses which involved the making of false declarations.
facts.F6: The agreement provided for 3 houses to be allocated to D1's side upon completion.
facts.F7: Two houses were given to D1's sons, which were sold immediately to the developer.
facts.F8: The keys to the third house, i.e. the Property, were given by the developer to the Plaintiff/Li Tsuen.
facts.F9: However, the title deeds, including a General Power of Attorney purportedly signed by the Plaintiff with the donee's particulars left blank (Purported GPA) and the Plaintiff's will, were given by the developer's solicitors to D1.
facts.F10: Seven years after the Plaintiff and his father have been in possession of the Property, without any formal demand, D1, as donee of the Purported GPA, transferred the Property to D2, his wife (the Transfer).
facts.F11: Li Tsuen passed away on 20 September 2016, aged 88.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff had to rely on the illegal development agreements to explain his registered title, part performance and proprietary estoppel by representation.
facts.F13: D1 had agreed to the Pre-Condition as part of the development agreement.
facts.F14: The Plaintiff had been paying rates for the Property from 30 May 2014.

facts.F1: LING TAT MING was the registered owner of the mezzanine floor of Shing Hing Building, 78-84 Lai Chi Kok Road, Kowloon.
facts.F2: LING TAO YEUNG was the holder of a light refreshment restaurant licence for the premises.
facts.F3: LING TAT MING let the premises to LI YUK SANG for a five-year term from 1 October 1989 to 30 September 1994 by an agreement in writing dated 10 October 1989.
facts.F4: LING TAO YEUNG permitted LI YUK SANG to use his light refreshment restaurant licence during the tenancy at a monthly licence fee of $2,000.

facts.F7: LI YUK SANG claimed that LING TAT MING orally agreed to renew the tenancy for a further two years at the market rent available in September/October 1994.
facts.F8: LI YUK SANG spent $1,000,000 in renovating the premises, but did not produce receipts for the work done.
facts.F9: Photographic evidence of the renovation work was also not produced.
facts.F10: LING TAT MING never made an oral agreement to renew the tenancy.

claim: Damages arising out of injuries sustained by the plaintiff when either he or a cart which he was pushing or both came into collision with the 1st defendant's private motor-car
requested_remedy: Damages arising out of injuries sustained by the plaintiff when either he or a cart which he was pushing or both came into collision with the 1st defendant's private motor-car
parties: Defendant: 1st defendant (owner and driver of the private motor-car), 2nd defendant (driver of another car), and 3rd defendant (owner of the car driven by the 2nd defendant)

facts.F1: The accident occurred on 12th November 1968, when the plaintiff was pushing his cart across Castle Peak Road.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was injured when his cart and/or he himself came into collision with the 1st defendant's private motor-car.
facts.F3: The Statement of Claim recited two collisions, the first between the car owned and driven by the 1st defendant and a car driven by the 2nd defendant and owned by the 3rd defendant; the second collision recited was one between the plaintiff and the motor-car owned and driven by the 1st defendant.
facts.F4: At the hearing, the only evidence as to the actual collision was given by the plaintiff who said that he saw no second car and knew nothing of any collision between two cars.
facts.F5: The 1st defendant admitted to a collision between his motor-car and the plaintiff's cart upon the pleadings.
facts.F6: The plaintiff was taking a route across Castle Peak Road at a point without a zebra crossing, however another zebra crossing was available a short distance away.
facts.F7: The plaintiff waited about one minute for a number of cars to pass, and estimated the 1st defendant's car was at a distance of 200 yards (600 feet) from him when he started to push his cart across the road.
facts.F8: The 1st defendant's car had ample time to slow down and stop to let the plaintiff pass, but failed to do so, hitting the plaintiff.
facts.F9: The 1st defendant has not given evidence, and therefore did not dispute that his car collided with the plaintiff.
facts.F10: The plaintiff suffered injuries in the accident, including a partial rupture of the Achilles tendon of his left leg.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's claim for total loss of earnings for five months was not supported by evidence.
facts.F12: With proper treatment, the plaintiff would have made a full recovery by the date of the trial.

facts.F2: The previous tenancy was terminated on June 16th, 1988, by the serving of a notice under section 119(1) dated January 5th, 1988.
facts.F3: The respondent has no objection to the granting of a new tenancy, which should commence on June 17th, 1988.
facts.F4: The new tenancy is to be for 2 years and, other than the rent, is to be on the same terms and conditions as the previous tenancy agreement.

facts.F6: The renovation work has caused disturbance and noise, which has affected the rental value of the premises.
facts.F7: Miss Savage, a chartered surveyor, assessed the prevailing market rent of the unrenovated flat as $28,000.00 per month, considering the disturbance caused by the renovation work.

facts.F9: There were comparable lettings in The Rozlyn and other similar premises in the area.
facts.F10: The agreements of the leases to new tenants could not be expected to completely reflect the degree of disruption caused by the renovation work.
facts.F11: There is a difference in rents for renovated and unrenovated flats in similar older developments.

facts.F1: This litigation arose out of a dispute about the Plaintiffs’ right of way over Lot 695 in Sai Kung.
facts.F2: The parties are landowners and/or residents of different lots of land in Demarcation District 247 which includes Ngau Pui Wo and Tai Lam Wu.
facts.F3: The Plaintiffs acquired their properties in 2005 and 2006.
facts.F4: The 1st Defendant is the village representative of Tai Lam Wu and Ngau Pui Wo.
facts.F5: Prior to 1993, Lai Yuk Kee and three others were the registered owners of seven lots of land in Demarcation District 247 including Lot 695.
facts.F6: On 7 January 1993, they assigned the seven lots of land to the 2nd Defendant, who is Lai’s step-daughter.
facts.F7: The 2nd Defendant divided Lot 695 into ten sections and assigned them to ten different purchasers for a consideration of $76,230 each on 30 November 1993.
facts.F8: Then between August and October 1997, eight of the ten sections of Lot 695 were assigned to Lai for the same consideration.
facts.F9: Sections C and F of Lot 695 remain under the ownership of the purchasers.
facts.F10: Lai is the registered owner of the other eight sections including the remaining portion of Lot 695.
facts.F11: The only vehicular access to Ngau Pui Wo is via a side-road from Wilson Trail in the neighbouring Tai Lam Wu Village.
facts.F12: The Suit Road runs over part of Lot 695C, Lot 695F and Lot 695RP, but the substantial part of the Suit Road is built on Government land.
facts.F13: In October 2005, the 2nd Plaintiff’s husband began renovating the house on Lot 590.
facts.F14: The 1st Defendant tried to block up the Left Limb Road with boulders.
facts.F15: In April 2006, the 1st Plaintiff started to renovate its house on Lot 841.
facts.F16: On 24 September 2006, the 1st Defendant used boulders and chain to lock up part of the Suit Road within Lot 695 to prevent vehicular access.
facts.F17: On 22 November 2006, the Plaintiffs issued the present writ of summons and then the inter-parte summons seeking an injunction to compel the 1st Defendant to remove the blockade.

claim: Challenge to the validity of the New Territories Land (Exemption) Ordinance on the ground that it infringes provisions of the Bill of Rights and the Letters Patent.
requested_remedy: Challenge to the validity of the New Territories Land (Exemption) Ordinance on the ground that it infringes provisions of the Bill of Rights and the Letters Patent.

facts.F1: The New Territories Land (Exemption) Ordinance was passed by the Legislative Council and assented to by the Governor of Hong Kong on 23rd June 1994.
facts.F2: The Exemption Ordinance exempts rural land in the New Territories from the application of Part II of the New Territories Ordinance, which recognizes and enforces Chinese custom or customary rights affecting land.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff, a well-known leader in the New Territories, commenced the action to challenge the validity of the Exemption Ordinance.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff relies on the Proclamation made by Governor Sir Henry Blake in 1900, which promised to safeguard the commercial and landed interests and not to interfere with the usages and good customs of the indigenous inhabitants of the New Territories.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff's challenge is in respect of section 3(a) and section 10 of the Exemption Ordinance, which he says are contrary to the provisions of the Letters Patent and the Basic Law.
facts.F6: China will resume the exercise of sovereignty over Hong Kong on 1st July 1997.
facts.F7: On 1st July 1997, courts of the Special Administrative Region (SAR) shall come into existence with the power of interpretation of the Basic Law.

facts.F5: Four of the Company's staff representing 50% of its workforce also left to join Lam's companies Topbest Technology Ltd and Lawgicware International Limited.
facts.F6: In mid-August 1999, there were negotiations for the purchase of Lam's interest in the Company by the Yeung family but no agreement was reached.
facts.F7: Since August, the Company has been funded by the Yeung family alone.
facts.F8: As at 30 September 1999, according to the latest management accounts, the outstanding amount due from the Company to the 2nd respondent was approximately $700,000 whilst Lam owed the Company over $950,000.
facts.F9: On 23 September 1999, solicitors for the 2nd respondent demanded that the Company repay the 2nd respondent the shareholder's loan and on 4 October 1999, a writ was issued against the Company for some $700,000.
facts.F10: The 2nd respondent failed to discharge the burden of proof to show that there was an absence of 'clean hands' on the part of the petitioner.
facts.F11: The petitioner's misconduct was not the cause of the breakdown in confidence.

claim: Claims US$34,020 under the letter of credit and/or the contract for failure to pay for the supplied automatic FAC'SIM production certifier
requested_remedy: Claims US$34,020 under the letter of credit and/or the contract for failure to pay for the supplied automatic FAC'SIM production certifier

facts.F1: The plaintiff and the defendant entered into a contract on 29 October 1993, where the plaintiff supplied an automatic FAC'SIM production certifier for 3.5" MFD to the defendant.
facts.F2: The defendant provided an irrevocable letter of credit drawn on the Dao Heng Bank to secure payment.
facts.F3: The plaintiff presented documents to the Dao Heng Bank for payment under the letter of credit.
facts.F4: The Dao Heng Bank advised the plaintiff's bank that payment under the letter of credit was refused due to discrepancies.
facts.F5: The discrepancies were referred to the defendant for acceptance, but the defendant refused to confirm acceptance of the delivery under the letter of credit.
facts.F6: The letter of credit was issued by the Dao Heng Bank and dated 23 November 1994, with the plaintiff as the beneficiary and the defendant as the applicant.
facts.F7: The letter of credit required a cargo receipt, quality approval certificate, and other documents to be presented.
facts.F8: The quality approval certificate was dated 12 December 1994 and signed by the defendant, referring to the letter of credit and the supply of 1 set of Automatic FAC'SIM 3.5" MFD Production Certifier including 6 modules.
facts.F9: The Dao Heng Bank issued an Advice on Refusal on 23 December 1994, stating that the documents did not comply with the terms and conditions of the credit.
facts.F10: The defendant claimed that the machine supplied by the plaintiff was defective and that it justifiably terminated the agreement.
facts.F11: The defendant's defence of defective goods and termination of the contract is a triable issue.
facts.F12: The letter of credit does not constitute a separate contract between the plaintiff and the defendant, but rather a means of payment under the contract of sale.

facts.F2: The accident occurred on 10 February 2004, when the Plaintiff and his colleagues were assigned to paint a transmission tower situated on Kau Yi Chau, a remote island of Hong Kong.
facts.F3: The tower was a lattice structure with four vertical columns interconnected by diagonal struts, and six levels of platforms, each about 15 ft. high.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff was supplied with personal protective equipment, including an upper chest harness, a lower pelvic harness, an independent lifeline, a 31 in. lanyard, a 9 in. lanyard, a figure-of-eight ring, and a number of carabineer hooks.

parties: Plaintiff: Foshan Sundy Trade Co. Ltd.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff received an order from Bliss Success Limited (BSL) for the purchase of 30,186 pieces of ladies jeans (the Goods) in May 2005.
facts.F2: The selling price of the Goods was agreed at US$114,706.80, evidenced by an invoice dated 30 May 2005.
facts.F3: The Goods were delivered into the custody of the Defendant, as the carrier, who packed the Goods inside 9 containers for shipment to the United States in late May 2005.
facts.F4: Miss Liang of the Plaintiff came to the Defendant's office and paid the Defendant the relevant freight and charges for the shipment of the Goods on about 1 June 2005.
facts.F5: The Defendant handed over to Miss Liang the original Bill of Lading No. AHK50602006A, with no adverse clausing.
facts.F6: The Bill of Lading named the Plaintiff as the Shipper, to order of HBZ Finance Ltd. as the Consignee, and BSL as the Notify Party.
facts.F7: The Goods under the Bill of Lading were shipped from Hong Kong to the United States in mid-June 2005.
facts.F8: BSL informed the Defendant that they had lost the Bill of Lading and asked the Defendant to release the Goods to them.
facts.F9: The Defendant released the Goods to BSL upon securing a letter of Indemnity and Guarantee issued by Israel Discount Bank of New York dated 15 June 2005.
facts.F10: BSL provided 3 advertisements dated 22, 23 and 24 of July 2005 in a newspaper saying that the original Bill of Lading was lost by BSL.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff sent letters to the Defendant asking for return of the Goods on the ground that the Plaintiff was the holder of the original Bill of Lading in March 2006.
facts.F12: The original Bill of Lading was issued, and the carrier was under the obligation to deliver the Goods to the holder of the bill upon presentation of the original bill.
facts.F13: The Defendant was informed that BSL had lost the Bill of Lading.
facts.F14: The Defendant checked if the Goods had been delivered without production of the original Bill of Lading

requested_remedy: Gratuitous payments not within any of the authorized objects of the companies
parties: Plaintiff: Stable Investment Ltd. and Mosbert Acceptance Ltd.

facts.F1: The plaintiff companies in liquidation, Stable Investment Ltd. and Mosbert Acceptance Ltd., made payments to the defendant between 1973 and 1975.
facts.F2: The payments were recorded in the companies' journals as loans, except for two payments made as 'payments to Dr. J.T. McAlister on your behalf'.
facts.F3: The plaintiffs in liquidation, through the Official Receiver, seek to recover over HK$20 million from the defendant.
facts.F4: The companies' Memoranda of Association do not authorize gratuitous payments, except for specific purposes unconnected with the matters in dispute.
facts.F5: Sub-clause 3(x) in the Memorandum of Mosbert Acceptance Limited allows the company to deal with monies not immediately required.
facts.F6: Gratuitous payments out of a company's funds require either express authorization in the Memorandum of Association or an ancillary power that is reasonably incidental to the attainment or pursuit of one or more of the company's expressed objects.

claim: The Plaintiff seeks the following information from the Banks: (1) The current balance of the Accounts as of the date of the Order to be made; (2) The account opening documents for the Accounts; (3) The bank statements of the Accounts, from the date of transfer to the date of the Order to be made; and (4) Transaction details relating to onward transfers from the Accounts.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff seeks the following information from the Banks: (1) The current balance of the Accounts as of the date of the Order to be made; (2) The account opening documents for the Accounts; (3) The bank statements of the Accounts, from the date of transfer to the date of the Order to be made; and (4) Transaction details relating to onward transfers from the Accounts.
parties: Defendant: HANG SENG BANK, LIMITED and THE HONGKONG AND SHANGHAI BANKING CORPORATION LIMITED

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was the victim of an investment scam perpetrated by a female named Wong Tingting (Wong) who befriended and persuaded him into paying US$480,000 (approximately HK$3.74 million) (the 'Stolen Monies') to the Accounts.
facts.F2: The Stolen Monies were supposedly for the purpose of trading spot gold through an account in the name of the Plaintiff at Red Sun Capital, a foreign exchange broker recommended by Wong.
facts.F3: Huge profits were allegedly made from executed trades, but the Plaintiff was not able to withdraw monies from the purported 'trading accounts', unless a hefty fee, being 10% of the profits, was paid to Red Sun.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff did investigation and discovered that Red Sun was a real company in Hong Kong but had a different website from the one with which the Plaintiff created his trading account.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff seeks information from the Banks to identify the wrongdoers and to trace and recover the stolen Monies.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff served the Originating Summons on the Banks, neither of which contested the proceedings and did not appear.
facts.F7: The wrongdoers who own and/or operate the Accounts have been unjustly enriched at the expense of the Plaintiff.
facts.F8: The Banks have information available to them which has been derived from its innocent role in the fraud as custodian of the Accounts.

parties: Defendant: KONG HING WAH formerly trading as E AND C-T ENGINEERING CO.

facts.F1: The applicant was employed by the respondent as an air-conditioning apprentice.
facts.F2: On 26 June 2017, the applicant was working at the back lane of a vegetable stall in Yuen Long, New Territories and was standing on an A-shape ladder to dismantle a split type air-conditioner at a height of about 15 feet above the ground.
facts.F3: The applicant suffered from an electric shock and fell down from the ladder, injuring his left wrist, right middle finger, low back, and neck.
facts.F4: The applicant was 34 years old at the time of the accident.
facts.F5: The applicant attended the A&E Department of Pok Oi Hospital on the day after the accident and was put on left wrist cast for his left wrist injury.
facts.F6: The applicant was followed up at the A&E follow-up clinic on 7 July 2017 and 21 July 2017, and was referred to the Orthopaedic Clinic for further assessment.
facts.F7: The applicant’s left wrist pain was treated conservatively, and his right middle finger swelling was treated with operation on 19 December 2017.
facts.F8: Between 10 January 2018 and 31 January 2018, the applicant attended 2 sessions of physiotherapy at the Physiotherapy Department of the Tin Shui Wai Hospital.
facts.F9: The applicant’s monthly earnings at the time of the accident was $18,750 ($750 x 25 working days).
facts.F10: The applicant still experiences residual pain in his back and right middle finger.
facts.F11: The compensation for permanent partial incapacity under section 9 is calculated as 3% of the applicant’s monthly earnings at the time of the accident multiplied by 96 months.
facts.F12: The compensation for temporary incapacity under section 10 is calculated as the periodical payments due to the applicant for the periods of absence from duty certified by the Board.

facts.F1: The validity of the purported arbitration agreement in this case is to be governed by English law.
facts.F2: On 28 March 2019, OCBC issued the notice to commence arbitration ('the Arbitration Notice').
facts.F3: Commencement of arbitration was plainly OCBC’s act to preserve its claim pending resolution of the jurisdictional dispute rather than submission to arbitration.
facts.F4: The arbitration agreement in the Charterparty has not been incorporated into the Bills of Lading by reference.
facts.F5: General words of incorporation in a bill of lading will not normally be sufficient to incorporate an arbitration clause in a charterparty under English law.

parties: Plaintiff: Ting Kam Yuen, the lawful attorney for and on behalf of the Dependants of Tong Kwok Fong, deceased, and as the Personal Representative of the Estate of Tong Kwok Fong, deceased
Defendant: Cheung Wing Kin, the Representative of the Estate of Cheung Tak Ming (deceased) and Cheung Wing Kin, the Representative of the Estate CHOW TAI HO (deceased)

facts.F1: Tak Ming’s vessel went for a fishing trip on 14 March 1993, and a collision occurred between the vessel and a ship at around 5 am on 15 March 1993.
facts.F2: Tak Ming died after being rescued by a container ship, MV Kuo Chang, more than an hour later.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff and the Defendants disagree on whether Tak Ming survived Chow or vice versa.
facts.F4: Section 11 of the Conveyancing and Property Ordinance, Cap.219 provides that where two or more persons die in circumstances rendering it uncertain that any one of them, or which of them, survived the other or others, such deaths shall be presumed to have occurred in order of seniority.
facts.F5: The burden of proof is on the Plaintiff to demonstrate, with evidence, a defined and warranted conclusion that the younger person had died before the older one.
facts.F6: The sea was calm and foggy at the time of the collision, and there was some visibility.
facts.F7: Other survivors would have responded to the incessant shouting of the brothers if they were present.
facts.F8: Chow, Kok, and Tong were all carried into the water by the sinking vessel and were unable to swim up again.
facts.F9: Chow had passed away shortly after the collision and Tak Ming survived her for no less than an hour.

facts.F1: The 1st plaintiff is a company incorporated under the laws of St Lucia and beneficially owned and controlled by Noble Group Holdings Limited.

facts.F11: The plaintiffs transferred the funds to the 1st defendant’s account as a result of a scheme of fraud perpetrated against them.

requested_remedy: The plaintiff sought the determination and/or construction of three questions of law, including whether Section 12 of the Sale of Goods Ordinance applies to the Sales Contract, whether the defendant's emails constituted reasonable notices to the plaintiff, and whether the defendant was entitled to terminate the Contract with immediate effect on 27 May 2021

facts.F1: On 17 April 2020, the plaintiff as buyer and the defendant as seller entered into a contract for the sale and purchase of steel bars (the contract) for a 2-year period commencing 1 May 2020
facts.F2: Clause 12 of the Contract stipulates that payments are to be made within 30 days from the date of delivery, and if payments are not received within the stipulated period, the defendant shall have the right to suspend further delivery of commodities under the Contract and/or terminate this Contract
facts.F3: Between 1 May 2020 and 27 May 2021, the plaintiff placed 24 purchase orders with the defendant
facts.F4: By May 2021, the defendant had sent several emails to the plaintiff requesting payment, reminding them that payments aggregating in excess of $901,000 were overdue and that the defendant had the right to suspend delivery of commodities immediately and/or terminate the contract
facts.F5: By 27 May 2021, the overdue payments exceeded $2.9 million, and the defendant exercised its right to terminate the contract
facts.F6: The plaintiff received a request to collect a cheque for the overdue payments on 27 May, and the defendant deposited the cheque with the bank the following day
facts.F7: Apart from the delivery made of a purchase order on 31 May, the defendant has refused to further supply steel bars to the plaintiff
facts.F8: The plaintiff commenced this action on 12 January 2022 and issued the present summons on 22 April 2022
facts.F9: The contract was for the supply of a large quantity of steel bars over a two-year period
facts.F10: The total value of the commodities under the contract was $49 million
