claim: Claim for value of goods sold and services rendered to the Defendant, totaling $357,880
requested_remedy: Claim for value of goods sold and services rendered to the Defendant, totaling $357,880

facts.F1: The Plaintiff agreed to sell 3 units of garbage compactors to the Defendant on September 5, 2005, at a total price of $564,300.
facts.F2: The Defendant paid 40% of the price as deposit for the 3 garbage compactors in early October 2005.
facts.F3: The Defendant tendered a cheque for the remaining 60% of the price, but with the condition that if the equipment malfunctioned within 3 days, it would countermand payment.
facts.F4: The Defendant collected the 3 garbage compactors on October 31, 2005, but later discovered malfunctions and notified the Plaintiff to withhold payment.
facts.F5: The Defendant appointed a firm of surveyors, Flying Horse, to inspect the garbage compactors, and the preliminary report stated that the compactors were not brand new machines.
facts.F6: The Defendant's solicitors demanded the Plaintiff to agree to the rescission of the agreement and return the paid deposit.
facts.F7: The final survey report by Flying Horse identified various defects and abnormalities in the garbage compactors.
facts.F8: The Defendant acquired 3 replacement garbage compactors elsewhere at a total price of $375,000.
facts.F9: The Defendant's company director, Madam Chung Wai Ming, testified that the Plaintiff's representative, Mr. Willie Chan, assured her that the garbage compactors were brand new and well-functioned.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff's representative, Mr. Chan, explained that the compactors were shipped from overseas and exposed in an open area, resulting in some rust on the compactors.
facts.F11: The Defendant's staff noticed excessive and obvious rust on the compactors during inspections.
facts.F12: The compactors had been stored for about 2 years.

claim: Specific performance of the sale and purchase agreement under Order 86
requested_remedy: Specific performance of the sale and purchase agreement under Order 86

facts.F1: On 25 November 1996, the plaintiff and defendant entered into a provisional agreement for sale and purchase of a flat in Shatin.
facts.F2: The agreed price was $12,550,000, consisting of a $500,000 initial deposit, a $755,000 further deposit upon signing of the Formal Agreement on or before 10-12-1996, and a balance of $11,295,000 upon completion on or before 7-01-1997.
facts.F3: The agreement required the seller to deliver vacant possession of the premises to the Purchaser upon completion.
facts.F4: Clauses 6 and 7 of the agreement stipulated that the seller could back out of the sale by returning the initial deposit plus an equal sum and paying stamp duty if he failed to complete the sale in accordance with the agreement.
facts.F5: On 6, 9 and 10 December 1996, the Purchaser's solicitors requested a draft sale and purchase agreement from the Seller's solicitors.
facts.F6: The Purchaser's solicitors delivered a formal agreement signed by the Purchaser, along with the further deposit cheque, on 10 December 1996.
facts.F7: The Seller's solicitors returned the formal agreement and cheque, and sent their own cheque for $1 million, purporting to act under clause 7, on 12 December 1996.
facts.F8: The Seller's solicitors claimed the Seller had the right to back out of the sale under clause 7, even though the deadline for signing the formal agreement had passed.
facts.F9: The seller's obligation to complete the sale included executing the assignment and doing what else was required of him under the agreement leading to that final act.
facts.F10: The signing of a formal agreement on or before 10 December 1996 was part of the seller's obligation to complete the sale.
facts.F11: The seller's failure to sign the formal agreement on or before 10 December 1996 meant he had failed to complete the sale in accordance with the agreement.
facts.F12: The seller delayed exercising his rights under clause 7 for 2 days after the deadline for signing the formal agreement had passed.

claim: For damages for breach of contract and/or duty against the defendants as Owners/Charterers of the ship or vessel 'Virginia Moon' in and about the loading, handling, custody care and discharge of the plaintiffs' cargo on board the ship 'Virginia Moon' in the year 1979.
requested_remedy: For damages for breach of contract and/or duty against the defendants as Owners/Charterers of the ship or vessel 'Virginia Moon' in and about the loading, handling, custody care and discharge of the plaintiffs' cargo on board the ship 'Virginia Moon' in the year 1979.
parties: Plaintiff: CHINA STEEL CORPORATION and CHINA SHIPBUILDING CORPORATION

facts.F1: The writ was issued on the 22nd November 1980 with an endorsement claiming damages for breach of contract and/or duty against the defendants as Owners/Charterers of the ship or vessel 'Virginia Moon'.
facts.F2: One year later the plaintiffs wholly discontinued the action against the 2nd defendant Fairmont Shipping (H.K.) Ltd.
facts.F3: The writ was served on Virginia Panama by leaving a copy of it at the offices of Fairmont Shipping (H.K.) Ltd., 26th floor, Bank of American Tower, 12 Harcourt Road, Hong Kong.
facts.F4: Fairmont Shipping filed an affirmation stating that they were the Hong Kong agents of Maglines Shipmanagement, Inc. and had no connection with Virginia Panama S.A. nor the 'Virginia Moon' from 21st July 1980.
facts.F5: An affidavit sworn by a partner in the solicitor's firm acting for the plaintiffs stated that the claim arises out of loss and damage to cargo carried on board the 'Virginia Moon' from Kobe, Japan to Kaoshiung, Taiwan in October 1979.
facts.F6: The cargo encountered heavy weather during the voyage, and deck lashings gave way resulting in deck cargo valued at US$363,700 being lost overboard and damage to other hatch covers amounting to US$211,832.
facts.F7: A cargo of ramming mass carried under deck was damaged by seawater, with surveyors advising that damage had been caused during transportation by sea.
facts.F8: Investigations in Panama showed that there would be little purpose in proceeding there, and it was impossible to say that Virginia Panama S.A. had positively established a place of domicile at any one place.
facts.F9: The Hong Kong Companies Register indicated that Mr. Robert Chao-Feng Ho, controller of Maglines Shipmanagement Inc. and Fairmont Shipping (H.K.) Ltd., resided at an address in Kowloon.
facts.F10: At the time the writ was served, it is necessary to look at the company's situation to determine if a foreign company has 'established a place of business' in Hong Kong.

lawsuit_type: Application to strike out service of writ

claim: The plaintiffs claim that the defendants, as transferees of the restaurant business, have incurred liability for their claims under the Transfer of Business (Protection of Creditors) Ordinance, Cap. 49, as the defendants did not give notice of the transfer according to the provisions of the Ordinance.
requested_remedy: The plaintiffs claim that the defendants, as transferees of the restaurant business, have incurred liability for their claims under the Transfer of Business (Protection of Creditors) Ordinance, Cap. 49, as the defendants did not give notice of the transfer according to the provisions of the Ordinance.
parties: Plaintiff: MAN YEE (a firm), CHOW KAM CHEONG, trading as CHEONG KEE ROASTED PORK, IP MOON CHUEN, trading as SHUN FAT MEAT COMPANY (PORK DEPARTMENT) and KWAN KOK HUNG, trading as HOP SHING HO TRADING COMPANY (a firm)
Defendant: CHI TAO ENTERPRISES COMPANY LIMITED trading as KAM TAO RESTAURANT

facts.F1: The four plaintiffs supplied goods to a restaurant trading under the name, the Perennial Restaurant, and were owed different sums of money for the goods.
facts.F2: In early December 1983, Perennial closed down and the plaintiffs were not paid for the goods supplied on credit.
facts.F3: In January 1984, the restaurant was re-opened as the Kam Tao Restaurant by the defendants, who were the owners of a chain of 13 restaurants.
facts.F4: The defendants had purchased the restaurant premises and a controlling interest in Perennial Restaurant Limited from the previous owners, and had surrendered the balance of the term of the ten-year lease.
facts.F5: The defendants also purchased the fixtures and fittings of the previous restaurant for a consideration of HK$349,178.
facts.F6: Madam Lee, a director of the defendant company, gave evidence that there was no attempt to prepare a valuation of the fixtures and fittings, and that their value was essentially nominal.
facts.F7: The amount of HK$349,178 was paid to meet any claims the employees of Perennial may have on the restaurant, including severance pay and arrears of wages.
facts.F8: The new restaurant operated from the same premises as the Perennial Restaurant.
facts.F9: The food served at the new restaurant was similar to that of the Perennial Restaurant.
facts.F10: The defendants operated the new restaurant under the same restaurant licence as Perennial.

lawsuit_type: Claim under the Transfer of Business (Protection of Creditors) Ordinance, Cap. 49

claim: The plaintiff claims against the IO for breaching the statutory duties under the Building Management Ordinance, Cap. 344 (the BMO), the Deed of Mutual Covenants of the Building (the DMC), nuisance and negligence causing the water leakage problem. Mr Kwok claims against the IO for both injunctive relief and damages.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims against the IO for breaching the statutory duties under the Building Management Ordinance, Cap. 344 (the BMO), the Deed of Mutual Covenants of the Building (the DMC), nuisance and negligence causing the water leakage problem. Mr Kwok claims against the IO for both injunctive relief and damages.
parties: Defendant: THE INCORPORATED OWNERS OF KENT BUILDING

facts.F1: The Building was constructed in 1966 and it is for residential use.
facts.F2: Mr Kwok acquired Flat 13B in or about May 1990 and has been its sole registered owner till now.
facts.F3: The roof of the Building (the Roof) consists of Roof A, which is the part of the roof immediately above Flat 13A and Roof B.
facts.F4: The IO acquired, among other things, Roof B by an assignment dated 30 June 2008 at the nominal price of HK$1.00.
facts.F5: In the minutes of a meeting of IO dated 27 March 2012, it was recorded that the owner of Flat 13B had sent to the IO a letter requesting for an extension of the Licence in respect of the Roof.
facts.F6: The IO refused to grant an extension and the Licence ceased to exist in 2013.
facts.F7: Mr Kwok caused the Flat 13B to be partitioned into 3 suites (known as Room A, Room B and Room C) and each of them has its own kitchen and washroom. They have been let out for rental profits.
facts.F8: At the Roof, there is a canopy (the Canopy) and a parapet wall (the Parapet Wall) and it is about 3 feet in height and 40 feet in length. The Parapet Wall separates Roof A and Roof B.
facts.F9: The Building has been managed by CITI-PRO Property Services Co., Ltd. (the Management Company).
facts.F10: By a renovation contract dated 31 August 2010, the IO engaged a contractor known as “差工建築工程有限公司” (the 1st Contractor) to carry out renovation works at the Building.
facts.F11: The 1st Contractor attended the meeting on 26 October 2010 where a resolution was passed to authorize the IO to remove the structures on the Roof.
facts.F12: The 1st Contractor completed the waterproofing works on the Roof including the Canopy after Mr Kwok demolished the toilet at Roof B and the IO demolished other structures on the Roof in 2013.
facts.F13: Another contractor, 国望建築工程有限公司 (the 2nd Contractor), was engaged by the IO to undertake waterproofing works on the Roof in 2014.
facts.F14: The 2nd Contractor reported that the waterproofing works on the Roof had been completed and a water test was administered and passed, as confirmed by the project consultant 谁帕建築审批公司 (the 2nd Consultant).
facts.F15: Despite the completion of such works, the water seepage problem actually persisted.
facts.F16: The IO engaged another contractor Kin Hei Engineering Limited (the 3rd Contractor) to carry out further water resistant works on the Roof in June 2016 and February 2017.
facts.F17: Mr Kwok commenced these proceedings against the IO on 29 March 2017.
facts.F18: The IO did not keep records and contractual notes on its instructions to Kin Hei Engineering Ltd.
facts.F19: The IO did not review and request professionals to check the overall condition of the Roof.
facts.F20: The IO did not provide notifications to the repairing personnel to pay attention to the waterproofing issue.
facts.F21: The IO was aware of the waterproofing problem for over a decade but failed to take proper action.
facts.F22: The IO did not properly delegate its duties to the building management and failed to superintend the performance of Kin Hei Engineering Ltd.

facts.F1: The respondent company has a sheet metal factory in Castle Peak Road.
facts.F2: On 4th July 1991, an application was submitted to the Labour Department, purportedly on behalf of the company, seeking authority for it to operate a special scheme of work for the employment of women and young persons in the factory.
facts.F3: Permission for that scheme was required by virtue of the provisions of the Women and Young Persons (Industry) Regulations.
facts.F4: The Labour Department sent a response dated 11th July granting permission, subject to certain conditions, including the maintenance of a register for workers employed in each group covered by the permission.
facts.F5: In January 1992, a Labour Department Inspector visited the factory premises and asked to see the register, but none was produced.
facts.F6: An information was laid alleging that the respondent failed to maintain a register of women and young persons.
facts.F7: The Crown relied on an admission by Madam Lam, an employee of the company, that no register was maintained.
facts.F8: Madam Lam was neither a director nor the secretary of the respondent company.
facts.F9: Madam Lam had been dealing with the Labour Department on behalf of the company regarding the special scheme.
facts.F10: She had signed the application for the special scheme and a statutory notice, Form LD334.
facts.F11: The Labour Department inspector spoke to Madam Lam at the factory during the visit in January 1992.
facts.F12: The respondent company had permitted Madam Lam to act on its behalf in its dealings with the Labour Department.
facts.F13: Madam Lam was authorized by the company to appear on its behalf at the hearing before the magistrate.

requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed that his termination of service was contrary to the Rules of Natural Justice and sought an order of certiorari
parties: Defendant: The Government of Hong Kong, later amended to Secretary of the Civil Service

facts.F1: The plaintiff joined the Royal Hong Kong Police Force on October 31, 1969, as a Probationary Police Inspector.
facts.F2: After 3 years of service, he was confirmed to the permanent and pensionable establishment and was promoted to the rank of Senior Inspector of Police.
facts.F3: In November 1975, he was transferred from the permanent and pensionable establishment to contractual terms of service.
facts.F4: In 1977, he passed the qualifying examination for promotion to the rank of Superintendent, but was not promoted.
facts.F5: On July 21, 1978, he received a letter from the Secretary for the Civil Service informing him of the government's intention to terminate his service.
facts.F6: The letter stated that the government had received allegations of the plaintiff's association with persons of undesirable character and his interest in a nightclub.
facts.F7: The plaintiff's solicitors replied to the letter, denying the allegations and requesting further information.
facts.F8: The government did not provide the requested information, and on September 25, 1978, the plaintiff received a letter terminating his service.
facts.F9: The plaintiff applied for an order of certiorari, claiming that he had not been given sufficient information to enable him to correct or contradict the allegations made against him.
facts.F10: There was correspondence between the parties before the termination of the plaintiff's service.
facts.F11: The Government did not afford the plaintiff an opportunity to be heard before the termination of his service.

parties: Plaintiff: Skillsoft Asia Pacific Pty Ltd

facts.F1: The plaintiff (Skillsoft) and the defendant (Ambow) entered into an agreement dated 30 April 2008, under which Ambow was appointed as the distributor of Skillsoft’s products in China.
facts.F2: The agreement contained various obligations on Ambow, including the provision of monthly Sales Reports in the agreed format and the maintenance of records relating to its distribution of Skillsoft’s products.
facts.F3: The agreement also provided for audit rights in favour of Skillsoft to determine whether applicable fees had been paid in accordance with the agreement and to ensure compliance with the terms of the agreement.
facts.F4: On 19 September 2011, Ambow issued a notice to Skillsoft to exercise an option to become a non-exclusive distributor of Skillsoft’s products from January 2012.
facts.F5: Skillsoft responded on 22 September 2011, stating that Ambow’s obligations to make pre-payment of licence fees would continue despite the change from an exclusive distributor to a non-exclusive one.
facts.F6: Ambow reacted on the next day by terminating the agreement on 31 December 2011.
facts.F7: Skillsoft contends that the agreement expired on 31 December 2013 at the end of its stated term of 5 years and 8 months, while Ambow says that the agreement expired on 31 December 2011 in accordance with its termination letter dated 23 September 2011.
facts.F8: There is a fundamental dispute between the parties on when the term of the agreement ended.
facts.F9: An upcoming trial is scheduled to determine the issues between the parties.

facts.F1: The plaintiff entered into a provisional agreement to buy the Flat from Endenne Development Limited on 7 April 1997.
facts.F2: Fung Ping Yan, a director of Endenne Development Limited, was also employed as a liaison clerk by the solicitors acting for the plaintiff.
facts.F3: The solicitors acting for the plaintiff were not provided with a No Objection Letter (NOL) from the District Lands Office Yuen Long (DLOYL) at the time of the sale, but were later provided with a fake NOL dated 13 December 1995.
facts.F4: The redevelopment in the Property was unauthorised and in breach of the Buildings Ordinance, as stated in a letter from DLOYL to solicitors acting for purchasers of the 1st floor unit in the Property dated 26 May 2000.

facts.F6: The plaintiff paid off the mortgage on 14 October 2005, having repaid the principal loan, plus interest and a pre-payment charge.
facts.F7: Fung knowingly made false representations to the plaintiff to induce him to buy the Flat.
facts.F8: The defendants provided a fake Approval Letter, exemption certificates, and NOL, as demonstrated by the letter from DLOYL to solicitors acting for purchasers of the 1st floor unit in the Property dated 26 May 2000.

parties: Plaintiff: Hang Yick Properties Management Limited
Defendant: The Incorporated Owners of Kam Fung Building, Yuen Long

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was appointed as the building manager of Kam Fung Building at Castle Peak Road, Yuen Long in 1988.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff's appointment was terminated in October 1994.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff claims to have incurred and accumulated a deficit of HK$267,540.07 between 1989 and October 1994.
facts.F4: The Defendant is the Incorporated owners of Kam Fung Building.
facts.F5: The Defendant alleges that the Plaintiff has breached the terms and conditions of the deed of mutual covenant.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff failed to deliver all books and accounts to the Defendant or the owners of the building.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff did not provide an accurate summary of all items of income and expenditure for the management of the building.
facts.F8: The Plaintiff did not report on the balance sheet as at the date of termination of the appointment of the manager.
facts.F9: The Defendant alleges that the Plaintiff's claimed expenses were not wholly, exclusively or properly incurred in the management of the building.
facts.F10: The trial of the action is scheduled to start on 21 June 2000 and end on 23 June 2000.
facts.F11: The Defendant complained that the vouchers, invoices, and other accounting documents for the period from February 1988 to June 1991 ('pre-1991') were not discovered by the Plaintiff until Thursday, 18 May 2000.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff's former solicitors had claimed that these documents were not in the Plaintiff's possession, but they were in fact possessed by the Plaintiff.
facts.F13: The Defendant is asking for the trial date to be vacated to deal with the recently discovered documents.
facts.F14: The Defendant took out another application to adjourn the trial fixed for 21 June 2000.
facts.F15: The Plaintiff argues that the late disclosure of the 'pre-1991' accounting documents has been corrected by the further discovery made on 18 May 2000.
facts.F16: The Plaintiff adduced evidence that there ought to be ample time for the Defendant to produce an accounting report by 21 June 2000.
facts.F17: The Defendant had an opportunity to compile an accountant's report by 21 June 2000 if it proceeds with due diligence after the discovery of the 'pre-1991' accounting documents.

facts.F1: The plaintiff is a company incorporated in Hong Kong carrying on the business of inter-dealing broking.
facts.F2: The 1st defendant (Chan) was formerly an employee of the plaintiff on its equity desk, and was the head of the equity desk.
facts.F3: The 2nd defendant (Kwok) was also formerly an employee of the plaintiff on its equity desk, and was the deputy head of the equity desk.
facts.F4: Chan and Kwok gave advanced notice to the plaintiff of their resignations and of the termination of their employment with the plaintiff at the end of the notice period specified in their employment contract.
facts.F5: They also reserved their right under s. 7(2) of the Employment Ordinance to leave the plaintiff earlier by paying or agreeing to pay the plaintiff wages in lieu of notice for the balance of the unserved notice period.
facts.F6: On the same day as Chan and Kwok sent their letters terminating their employment, 5 other brokers also sent almost identical letters terminating their employment with the plaintiff.
facts.F7: Chan and Kwok and the 5 other brokers all left to join Nittan Capital (Hong Kong) Limited (Nittan HK).
facts.F8: This was almost the whole of the plaintiff's equity desk.
facts.F9: The undisputed evidence is that the considerable portion of the income of Chan and Kwok over the said years was in the bonuses paid to them.
facts.F10: The bonuses payable under Chan's and Kwok's contracts of employment were not 'wages' within the meaning of s. 2 of the Ordinance.
facts.F11: The bonuses were payable as a matter of contractual obligation or were of a gratuitous nature, payable only at the plaintiff's discretion.
facts.F12: The plaintiff claimed that Chan and Kwok failed to comply with their statutory obligation to make full payment in lieu of notice, as the payments made did not include any bonus.
facts.F13: The plaintiff's claims were not for common law damages but simply for the sums claimed on the basis that each of Chan and Kwok had failed to comply with their statutory obligation to make full payment in lieu of notice.

claim: employees’ compensation
requested_remedy: employees’ compensation
parties: Plaintiff: CHEUNG KAI CHI for and on behalf of the Dependents of the deceased, CHEUNG KIN KEUNG
Defendant: CHUN WO CONTRACTORS LIMITED (1st Respondent) and CHUN WO FOUNDATIONS LIMITED (2nd Respondent)

facts.F1: The Deceased was employed as a welder ganger by the 2nd Respondent at a construction site near Choi Hung Park and Ride Development, and he was fatally injured near the back of a crawler crane on 13 March 2002.
facts.F2: The Labour Department’s investigation showed that the crawler crane created a trapping area between the rear carriage of the crane and the drill head when it was being operated for hoisting purposes.
facts.F3: A re-construction of the scene of the accident showed that a clearance between the dead end of the rear carriage of the crane and the drill head was about 15 centimetres.
facts.F4: The severity and multiplicity of the injury which resulted in the complete separation of the cervical vertebrae and severance of the Deceased’s spinal cord suggests that the injury was caused by mechanical force.
facts.F5: The driver of the crawler crane was being investigated for homicide but he was then operating the crane at the instruction of the foreman and the signaller, and it is unlikely that the incident was an act of revenge or a personal grudge between him and the Deceased.
facts.F6: The Deceased was last seen 35 minutes before the accident examining the drill head, and he was wearing protective clothes and gloves which would be worn by workers performing welding work which was the kind of which for which he was employed.
facts.F7: The Deceased was certified dead upon arrival at the hospital, with numerous abrasions and bruises over his body, fracture-separation between the 5th and 6th cervical vertebra with complete transaction of spinal cord, fractures of spinous processes of the 4th to 7th cervical and 1st to 7th thoracic vertebrae and fractures of left transverse processes of the 5th to 7th thoracic vertebrae.
facts.F8: The Deceased was 49 years old at the time of the accident, and his salary was in excess of $21,000 per month.
facts.F9: The driver of the crawler crane was operating the crane at the instruction of the foreman and the signaller.
facts.F10: The Deceased was last seen alive doing work-related activities.
facts.F11: The Deceased was crushed to death by the slewing motion of the crawler crane.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff agreed to sell and the Defendant agreed to purchase the Property at the price of HK$8,380,000.00, with completion to take place on or before 23 July 2008, according to an agreement in writing dated 15 February 2008.
facts.F2: The Defendant paid deposits of HK$838,000.00 or 10% of the purchase price as required.
facts.F3: The Defendant failed to complete the sale of the Property by paying the balance of the purchase price on 23 July 2008.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff accepted the Defendant's repudiation and forfeited the deposits by letter dated 23 July 2008.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff instructed Midland Realty Ltd. to offer the Property for resale at the price of HK$7,800,000.00 on 31 July 2008, which was later reduced to HK$5,350,000.00 on 5 November 2008.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff entered into a provisional agreement to resell the Property for HK$4,950,000.00 on 27 November 2008, and the sale was completed on 20 February 2009.
facts.F7: The open market value of the Property as at 23 July 2008 was HK$7,000,000.00, as indicated by the Joint Expert Report of the parties.
facts.F8: The property prices in the New Territories were relatively stable in July and August 2008, according to the price indices.
facts.F9: The global financial crisis caused an alarming slump in the property market starting from the end of September 2008.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff did not possess the information on the open market value of the Property at the time of resale.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff was advised by estate agents when fixing the resale price of the Property.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff did not commission expert valuation before fixing the resale price of the Property.

facts.F1: On 18 February 1972, the Plaintiff was injured in a traffic accident while a passenger in a car driven by a deceased person.
facts.F2: The deceased driver was prosecuted for careless driving and pleaded guilty, admitting the facts before the Magistrate.
facts.F3: The deceased driver had conceded that he felt sleepy prior to the accident and that the weather was fine and the road surface was good.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff claimed special damages, including family visits, Chinese medicine charges, extra nourishment, and other expenses.
facts.F5: The Defence disputed some of the special damages claims.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff was hospitalized for less than a month and treated as an out-patient for a little over a month.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff suffered no compound fractures, and his conditions were not serious.
facts.F8: The medical report from Queen Elizabeth Hospital stated that the Plaintiff's confinement and treatment were uneventful.
facts.F9: A surgeon testified that the Plaintiff would need a further operation, which would cost around $3,000, and require a 7-day hospital stay.
facts.F10: The deceased driver's admission of guilt and the facts conceded during the traffic prosecution were used as evidence of negligence.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff's medical history was considered in determining general damages.
facts.F12: The medical report from Queen Elizabeth Hospital and the surgeon's testimony were used to determine the extent of the Plaintiff's injuries.

facts.F1: Two almost simultaneous collisions occurred near the termination of the East Lamma Channel Traffic Separation Scheme, Hong Kong, at around 3:37am and 3:40am on 14 May 2011, among three container vessels: Xin Nan Tai 77, MCC Jakarta, and TS Singapore.
facts.F2: The 1st Collision was between Xin Nan Tai and Jakarta, and the 2nd Collision was between Jakarta and Singapore.
facts.F3: The weather was generally fine, and visibility was around 8 nautical miles.
facts.F4: Prior to the collisions, Jakarta and Singapore were outbound from Hong Kong, navigating in the outbound traffic lane of the Lamma Scheme on a south-easterly course.
facts.F5: Xin Nan Tai was navigating along the Dangan Shuidao Traffic Separation Scheme, steering a westerly course.
facts.F6: The collisions occurred in a crossing situation, with Xin Nan Tai being the 'give-way' vessel and Jakarta being the 'stand-on' vessel.
facts.F7: Around 03:34, Xin Nan Tai altered course 10 degrees to starboard.
facts.F8: Xin Nan Tai did not take early and substantial action to give way to Jakarta.
facts.F9: Jakarta did not maintain a proper lookout and observe Xin Nan Tai in good time prior to the 1st Collision.
facts.F10: Jakarta altered course to port in breach of COLREGS, but this breach did not contribute to the 2nd Collision.
facts.F11: Singapore is 5% to blame for the 2nd Collision.

facts.F2: The Defendants purported to rescind the agreement on 28 May 1998, citing that the property was included in an Outline Zoning Plan (OZP) No. S/H20/6 which showed that the site occupied by the oil depot and supplies building was zoned for Industrial use and the area bordering the basin was zoned for Cargo Handling Area.

facts.F6: The zoning of the site where the oil depot and supplies building now stand for Industrial use and the area bordering the basin for Cargo Handling Area do not produce any injurious or prejudicial effect on the Premises.
facts.F7: The Defendants indicated that they would refuse to complete, which led to the Plaintiff accepting the repudiation.

claim: The applicant claimed she would face a risk to her life if she was sent back to Indonesia due to the loan shark's threat to harm or kill her.
requested_remedy: The applicant claimed she would face a risk to her life if she was sent back to Indonesia due to the loan shark's threat to harm or kill her.

facts.F1: The applicant was born on 12/12/1984 in Purwosari village, Central Java, Indonesia.
facts.F2: Her parents and younger sister were in Indonesia.
facts.F3: She had education for 9 years.
facts.F4: She was a domestic worker in Malaysia (2006-2008), Singapore (2008-2010), and Hong Kong (2010-2015).
facts.F5: She was single.
facts.F6: She came to Hong Kong on 4/10/2017 as a domestic helper under a 2-year contract.
facts.F7: She was arrested by Immigration Officers for taking up unapproved employment.
facts.F8: She was sentenced to imprisonment for 4 months.
facts.F9: She lodged the non-refoulement claim in this case in July 2018.
facts.F10: In late 2017, her parents called her while she was in Hong Kong, informing her that they had borrowed a loan of 180 million Rupiah from a loan shark.
facts.F11: They could not repay by the deadline in January 2018 and had agreed that the applicant would marry the loan shark as an alternative for settling the loan when she returned to Indonesia.
facts.F12: The applicant did not know anything about the loan shark.
facts.F13: A few days later, she talked to the loan shark on the phone, asking for an extension of the deadline, but the loan shark refused and threatened to kill her if she refused to marry him.
facts.F14: She changed her phone number to stop any contact from her parents and the loan shark since the end of 2017.
facts.F15: She believed the situation remained the same, but she had no updated information about her parents, the loan, and the loan shark.
facts.F16: She thought the police would not help as this was a personal matter, and the police would not assist an ordinary woman like her.
facts.F17: She did not feel safe in Jakarta or Surabaya.
facts.F18: She had no relatives or friends who could offer a shelter elsewhere in Indonesia.
facts.F19: She refused to marry the loan shark as an alternative for settling her parents' loan.
facts.F20: She feared that her parents might force her to marry the loan shark.
facts.F21: She was in fear that the loan shark would harm or kill her if she returned to Indonesia.
facts.F22: The applicant applied for leave for judicial review of the decisions of the TCAB on 20/2/2019.
facts.F23: The notice of hearing was sent to her updated address, but there was no return of mail.

facts.F1: The plaintiff, Mr Chan, purchased a property called House Type 4A, No.10 of Gmelina Path, Palm Springs, Phase 1C in the New Territories (the Property) for $12.18 million under a provisional agreement dated 20 September 1997.
facts.F2: At the time of purchase, the property market in Hong Kong was very active, and many speculators, including Mr Chan, would give blank cheques and blank signed provisional agreements to estate agents to buy a property that could be quickly resold for a profit.
facts.F3: The plaintiff instructed the estate agent, Mr Wong, to find a property worth not more than $13 million and with a size of not less than 2000 sq. ft.
facts.F4: The defendant signed the provisional agreement on 20 September 1997 after being persuaded by Mr Wong.
facts.F5: The plaintiff did not see the Property before purchasing it, which was common practice among speculators in Hong Kong at the time.
facts.F6: The next day, the plaintiff, his wife, and another lady visited the Property with Mr Wong and saw the garden, various parts of the house, and a fibre glass structure on the roof that was not authorized by the manager of the building.
facts.F7: The plaintiff knew that the structure was unauthorised and might be removed by the manager, but he still wanted to retain it.
facts.F8: A supplemental agreement was signed on 8 October 1997 to retain the fibre glass structure on the roof.
facts.F9: The plaintiff tried to resell the house for a quick profit but failed due to a decline in the market price.
facts.F10: A notice was served by the manager to remove the fibre glass structure, and the plaintiff relied on clause 23(a) of the formal sale and purchase agreement to rescind the agreement and claim back his deposit.
facts.F11: There was an agreement contained in the document at p.206 that required the vendor to retain the fibre glass structure.
facts.F12: There was a document at p.207 that handed over the keys to the premises to the plaintiff and required him to assume all responsibilities, including paying all outgoings.

requested_remedy: confirmation of reduction of capital

facts.F1: The Company was incorporated in Hong Kong on 11 May 1990 and changed its name to its present name on 5 July 1990.
facts.F2: Its principal business is the trading of data and word processing consumable supplies.
facts.F3: The present authorised share capital of the Company is HK$8.5 million divided into 85,000 shares of HK$100.00 each, all of which had been issued and were fully paid up or credited as fully paid up.
facts.F4: There are only two shareholders, Fujicopian Company Limited and Fuji Kako Company Limited, both incorporated in Japan.
facts.F5: A special resolution was passed at a duly convened extraordinary general meeting on 22 December 2003, whereby it was resolved that the authorised and paid up capital is to be reduced from HK$8.5 million divided into 85,000 shares of HK$100.00 each to HK$1,955,000.00 divided into 85,000 shares of HK$23.00 each.
facts.F6: The Company had increased its capital in 1995 and 1996 to support its production line in Mainland China, but the production line was closed in 1999.
facts.F7: The board of directors considered that the capital of HK$8.5 million is in excess of the wants of the Company and proposed to reduce the capital to HK$1,955,000.00.
facts.F8: The financial statements as at 31 October 2003 showed that the Company had stable profits, with a profit for the financial year ended 2002 of HK$2,233,469.00 and a profit for the financial year ended 2003 of HK$2,360,837.00.
facts.F9: The Company had net current assets of HK$11,388,106.00 as at 31 October 2003.
facts.F10: The Company had current liabilities of HK$1,756,490.00 as at 31 October 2003, made up of trading and other payables, the amount due to Fujicopian Japan, and the amount due to Fujicopian USA.
facts.F11: The unaudited payment schedule of purchase creditors as at 31 July 2004 showed that the Company had made purchases from Fujicopian Japan of HK$9,503,106.00 from 1 November 2003 to 31 July 2004.
facts.F12: Fujicopian Japan, Fujicopian USA, and Palmetto Imaging Technology, LLC wrote letters stating they have no objection to the proposed reduction of capital.
facts.F13: The Company had properly explained the proposals to the shareholders.
facts.F14: The reduction of capital would not deplete assets available for the payment of debts.
facts.F15: The interests of creditors had been safeguarded.

claim: The Plaintiff claims damages for breach of contract for the Defendant's failure to accept the black cloth, which the Plaintiff alleges meets the contractual requirements.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff claims damages for breach of contract for the Defendant's failure to accept the black cloth, which the Plaintiff alleges meets the contractual requirements.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff and the Defendant entered into a contract on 24th May 1991 for the sale by the Plaintiff to the Defendant of a total of 21700 yards of corduroy cloth printed with a design.
facts.F2: On 20th June 1991, the Plaintiff produced samples for the Defendant's approval of the colour and design.
facts.F3: Changes were made to the colours and it was agreed that the black material would be printed only on one side to achieve a softer finish.
facts.F4: On 8th July, the Plaintiff produced further samples, which were stamped by the Defendant on the back to show they were approved.

facts.F1: Gavin Watson, the Plaintiff's managing director, and his friend Stephen Mansfield visited the Defendant's motor car showroom in Gloucester Road, Wanchai, on 6th May 2000.
facts.F2: Mr. Watson was highly knowledgeable about motor cars and was looking for a car for his wife, saw a Mercedes Benz S320 which seemed suitable, and spoke to the salesman, Mr. Michael Wong.
facts.F3: Mr. Watson was aware that the Defendant was not a Mercedes Benz authorised dealer and was keen to establish the provenance of the car, specifically that it was a brand new car manufactured in 2000.
facts.F4: Mr. Wong confirmed that the S320 was a 2000 model and had been imported directly from Germany, and later agreed to provide the Mercedes Benz S430, which had a larger engine, as an alternative option.
facts.F5: Mr. Watson purchased the S430 on 12th May 2000, with a purchase agreement describing the car as a 'Brand New 2000 M. Benz S430L' with a purchase price of $1,040,000.
facts.F6: The car was eventually delivered on 19th June 2000, with an invoice from AGA Motors describing the car as a 'Brand New 2000 M. Benz S430L'.
facts.F7: In August 2001, Mr. Watson took the car to Zung Fu, the authorised Mercedes Benz dealer, for servicing, and later received a letter stating that the date of manufacture of the car was 18th December 1998, not 2000.
facts.F8: The car had a complete electrical breakdown, and Mr. Watson sold it to a motor dealer for $490,000 on 8th February 2002.
facts.F9: A valuer, Mr. Raymond Lee, valued the car between $500,000 and $520,000, assuming it was a 1998 model, and between $680,000 and $700,000 if it were a 2000 model.
facts.F10: Mr. Watson relied on Mr. Wong's statement about the car's age in making the purchase.
facts.F11: The car was not manufactured in 2000, but in 1998.

claim: breach of a contract for sale and purchase of certain made-to-measure furniture and personal injury arising therefrom
requested_remedy: breach of a contract for sale and purchase of certain made-to-measure furniture and personal injury arising therefrom
parties: Defendant: MAJESTIC FURNITURE & INTERIOR DESIGN LIMITED

facts.F1: On 12 July 2008, Ellen visited Majestic’s store in North Point with a view to purchasing made-to-measure wooden household furniture.
facts.F2: Ellen was assured that the furniture sold by Majestic was made of E-1 grade timber and toxin-free plywood from Indonesia.
facts.F3: In reliance on the representations of the salesmen and the documents shown to her, Ellen agreed to purchase the furniture from Majestic at the price of HK$38,000.
facts.F4: Upon partial refund by Majestic in October 2008, the price paid by Ellen was reduced to HK$31,560.
facts.F5: On 5 October 2008, Majestic delivered the furniture to Ellen at her residence, but the furniture contained extremely high levels of formaldehyde and total VOC (Volatile Organic Compounds) and were not safe.
facts.F6: Ellen suffered personal injury as a result of exposure to toxins emitted from the furniture, including allergic symptoms in the eyes, throat, nose, lung and skin.
facts.F7: An expert report by Professor Christopher Y.H. Chao confirmed that the furniture was the source of the high level of toxins recorded in Ellen’s residence.
facts.F8: An expert report by Dr Joseph Pang confirmed that Ellen suffered personal injury as a result of exposure to the toxins emitted from the furniture.

facts.F8: The defendant alleged that the plaintiff had entered Hong Kong unlawfully on five occasions between 2000 and 2003 and was repatriated to the Mainland each time.
facts.F9: The plaintiff was charged with common assault and unlawful remaining in Hong Kong, and was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment.

facts.F2: The contract required prompt shipment from Italian main port within 60 days after receipt of letter of credit.
facts.F3: The plaintiff opened its letter of credit promptly but the defendant failed to ship on time.
facts.F4: The plaintiff waived the breach and amended its letter of credit two or three times to allow for late shipment.
facts.F5: On 6th November 1978, the plaintiff served notice on the defendant that they must ship no later than 20th November 1978.

facts.F9: The contract plates were scrap and could not be converted into high tensile or mild steel bars as claimed by the plaintiff.
facts.F10: The damages were assessed on the date of breach, 20th November 1978, which marked the end of the extended time of delivery.

requested_remedy: Application for an order under section 221 of the Companies Ordinance to summon three applicants, namely Francis Young, Benedict Joseph Young, and Cecilia Mary Young, to give information concerning the affairs of King's Dyeing and Weaving Factory Limited.
parties: Defendant: King's Dyeing & Weaving Factory Limited, Kazan Properties and Investment Ltd., Hyperion Corporation

facts.F1: The Official Receiver applied for an order under section 221 of the Companies Ordinance to summon three applicants, namely Francis Young, Benedict Joseph Young, and Cecilia Mary Young, to give information concerning the affairs of King's Dyeing and Weaving Factory Limited.
facts.F2: The Official Receiver was appointed as the provisional liquidator of King's Dyeing and Weaving Factory Limited on 25th July, and subsequently, Special Managers were appointed to assist in the winding-up process.
facts.F3: During the course of negotiations for the sale of King's principal business as a going concern, the Special Managers ascertained that King's had executed a debenture in favour of Kazan charging the assets of the company.
facts.F4: The circumstances surrounding the execution of the debenture by King's in favour of Kazan and the close relationship between King's and Kazan cried out for a full investigation.
facts.F5: The Official Receiver considered that it was necessary to investigate the beneficial ownership of Kazan through Hyperion and for this purpose to obtain access to all books and records that were not in his possession which related to the affairs of King's.
facts.F6: F. Young is a chartered accountant, a partner in the firm of K.K. Young & Co., and has been the auditor of King's.
facts.F7: B.J. Young is both a director of Kazan and Hyperion, and also a director of Ephfra and Anclar, which companies are also directors of Kazan.
facts.F8: C.M. Young appears to be employed as a book-keeper and has been the book-keeper of Kazan and also represented a nominee company as secretary.
facts.F9: The liquidator's report is kept hidden from the examinees.
facts.F10: Section 221 is to provide assistance to the liquidator to try and ascertain the truth about the affairs of the company as expeditiously and economically as possible.

facts.F2: On 12 March 2015, the applicant worked at an industrial building in Tuen Mun, a construction site in Sheung Shui, and the construction site at Sheung Shui Slaughterhouse.
facts.F3: After finishing the scaffolding work at the Slaughterhouse, the applicant went to a warehouse to tidy up the scaffolding tools and materials.
facts.F4: At the warehouse, the applicant's right ankle was cut by a sharp metal sheet at the bottom of the metal gate.
facts.F5: The applicant was driven to the warehouse by the 1st respondent in a truck belonging to the 2nd respondent.
facts.F6: The 1st respondent accepted that he was the sub-contractor of the 2nd respondent, and the 2nd respondent was a sub-contractor of the 3rd and/or 4th respondents.
facts.F7: The applicant filed an application for compensation for the injury, claiming he was an employee directly employed by the 1st respondent.
facts.F8: The 3rd and 4th respondents claimed that the work carried out by the applicant at the warehouse was not part of the work undertaken by them and sub-contracted to the 2nd respondent.
facts.F9: The applicant was employed by the 1st respondent at the material time.
facts.F10: The 1st respondent was driving the truck belonging to the 2nd respondent at the time of the accident.

facts.F1: Ngo entered into a provisional agreement to buy a flat from Endenne on 7 April 1997.
facts.F2: Fung, the director of Endenne, provided documents to Willis, the solicitor acting for Ngo, including an Approval Letter, exemption certificates, and a No-Objection Letter (NOL) from the District Lands Office, Yuen Long (DLOYL).
facts.F3: Willis drafted a Sale and Purchase Agreement (SPA) that included a term requiring Endenne to provide an NOL.
facts.F4: Fung provided a copy of the NOL to Willis after the SPA was signed.
facts.F5: Ngo purchased the flat and moved in, but later discovered that the redevelopment of the property was unauthorised and in breach of the Buildings Ordinance.
facts.F6: The DLOYL had not issued an Approval Letter, exemption certificates, or NOL for the property.
facts.F7: Ngo paid off the mortgage on 14 October 2005 and sought rescission of the Assignment and damages against Endenne and the Firm.
facts.F8: Endenne and its directors, Fung and Chan, made fraudulent misrepresentations to Ngo by providing false documents.
facts.F9: The Assignment was dated 26 May 1997
facts.F10: Payment of damages plus interest by the 3 Defendants is a condition for the rescission of the Assignment.

facts.F8: The door existed and was used from 1965 to 2004.
facts.F9: The door has not been proved to have been an illegal structure.
facts.F10: The door was used for nearly 40 years as a door.

claim: The plaintiff claims for injury, loss and damage suffered due to the collision of the public light bus driven by the defendant
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims for injury, loss and damage suffered due to the collision of the public light bus driven by the defendant

facts.F1: The plaintiff was a passenger on a public light bus driven by the defendant when it collided with another vehicle on Castle Peak Road on 27th May, 1978.
facts.F2: The defendant claimed that the vehicle went out of control due to a punctured tyre.
facts.F3: The plaintiff was not paying attention when the accident occurred and woke up in a hospital.
facts.F4: The defendant initially stated to the police that the oncoming car crossed the double white line and rammed the public light bus.
facts.F5: However, the defendant later stated in the witness-box that he was driving at about 30 m.p.h. when the accident occurred.
facts.F6: The Motor Investigation Bureau's report and the defendant's initial statement to the police contradict the defence filed in the case.
facts.F7: The plaintiff suffered a ruptured right eyeball, multiple lacerations, and fractures in three different bones of the upper face.
facts.F8: The plaintiff underwent two operations and was in hospital for a week.
facts.F9: The plaintiff lost his vision completely and eventually had to have the eyeball removed and replaced with a glass eye.
facts.F10: The plaintiff, a 62-year-old dispenser at a maternity home, now has difficulty reading, watching TV, and judging distances.
facts.F11: The vehicle had a punctured tyre at the time of the collision.
facts.F12: The accident occurred when the oncoming car crossed the double white line and rammed the public light bus, as stated by the defendant initially.
facts.F13: The defendant was driving at about 30 m.p.h. when the accident occurred.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was employed by the 1st Defendant as a demolition worker.
facts.F2: On 31 January 1982, the 1st Defendant fell through a hole in the upper floor and landed on the Plaintiff's head, causing a Jefferson fracture (broken neck).

facts.F4: The Plaintiff has always worked in laboring jobs, first as a mason and then as a demolition worker.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff is married with two children, a married daughter and a 14-year-old son, and has been unable to send them money since the accident.

facts.F8: The Plaintiff has permanent disabilities, including pain over his neck and shoulder, limitation of neck movements, intermittent numbness of his arms and hands, and weakness of his right hand and both lower limbs.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff is now only fit for a job such as a watchman, liftman, or caretaker.
facts.F10: Dr. Wedderburn and Dr. Ng Shi Hon agreed that the Plaintiff should not have the surgery offered.
facts.F11: Dr. Ng estimated the Plaintiff's loss of earning capacity at 20% of the whole man.
facts.F12: Dr. Mao assessed the Plaintiff's impairment at 14% of the whole man.
facts.F13: The Plaintiff's age, health, and disability were considered in determining the multiplier for future loss of earnings.

requested_remedy: Repayment of a loan due under a loan agreement dated 18 July 2000 ('the Loan Agreement') and a claim under Section 60 of the Conveyancing and Property Ordinance, Cap. 219
parties: Defendant: B-Tech (Holdings) Limited (1st Defendant), Coupeville Limited (2nd Defendant), Easycom Limited (3rd Defendant), Thing On Enterprises Limited (4th Defendant)

facts.F1: The Plaintiff, Ampittia Inc., is a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands.
facts.F2: The 1st Defendant, B-Tech (Holdings) Limited was formerly known as Dong-Jun (Holdings) Limited and is a company incorporated in Bermuda.
facts.F3: The 2nd Defendant, Coupeville Limited, is a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and a wholly owned subsidiary of the 1st Defendant.
facts.F4: The 3rd Defendant, Easycom Limited, was a company incorporated in Hong Kong and a wholly owned subsidiary of the 2nd Defendant.
facts.F5: The 3rd Defendant is the registered owner of a commercial property known as Levels 1-3 of Harvest Building with 50 car-parking spaces situate at No. 585 Longhua West Road, Xuhui District, Shanghai, China ('the Shanghai Property').
facts.F6: The 1st Defendant is the holding company in the Group and the Shanghai Property was acquired by the Group in March 2000 at a consideration of HK$88 million.
facts.F7: The 4th Defendant, Thing On Enterprises Limited, is a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and is owned by Wong Chung Tak, a businessman with extensive interest in business activities including diamond trading, securities and commodities dealings, property development and investment in Hong Kong, China and elsewhere.
facts.F8: On 19 January 2001, the 1st and the 2nd Defendants accepted an offer of the 4th Defendant to purchase the entire issued share capital of the 3rd Defendant at HK$25 million.
facts.F9: A formal agreement for sale and purchase dated 31 January 2001 was entered into by the 2nd Defendant as the vendor, the 1st Defendant as the covenantor and the 4th Defendant as the purchaser.
facts.F10: The Injunction Order was hybrid in nature and contained a Mareva Injunction restraining the 1st Defendant from disposing of or dealing with its assets and an interim injunction against all the Defendants to restrain disposal of the shares of the 3rd Defendant and/or the Shanghai Property.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff’s summons was issued on 5 February 2001 for continuation of the Injunction Order.
facts.F12: The 1st to 3rd Defendants and the 4th Defendant issued summonses on 8 and 13 February 2001, respectively, seeking discharge, alternatively variation of the Injunction Order.
facts.F13: The 1st Defendant has an unaudited net asset value of approximately HK$298.9 million as at 30 September 2000.
facts.F14: The 1st Defendant had received letters before actions from solicitors representing certain creditors demanding repayment of loans in the total principal amount of HK$40.5 million.
facts.F15: The 1st Defendant entered into a Placing Agreement and the Property Agreement on 19 January 2001 to raise funds to improve the liquidity position and with a view to reducing the indebtedness of the Group.
facts.F16: Eugene Chuang acting on behalf of the Plaintiff and Vincent Wong Chun Hung ('Vincent Wong'), the Chairman and Executive Director of the 1st Defendant, allegedly made an oral agreement on or about 28 September 2000 extending the repayment date under the Loan Agreement from 18 October 2000 to 17 April 2001.
facts.F17: There was conflicting expert opinion on the valuation of the Shanghai Property.
facts.F18: The 1st Defendant has several other assets besides the Shanghai Property that could be utilized to satisfy its creditors.
facts.F19: The Plaintiff failed to provide a true picture of the financial situation of the 1st Defendant at the ex parte stage.

lawsuit_type: Discharge of an ex parte injunction ('the Injunction Order')

facts.F1: The accident occurred on September 6, 1971, in Tai Po Road near the 16½ mile post, New Territories.
facts.F2: The accident happened at a straight stretch of the road without any speed limit for traffic.
facts.F3: The road was 20 feet, 10 inches wide for a two-way traffic, with each side being approximately 10 feet, 5 inches wide.
facts.F4: There were four trees on the side of the road where the accident happened, with two trees protruding onto the road beside the kerb.
facts.F5: The deceased, Tong Fong, worked as a casual labourer in a wood factory owned by Tang Hong.
facts.F6: The deceased had just finished work and was about to go home when the accident occurred.
facts.F7: Tang Hong, an eyewitness, saw the deceased looking to the direction of Sheung Shui and then taking one step onto the road.
facts.F8: The defendant was driving at a speed of about 30 miles per hour.
facts.F9: The defendant claimed that he saw a white object in front of his car about 2 yards away and took avoiding action, but had to swerve back to the left due to an oncoming bus.
facts.F10: The defendant's vehicle, a Land Rover, had a slight dent on the front left wing.
facts.F11: A police officer drew a sketch showing the various positions of the bloodstained patches on the road and the position of the defendant's vehicle.
facts.F12: The deceased must have stepped down to the road without looking to the direction of the oncoming traffic.
facts.F13: The defendant would not be in a position to avoid the accident anyway, having regard to the circumstances.
facts.F14: At 30 miles per hour, a vehicle would have covered approximately 45 feet in one second, making it difficult for the defendant to avoid the accident.
facts.F15: The defendant must have swerved slightly his vehicle, but not sufficiently to avoid the deceased.

requested_remedy: The claimants sought damages for the death of Khalid Mehmood due to the accident at the workplace.
parties: Plaintiff: BUSHRA BIBI AND NABELA QOSER, the co-administrators of the estate of KHALID, MEHMOOD, the deceased
Defendant: METHOD BUILDING & ENGINEERING WORKS LIMITED (in liquidation), LEIGHTON CONTRACTORS (ASIA) LIMITED and SAFEWELL GONDOLA (HK) LIMITED

facts.F1: The deceased was employed by the 1st defendant to carry out works in relation to the construction of certain aviation fuel facilities in Tuen Mun Area 38 in the New Territories.
facts.F2: The 2nd defendant was the principal contractor at the site and the 1st defendant was its sub-contractor in relation to some of the works being carried on at the site.
facts.F3: The 3rd defendant was responsible for the supply, installation and maintenance of suspended working platforms (gondolas) to be used for the work to be carried out.
facts.F4: On 2 July 2009, the project manager of the 1st defendant instructed the deceased and his team to remove rubbish, tools and other materials from inside Aviation Fuel Tank No. 5 and to carry out cleaning work inside the Tank.
facts.F5: The deceased and his co-workers started work and manually moved out safety harnesses, brushes, old cans and other items through the entrance.
facts.F6: A gondola that had been resting on the floor of the Tank was raised a certain distance from the ground so to enable cleaning work to be done on that part of the floor of the Tank that was immediately below the gondolas.
facts.F7: The deceased attempted to climb onto the working platform of the gondola but failed, and fell 22 metres and suffered multiple injuries from which he died.
facts.F8: The accident was reported and investigated by Mr. Chu Yan Chung, an Occupational Safety Officer of the Labour Department.
facts.F9: An inspection of gondola No. 2 revealed that the three-position control switch was stuck at the 'up' position and that the emergency stop button had not been activated.
facts.F10: The deceased faced a dilemma caused by the negligence of the 1st and 2nd defendants.
facts.F11: The deceased reacted to the dilemma by acting to protect the property of the 1st and 2nd defendants.
facts.F12: The deceased’s action was an ill-judged decision, taken on the spur of the moment, to safeguard the property of his employer, without properly appreciating the severity of the risk involved.

facts.F11: The plaintiff was required to manually push the load over the edge of the pitched roof as the load was caught on the roof when being lowered.
facts.F12: The accident occurred at the Tin Shui Wai Site.

facts.F1: The plaintiff is an inter-dealer broker, and the defendants are its former employees working in its Equity Desk.
facts.F2: The contracts of employment required a six-month notice for termination, but the contracts also provided that the notice could not expire before 8 January 2008.
facts.F3: The defendants notified the plaintiff on 30 November 2006 that they would terminate the contracts by paying the plaintiff wages in lieu of notice.
facts.F4: The defendants tendered payments of wages to the plaintiff which were calculated up to 8 January 2008, but the plaintiff disputes the adequacy of the payments.

facts.F6: The bonuses in question were provided in two letters of the plaintiff dated 3 February 2005 and addressed to the 1st and 2nd defendants respectively.
facts.F7: The 1st and 2nd defendants had received bonuses pursuant to the terms of the letters in April and October 2006.
facts.F8: The plaintiff claims these bonuses from the defendants under section 7 of the Employment Ordinance on the basis that these bonuses 'would have accrued' to them during the period of notice of termination.
facts.F9: The plaintiff has pleaded in its Amended Statement of Claim that the bonuses that would have accrued to the 1st and 2nd defendants in 2007 were the same as those accrued to them in April and October 2006.
facts.F10: The defendants oppose the plaintiff's proposed re-amendment to the Amended Statement of Claim, arguing that the proposed amendments are inconsistent, immaterial, and useless to the matters in issue.
facts.F11: The plaintiff seeks to calculate the bonuses from the business that would have been done for it had the seven former employees remained with it.

facts.F2: The PA stated that the purchase price was HK$1,900,000.00 and the plaintiff paid deposits of HK$570,000.00.
facts.F3: The plaintiff had previously purchased a Small House in 1994 and was aware of the need for consent from the District Lands Office (DLO) and premium payment.

facts.F10: The purchase price and the current market value of the property had a difference of HK$330,000.00.

facts.F3: The relevant terms of the Agreement are Clause 15.01, 15.04, 16.01, 20.02, 20.03 and 20.04.
facts.F4: A requisition on title was raised by the plaintiffs concerning the original of a Power of Attorney (POA) dated 23 May 1997.

facts.F2: The plaintiff in HCA 524/2012 ("Capital Wealth Finance") is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the plaintiff in HCA 522/2012 ("Capital Wealth Corp").
facts.F3: The defendant in both actions ("Mayer") is a Cayman Island company, the shares of which are listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
facts.F4: The plaintiffs claim that they have advanced two loans in the respective sums of $10,000,000 and $5,500,000 to Mayer on 28 June 2011.
facts.F5: Mr Lam Chin Chun ("Mr Lam"), the plaintiffs' Chief Executive Officer, says that he has agreed to provide the loans at the request of Mr Lai Yueh Hsing ("Mr Lai"), a director of Mayer.

facts.F8: There is no dispute that the two sums were paid into Mayer's account with HSBC on 28 June 2011.
facts.F9: Mayer denies the alleged loans.
facts.F10: Mayer produced a written Agreement between Mayer and Golden Tex dated 28 April 2011 for the sale and purchase of the shares in Advance Century.
facts.F11: The consideration provided in that agreement was precisely $15,500,000.
facts.F12: Mayer has also produced a notice from Golden Tex dated 28 June 2011, informing Mayer that the full consideration of HK$15,500,000.00 (US$2,000,000) has been fully settled to Mayer's HSBC saving account.

facts.F14: After 9 months, Mayer suddenly received a letter dated 22 March 2012 from the Plaintiffs' solicitors demanding repayment of the alleged loans.
facts.F15: The plaintiffs have not recorded the transactions in their own books and accounts.

facts.F6: The 2nd defendant met the 1st and 2nd instalment payments in the total sum of HK$1,000,000.00 under the 1st Deed, but no other payment was made.
facts.F7: The 2nd Deed was entered into by the plaintiff, the 1st defendant, and the 2nd defendant on 27 August 2001, with a revised payment schedule, after the 1st defendant's debt had grown to HK$6,712,954.40 by July 2001.

claim: The applicants claim to be the children of the deceased, Chan Lai Fong, for the purpose of the Intestates' Estates Ordinance (Cap. 73) and to be entitled to inherit her estate.
requested_remedy: The applicants claim to be the children of the deceased, Chan Lai Fong, for the purpose of the Intestates' Estates Ordinance (Cap. 73) and to be entitled to inherit her estate.
parties: Plaintiff: YAM YING HUNG, YAM CHOR WUNG, YAM YING KWAN, YAM PUI CHUN, YAM YING YOWN, YAM YING CHEUNG, YAM BIG CHUN

facts.F1: The applicants are children of Yam Wai Cho, who married Madam Lai Wan Chee in 1917 according to Chinese rites and custom.
facts.F2: Madam Lai Wan Chee died in 1940, and Mr. Yam Wai Cho married Madam Chan Lai Fong in 1941, also according to Chinese rites and custom.
facts.F3: The applicants were raised by Madam Chan Lai Fong, who never had any children of her own.
facts.F4: After the applicants got married, they continued to support and maintain Madam Chan Lai Fong financially until her death in 2001.
facts.F5: The applicants were treated as Madam Chan Lai Fong's children, and she was treated as their mother, within the family and in dealings with people outside the family.
facts.F6: The legislative intention behind the repeal of section 2(2)(b) of the Intestates' Estates Ordinance in 1995 was to bring the law in line with current day community expectations and remedy various legal inconsistencies and anomalies.
facts.F7: In Chinese customary law, the concept of 'tin fong' (田房 or 填房) refers to a second wife who marries into a family and 'fills up' the vacancy left behind by the former wife, becoming the mother of all children born by the previous wife.

claim: The plaintiff claims for injunctive relief relating to the use of the ground floor and cockloft of Wing Ming Industrial Centre
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims for injunctive relief relating to the use of the ground floor and cockloft of Wing Ming Industrial Centre
parties: Plaintiff: The Incorporated Owners of Wing Ming Industrial Centre
Defendant: ManTex Supplies Company Limited, China Asset Holdings Limited and Babies Trendyland Limited

facts.F1: The plaintiff is the Incorporated Owners of Wing Ming Industrial Centre, a multi-storey building.
facts.F2: Wing Ming Garment Factory Limited is the registered owner of the ground floor and cockloft of the Building.
facts.F3: The 1st defendant, ManTex Supplies Company Limited, entered into a tenancy agreement with Wing Ming to lease the ground floor and cockloft for a term of two years.
facts.F4: The tenancy agreement restricts the use of the premises to light industrial purposes only.
facts.F5: The 2nd defendant, China Asset Holdings Limited, occupies part of the ground floor and operates a Chinese medical clinic.
facts.F6: The 3rd defendant, Babies Trendyland Limited, occupies part of the ground floor and the entire cockloft and uses it for its business, including trading of children's wear.
facts.F7: The Building is subject to a Deed of Mutual Covenant and the Land Grant, which restrict the use of the building to industrial or godown purposes.
facts.F8: The Occupation Permit prescribes the approved or permitted user of the various parts of the building, including the ground floor and cockloft.
facts.F9: Wing Ming commenced proceedings against the 1st defendant for breach of the user clause in the tenancy agreement and the Deed of Mutual Covenant.
facts.F10: The plaintiff demanded that the defendants cease using the premises for purposes other than those permitted by the Land Grant and the Occupation Permit.
facts.F11: The defendants replied that they were in the process of applying to the relevant authorities to change the permitted use of the premises.
facts.F12: The defendants have not yet secured approval from the Lands Department to change the permitted use.
facts.F13: The evidence of Mr Lau, an Authorized Person and Chartered Building Surveyor, indicates in his analysis that applying for a temporary waiver and change of use is part of the process.

facts.F2: The minor plaintiff was born on the 31st July 1965.
facts.F3: The minor plaintiff joined the defendant company in March 1978 without an identity card and at the age of 12.
facts.F4: The minor plaintiff worked on a copper wire machine and had an accident on the 31st of August 1978, where a piece of copper wire snapped and hit him in his left eye.
facts.F5: The minor plaintiff's left eye is now completely useless and he has impaired vision in his right eye.
facts.F6: The minor plaintiff was in hospital for 7 days and underwent an operation.

facts.F11: The minor plaintiff was not instructed or supervised to clear the reels of copper wire before commencing work.
facts.F12: No protective goggles were provided to the minor plaintiff.
facts.F13: The minor plaintiff's earning capacity had been reduced by 1/3 due to the accident.

facts.F1: Far East PCB Ltd. (FEPCB) and Far East Laminators Ltd. (FEL) were involved in a dispute over an agency agreement.
facts.F2: FEL had collected money from the sales of printed circuit boards (PCBs), but had not accounted for the monies received to FEPCB since June 1994.
facts.F3: The agency agreement was terminated by FEPCB on October 5, 1994.

facts.F5: An escrow account had been set up to hold the disputed monies.
facts.F6: FEL claimed that it had a 10-year license to use the machinery at the Dongguan factory for the manufacture of PCBs.

facts.F8: FEL also claimed that it had paid approximately HK$2 million for the construction of the factory.
facts.F9: The business license of the factory was obtained by Mr. Johnson Yee in his name.
facts.F10: An industrial waste-water license was obtained by Miss Ann Choy.
facts.F11: FEL had paid HK$3 million to FEPCB which it did not dispute.
facts.F12: FEL had been acting as an agent for FEPCB but had failed to account for monies received from customers since June 1994.
facts.F13: FEL owed HK$3 million to FEPCB which it did not dispute.

facts.F1: The plaintiff entered into a contract to buy 146,250 unisex ski turtle neck pullovers together with quota to be manufactured in the People’s Republic of China (‘PRC’) at a price of US$301,396.88 CIF Hamburg.
facts.F2: The garments were to be delivered by the defendant to the plaintiff at the end of July 1986.
facts.F3: The plaintiff in turn was under contract to resell the pullovers, at a profit, to Wachsmuth & Krogmann, a wholesaler carrying on business in West Germany.
facts.F4: The defendant, in order to supply the garments to the plaintiff, entered into a contract with the Guangdong Branch of China National Textiles Import & Export Corporation (‘Chinatex’) for the garments to be manufactured in the PRC.

facts.F6: The export of garments manufactured in the PRC to West Germany is governed by an agreement between the PRC and the European Economic Community (‘EEC’) approved by the latter on 8th April 1986.
facts.F7: The plaintiff and the defendant had difficulties in resolving the category problem, with the PRC classifying the garments as Category 83 and West Germany classifying them as Category 5, while the contract specified Category 4.
facts.F8: The PRC refused to grant a Category 4 quota, making it impossible for the defendant to perform the contract.
facts.F9: The plaintiff refused to furnish an amended letter of credit within a reasonable time.

claim: Claims damages for injuries sustained in a road accident
requested_remedy: Claims damages for injuries sustained in a road accident
parties: Plaintiff: No explicit mention of the plaintiff's name
Defendant: No explicit mention of the defendant's name

facts.F1: The accident occurred on 30th March 1978 at Shing Mun Road in Tsuen Wan.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was struck by the near-side of a lorry driven by the defendant while walking close to the kerb.
facts.F3: The plaintiff sustained injuries which led to the amputation of his right leg and was confined in hospital and rehabilitation centre for a considerable period.
facts.F4: The defendant was unaware of the accident until he was stopped by a private car a few bends further down the Shing Mun Road.
facts.F5: The plaintiff's evidence varied between different courts, stating he took 'about 2 paces' and 'about 10 paces' before being struck by the lorry.
facts.F6: The eye-witness, Madam Kwan, described a man being hooked by a lorry from behind but could not specify which part of the lorry did the damage.
facts.F7: The road was straight with no traffic and few pedestrians at the time of the accident.
facts.F8: The defendant was driving slowly with a clear unobstructed front view and no distractions.
facts.F9: The plaintiff was fitted with a prosthesis but had a non-functional stump and 40% loss of functions.
facts.F10: The plaintiff was unable to drive and had sold his second-hand lorry purchased prior to the accident.
facts.F11: The plaintiff had a daily taking of $100 in 1978 but by the date of trial it was $120.
facts.F12: The plaintiff stayed in hospital for two months and nine months in the Centre and then joined a Training Institution for electronic products.
facts.F13: The plaintiff stepped down onto the road to make a detour around the obstruction caused by the parked vehicle.
facts.F14: The plaintiff was struck by the nearside slight protrusion of the defendant's lorry while on the road.

facts.F1: Madam Ho See Fung, deceased, who passed away in Hong Kong on 27 February 2011, was married to Wong Chun Kai in the Mainland China.

facts.F5: The Deceased executed a Tenancy Agreement in respect of Shop 7C in favour of Wai Wa for a term of 20 years at the rent of HK$1,000 per month on 25 December 2010.
facts.F6: The Tenancy Agreement stated the allegation regarding Ming Yau's aforesaid false representation and stated her wish that Shop 7C should be equally shared by her children.
facts.F7: Ming Yau claims that he paid the purchase price of Shop 7C, while the plaintiff claims that the Deceased paid the purchase price of Shop 7C.

facts.F9: The earnings derived from Hawker Stall/Ching Ping Domestic Goods belonged to the Deceased.

claim: The Plaintiffs contend that the Defendants have no 'sole and exclusive right and privilege to hold, use, occupy and enjoy' the space in the basement marked on the basement plan in pink which is bordered by the staircase on the east

facts.F1: The Defendants agreed to sell to the Plaintiffs, apartment A on the ground floor of Bisney Villas, together with car park space No. 2 in the basement, part of the basement, part of the yard and the flower bed in the basement by an agreement dated 29th May 1997
facts.F2: The Defendants derive their title from an assignment dated the 20th January 1994 which purports to vest in them the sole and exclusive right and privilege in respect of the space in the basement
facts.F3: The assignment to the Defendants' predecessor in title - Thelma Maria Chan, conveys 'full and exclusive right and privilege' in respect of all that space on the basement
facts.F4: The assignment from the developer, Chinsam Enterprises Limited, as first owner, was dated 12th March 1974
facts.F5: Chinsam Enterprises conveyed to Joseph Kwong, the second owner, apartment “A” on the second floor, with corresponding part of the roof, and car parking space No. 3, and reserved to itself individual five equal sixth parts, with exclusive use of all other apartments, car parking spaces, yard on the ground floor, flower beds on the basement, other portion of the roof, and all other self-contained portions of the said building by an indenture dated 1st February 1974
facts.F6: A plan of the basement was annexed to the indenture, which appears to show car park space 5 (instead of 3) as the designated one, but does show other self-contained portions of the said building including a portion running to the left of the staircase marked “staircase in common use.”
facts.F7: The area described as “space on the basement” is clearly identified in the plan annexed to the assignment to Thelma Maria Chan
facts.F8: The Deed of Mutual Covenant was executed on the same date as the assignment to Mr. Kwong, which purports “to define their respective rights and interest of and in the said premises and the said building.”
facts.F9: Clause 1 of the Deed recites that the parties have the sole and exclusive ownership of the portion of the building, with the appurtenances thereto
facts.F10: Clause 2 deals with common access to and entitlement to use of the common parts - entrance halls, staircases, landings and passages - for the proper use and enjoyment of the portion of which he has exclusive use, occupation and enjoyment
facts.F11: The 'space on the basement' was assigned to Thelma Maria Chan nearly 24 years prior
facts.F12: The first owner, the developer, reserved the specific areas, including 'other self-contained portions', which included the 'space on the basement'
facts.F13: The assignment to Thelma Maria Chan was made almost six weeks after the first assignment, indicating the clear intention of the first owner to reserve the space on the basement to itself and assign it to Thelma Maria Chan

facts.F5: After starting work, the Plaintiff discovered the gun was blocked and squatted down to clear the nozzle with a pin.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff said he did not know why white wash came to be splashed to his eyes, but the likely cause was the white wash being diverted by the pin and his fingers.

facts.F10: The Plaintiff did not turn off the pump before clearing the nozzle.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff knew that it was the practice to wear goggles when painting with white wash, but goggles were not provided by the Defendants.

facts.F1: The wash-basin fell from the 18th floor level of the hoist.
facts.F2: The plaintiff was employed by the 1st defendant, and the 2nd defendant had subcontracted the plumbing work from the 3rd defendant.
facts.F3: The hoist was an open metal frame erected in an angle of Block 1, close to its side and running from the ground floor level to the 18th floor.
facts.F4: The platform was operated by an operator at the ground level, within Block 1, who was not able to see the platform once it got above the 1st floor ground level.
facts.F5: There were sockets at each level into which a push bell button could be plugged, enabling the unloading workers at that level to signal the operator when to go up, down or to stop.
facts.F6: The platform was a bare, unenclosed platform without any boards or fencing on the sides.
facts.F7: On the morning of the accident, the plaintiff and two colleagues were loading sanitary ware onto the hoist platform to send it up to the 18th floor.
facts.F8: After the first load went up, the plaintiff and his colleagues loaded another load while Mr. Yuen, the 1st defendant, was present, and then while the platform was ascending, they began fetching more items of sanitary ware from a nearby stack.
facts.F9: The plaintiff was struck by a wash-basin and was knocked unconscious and taken to Princess Margaret Hospital where he did not regain consciousness for 10 days.
facts.F10: The plaintiff was acting in accordance with the usual practices on the construction site.
facts.F11: The 1st defendant, Mr. Yuen, caused the platform to go up with its load unenclosed and without any fastening or precaution whatsoever against slippage or falling.
