facts.F1: The Plaintiff bought a BMW in 1995 through her then fiancé and now husband, Cheung Wing Chau.
facts.F2: The car overheated in May 1996, and Cheung Wing Chau arranged for the car to be towed to the Defendant's garage in Hung Hom for repairs.
facts.F3: The Defendant was asked to obtain a Certificate of Roadworthiness for the car.
facts.F4: The Defendant initially quoted a price of $20,000.00 for a new cylinder head, but later agreed to replace it with a second-hand part for $5,000.00.
facts.F5: The Defendant obtained a Certificate of Roadworthiness for the car on the second attempt on June 4, 1996.
facts.F6: The Defendant did not give Cheung Wing Chau an invoice or a copy, but informed him of the amount due over the telephone.
facts.F7: Cheung Wing Chau paid the Defendant $10,000.00 and $5,000.00 on account of the repairs, but the car was not returned.
facts.F8: The Plaintiff and Cheung Wing Chau renewed the vehicle licence and insurance for the car in August 1996.
facts.F9: The Defendant claimed that Cheung Wing Chau had agreed to pay $35,000.00 for the repairs and storage, but Cheung Wing Chau denied this.
facts.F10: The police were involved twice, in January 1997 and June 1997, but were unable to resolve the matter.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff issued a writ in July 1997.
facts.F12: The Defendant rented premises at $8,000.00 per month to store the car from November 1997.
facts.F13: The hire purchase agreement for the car was paid off in July 1998, with payments of approximately $126,000.00.
facts.F14: The Plaintiff and Cheung Wing Chau continued to make payments under the hire purchase agreement despite not having possession of the car.
facts.F15: The Defendant was paid $15,000.00 on account of his work but still refused to return the car.

facts.F1: A sale contract was entered into between Swiss and Xiamen C & D (XCD) on 18 July 2008 for the sale of 45,000 WMTs (+/-10%) of iron ore fines at US$183 per DMT (Dry Metric Ton) CFR FO.
facts.F2: The payment was to be made by irrevocable letter of credit (payable at sight) issued by a Mainland or Hong Kong bank.
facts.F3: The letter of credit was issued by the Bank's Xiamen Branch on 22 July 2008 for US$8,235,000 in favour of Swiss as beneficiary.
facts.F4: Swiss caused a cargo of 44,500 WMTs iron ore fines to be loaded on board a vessel in India and then shipped to the Mainland between 19 and 23 July 2008.
facts.F5: The cargo arrived in Fangcheng on 2 August and was discharged on 3 August 2008.
facts.F6: On 30 July 2008 Swiss presented documents to Bangkok Bank to obtain payment under the letter of credit.
facts.F7: On 4 August 2008 Bangkok Bank posted the documents to the Bank, which received them on 6 August 2008.
facts.F8: On 11 August 2008, the Bank issued SWIFT message MT752 to Bangkok Bank, stating that it would reimburse at sight basis for credit terms.
facts.F9: On 12 August 2008, the Bank countermanded MT752 by a SWIFT message MT799.
facts.F10: On 13 August 2008, the Bank identified 4 discrepancies in the presented documents by a SWIFT message MT734.
facts.F11: The discrepancies included: (1) Short drawn, (2) Partial shipment, (3) Total cargo value of the bills is less than the tolerance amount of the L/C, and (4) Total cargo value of the bills before price adjustment, bonus, and penalty is less than the tolerance amount of the L/C.
facts.F12: On 14 August 2008, Bangkok Bank on Swiss' behalf objected to the Bank's refusal to pay.
facts.F13: Negotiations took place between Swiss and XCD, and on 22 September 2008, Swiss agreed to reduce the price of the cargo from US$183 per DMT to US$128 per DMT CFR FO.
facts.F14: The value of the cargo shipped dropped to US$5,122,240, and an addendum to the Sale Contract was executed to record this price reduction.
facts.F15: On 25 September 2008, the Bank paid US$5,122,240 to Swiss.
facts.F16: The Bank had five days to decide whether the presentation was compliant under UCP 600.
facts.F17: The Bank issued a SWIFT message MT752 representing its intention to honour the presentation on 11 August 2008.

claim: Exemption from rating under the exempting provisions of sub-section (1) of section 36 of the Rating Ordinance
requested_remedy: Exemption from rating under the exempting provisions of sub-section (1) of section 36 of the Rating Ordinance

facts.F1: The appellant, SHAM KA KEI, occupies a tenement used for breeding goldfish for display purposes.
facts.F2: The appellant relies on the exempting provisions of sub-section (1) of section 36 of the Rating Ordinance, specifically paragraph (a) relating to agricultural land, and the definition of 'agricultural land' contained in sub-section (4).
facts.F3: Sub-section (4) of section 36 defines 'agricultural land' as land used as farm land, a fish pond, a market garden, an orchard or for animal husbandry.
facts.F4: The respondent, COMMISSIONER OF RATING & VALUATION, submits that the intention of the legislature was to exempt only fish ponds for breeding fresh water fish for human consumption, as they existed in Hong Kong in 1973.
facts.F5: The respondent refers to 'Hong Kong 1973, Report for the year 1972', chapter 5, which mentions fish ponds for breeding fresh-and brackish water fish farming, but does not mention goldfish.
facts.F6: The respondent submits that the absence of any reference to goldfish in the report supports their interpretation.
facts.F7: The appellant's goldfish are bred for display purposes, not for human consumption.
facts.F8: Historically, fish ponds in Hong Kong were used for breeding fresh water fish for human consumption, but are now increasingly used for breeding goldfish and other tropical fish.
facts.F9: The appellant's 'ponds' are in fact tanks, according to the respondent.
facts.F10: According to the case Cresswell (Valuation Officer) v. BOC, Ltd., the ordinary meaning of the expression 'fish pond' in an agricultural context should be considered.
facts.F11: The legislature would have specifically mentioned fish if they had intended to include it under 'animal husbandry'.

claim: The plaintiff claimed that the agreement had been validly terminated by the plaintiff, and sought the return of the deposits, or declarations that would entitle them to this.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed that the agreement had been validly terminated by the plaintiff, and sought the return of the deposits, or declarations that would entitle them to this.
parties: Defendant: LEE HOI WING & LI TUNG PING THE MANAGERS OF LI TAK WO TSO

facts.F1: In early 1998, the defendants, Mr. Lee Hoi-wing and Mr. Li Tung-ping, were negotiating to sell a large plot of land in the New Territories to Winghing Investments Limited.
facts.F2: The property was not owned by either Mr. Lee or Mr. Li, but by two Tsos, the Li Tak Kau Tso and the Li Tak Wo Tso.
facts.F3: The managers of the Tsos had passed away in the early 1940s, and Mr. Lee and Mr. Li were not in a position to sell the property.
facts.F4: Sales of land owned by a Tso required the consent of the government acting through the relevant District Office.
facts.F5: Winghing was also involved in negotiations for the purchase of three other properties from other vendors in the same area.
facts.F6: Mr. Lee informed Winghing that it would take around three to five years to obtain the necessary agreements from the members of the Tsos and the consent of the District Office.
facts.F7: The agreement for sale and purchase was signed on 15 June 1998, with a completion date dependent on the receipt of the District Office’s consent.
facts.F8: Winghing paid a further deposit of HK$744,192.80, taking the total deposit to 10% of the purchase price.
facts.F9: After the agreement was signed, Mr. Lee and Mr. Li obtained the necessary agreements from the members of the Tsos and lodged the applications with the Northern District Office.
facts.F10: The District Office’s consent was eventually obtained on 27 October 1999, and the defendants called on Winghing to complete the sale and purchase within 14 days.
facts.F11: Winghing failed to complete the sale and purchase and commenced proceedings against Mr. Lee and Mr. Li, claiming that the agreement had been validly terminated.
facts.F12: Winghing was aware of the formalities that needed to be completed before completion could take place, including the consent of the District Office.
facts.F13: Winghing had been offered the opportunity to include a cut-off date or long-stop date in the agreement to protect its position in the event of delays.

Defendant: ['Man King Wah Josh trading as Shun Tim Meat Company (1st Respondent)', 'Zurich Insurance Company Limited (2nd Respondent)']

facts.F1: The deceased employee Wu Chuqing died on 28 September 2015 due to complications and multiple organ failure caused by streptococcus suis infection.
facts.F2: The deceased cut his left forearm while cutting a pig's trotter at work on 30 August 2014 and sought treatment at the Accident & Emergency Department of the Caritas Medical Centre.
facts.F3: A year later, the deceased was admitted to the Department of Medicine at the Yan Chai Hospital for fever and progressive dyspnoea for 2 weeks and was diagnosed with infective endocarditis.
facts.F4: The original Application was made on 27 July 2016, which was within the statutory 24th month period for making such application.
facts.F5: The applicant received advice from experts that the cause of death was the result of swine flu, which was an occupational disease, and not the accident that happened in August 2014.
facts.F6: The applicant applied to the Director of Legal Aid (DLA) to seek counsel's opinion, and the DLA did not give approval until 5 July 2018.
facts.F7: Counsel advised the applicant to re-amend the Amended Application to plead that the deceased died from an occupational disease.
facts.F8: Solicitors for the applicant wrote to the respondents for agreement to re-amend the Amended Application, but it was not until 2 November 2018 that Solicitors for the respondents indicated that the proposed re-amendment would be objected to.
facts.F9: The applicant's solicitors issued the present Summons for Re-amendment on 22 November 2018.

claim: The applicant applies under sections 111 and 122 of the Companies Ordinance, Cap 32 (“the Ordinance”) for extension of time to hold its AGM and lay its accounts before its shareholders at the AGM.
requested_remedy: The applicant applies under sections 111 and 122 of the Companies Ordinance, Cap 32 (“the Ordinance”) for extension of time to hold its AGM and lay its accounts before its shareholders at the AGM.

facts.F1: The applicant is a public company admitted to the Alternative Investment Market (“AIM”) of the London Stock Exchange (“LSE”) and is thus subject to the AIM Rules.
facts.F2: The applicant has obtained a prior order from Mr Justice To on 6 January 2012 to hold its 4th AGM on 20 January 2012 out of time.
facts.F3: The financial year end of the applicant is 30 June.
facts.F4: Pursuant to sections 111 and 122(1A) of the Ordinance, Article 155(C) of the applicant’s Articles of Association and Rule 19 of the AIM Rules, the applicant must hold its 5th AGM on or before 30 December 2012; and the AGM notice and the AGM notice and the profit and loss accounts (“the annual report”) must be issued to its shareholders within 21 days, ie on or before 9 December 2012.
facts.F5: The annual report was signed by the board of directors and sent to each of the shareholders on 2 January 2013 and uploaded to the applicant’s website.
facts.F6: The applicant and its former auditors had a dispute over audit fees and the scope of the engagement for the 2011 audit.
facts.F7: The new auditors were appointed on 5 October 2012, ie 3 months after the end of the financial year.
facts.F8: The former auditors had withheld material documents and so transition to the new auditors was impeded. It also took time for the new auditors to settle in and prepare the audited accounts.
facts.F9: The applicant’s Finance Manager deposed to the fact that the board recognized the importance of strong corporate governance, underwent a re-organization and made some key appointments, which included experienced accountants in the senior management.
facts.F10: It is the 2nd application of its kind made by the applicant.
facts.F11: The shareholders were aware of the financial position of the company in question and thus were not prejudiced by the non-compliance.
facts.F12: The delay was not deliberate.

claim: The Applicant claimed that he suffered personal injury by accident on the 30 May 2003, arising out of and in the course of employment, due to a near-accident with an old person pushing a wooden cart near Central Market.
requested_remedy: The Applicant claimed that he suffered personal injury by accident on the 30 May 2003, arising out of and in the course of employment, due to a near-accident with an old person pushing a wooden cart near Central Market.

facts.F1: The Applicant was a tram driver.
facts.F2: On 30 May 2003, the Applicant was driving tram TRM137 along Des Voeux Road Central westbound.
facts.F3: Near Central Market, an old person pushing a wooden cart emerged from the back of an eastbound tram next to TRM137.
facts.F4: The Applicant claimed to have immediately applied the brake to halt the tram to prevent it from hitting the old person, resulting in a sprained right wrist, ankle and neck.
facts.F5: The Applicant continued driving the tram but eventually stopped at Kennedy Town Terminal, where he took analgesic and continued to work.
facts.F6: When the tram arrived at North Point Tram Terminal in the afternoon, the supervisor instructed the Applicant to drive the tram back to Whitty Street Depot and to write and submit a report.
facts.F7: The Applicant submitted a report and waited for further instructions, during which time he felt pain and discomfort and requested an ambulance to take him to hospital.
facts.F8: The Respondent denied that the Applicant suffered an accident on the day and in the manner alleged, and put the Applicant to strict proof.
facts.F9: Chan Shih Yao, the Respondent's manager, gave evidence that he saw the Applicant using the DVD braking system before the Central Market stop, which is against normal operating procedures.
facts.F10: The Applicant may have made up the accident to account for his having used the DVD braking system and to avoid the consequences of doing so.
facts.F11: The Applicant used the DVD braking system before the Central Market stop.

claim: claims against the Defendants sea carriers for the misdelivery of 5 shipments of goods under 5 different sets of Bills of Lading
requested_remedy: claims against the Defendants sea carriers for the misdelivery of 5 shipments of goods under 5 different sets of Bills of Lading
parties: Plaintiff: The Owners of Cargo Lately Laden on Board the Ship or Vessel ‘BRIJ’, The Owners of Cargo Lately Laden on Board the Ship or Vessel ‘MURTER’, The Owners of Cargo Lately Laden on Board the Ship or Vessel ‘AL SALIMIAH’ (ALL collectively referred to as Glory Products Co. Ltd.)

Defendant: The Owners and/or Demise Charterers of the Ship or Vessel ‘BRIJ’, The Owners and/or Demise Charterers of the Ship or Vessel ‘MURTER’, The Owners and/or Demise Charterers of the Ship or Vessel ‘AL SALIMIAH’ (ALL collectively referred to as Defendants)

facts.F1: The Plaintiff, Glory Products Co. Ltd., was a seller and exporter of garments in Hong Kong for export to South America.
facts.F2: The garments were made in China, put into containers, and then shipped from Chinese ports to Hong Kong where they were transshipped on vessels operated by CAVN (but owned by the Defendants) for carriage from Hong Kong to Venezuela.
facts.F3: The goods in question were sold to buyer, Acetex International SA (Buyer) who operated in the Venezuela ports by its agent Francisco Amaya (Amaya) and its customs agent Oran (Oran).
facts.F4: The Plaintiff effected its shipment of the goods from China to Venezuela by going to a freight forwarder, Wing Tung Wei (China) Ltd. (WTW) which also operated its shipping side under the name of Talent Express Line (Talent).
facts.F5: WTW issued to the Plaintiff, Talent bills of lading, such as the Talent Bills in this case, which were then used by the Plaintiff as documents of title through the bank to obtain payment from the Buyer under the appropriate letters of credit.
facts.F6: Unknown to the Plaintiff, by arrangement between WTW and Hong Kong Maritime Co. Ltd., the Hong Kong agent of CAVN, CAVN issued to WTW as shipper, bills of lading of CAVN evidencing the shipment of the goods to Venezuela corresponding in most particulars to the shipment under the Talent Bills.
facts.F7: The goods arrived in Venezuela and were required under Venezuelan law to be handed to the Venezuelan Customs.
facts.F8: The goods were stored in warehouses controlled by the Venezuelan Customs and were then released by the Venezuelan Customs to Oran, who was acting as customs agent on behalf of Amaya, the Consignee under the CAVN Bills.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff started to make inquiries about the goods long after the delivery of the goods by the Venezuelan Customs to Amaya.
facts.F10: The existence of the CAVN Bills was discovered, and eventually, these proceedings were instituted against the Defendants.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff was not named as Shipper in the CAVN Bills.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff did not know about the existence of the CAVN Bills.
facts.F13: The CAVN Bills were delivered to Amaya in accordance with the contract and not in breach of it.

facts.F1: The writ of summons was issued against the defendant on 7 October 2021, and it was served on the defendant on 11 October 2021.

facts.F4: The defendant had parked 9 private vehicles at the Car Park since 24 June 2020 and had not paid parking charges totaling $355,572 up to 30 September 2021.
facts.F5: The plaintiff had sent numerous letters to the defendant demanding payment of parking charges, including two letters dated 7 December 2020 and 17 December 2020.
facts.F6: The plaintiff gave written notice to the defendant on 28 September 2021 about its intention to sell the Private Vehicles upon expiry of 7 days should the defendant not remove them from the Car Park by paying off the arrears of parking charges.
facts.F7: The defendant failed and/or refused to remove the Private Vehicles and to repay the said arrears despite the expiry of the written notice.
facts.F8: The plaintiff operated and operates a carpark located at lower basement floor to fifth floor of a building in Aberdeen (the Car Park), and the defendant is the registered owner of the 9 private vehicles (the Private Vehicles).

facts.F10: A declaration was sought by the plaintiff that property of the 9 private vehicles had passed from the defendant to the plaintiff pursuant to clause 7 of the Conditions of Parking.
facts.F11: The plaintiff sought authority to impound and to tow the Private Vehicles away from the Car Park, as well as to sell all the said Private Vehicles.
facts.F12: The defendant was absent and did not provide a defense.

claim: The plaintiff claims the equivalent of a sum of £1,000 which was admittedly paid by him to the defendant.
requested_remedy: The plaintiff claims the equivalent of a sum of £1,000 which was admittedly paid by him to the defendant.

facts.F1: The plaintiff and defendant were formerly patient and herbalist and became friends and later became partners in a medicine business.
facts.F2: In January 1966 the plaintiff sent to the defendant a draft for st. £1,000.
facts.F3: Issue has been joined as to the purpose for which the payment was made.
facts.F4: The parties first became acquainted in 1960 when the plaintiff was on a visit to Hong Kong.
facts.F5: The plaintiff was working as a farmer in New Zealand and he saved a substantial sum of money.
facts.F6: The plaintiff and defendant had a discussion about going into partnership for the marketing of medicine.
facts.F7: The dispute between the parties centers on the purpose for which the £1,000 was sent to the defendant.
facts.F8: The plaintiff's version of events is that the £1,000 was sent to the defendant for safe custody pending the plaintiff's return to Hong Kong from New Zealand.
facts.F9: The defendant's version of events is that the £1,000 was sent as a contribution to the partnership funds.
facts.F10: There were transactions between the parties related to two flats.
facts.F11: The plaintiff says that he himself paid $19,775 in respect of one flat (No.23) and $16,775 in respect of the other flat (No.25).
facts.F12: The defendant says that the payment of $16,775 in respect of No.25 was made from the £1,000 sent by the plaintiff.
facts.F13: The plaintiff says that he gave the defendant £1,000 to be used for the purchase of flat No.23.
facts.F14: The defendant used part of the £1,000 to pay for flat No.25 and kept the balance as part of the partnership funds.
facts.F15: There was correspondence between the parties regarding the payment and the use of the £1,000.
